name: Butter
names: ထောပတ် htaw pat

entries.heading: Butter (Afghan sheep/goat butter; yak butter in the highlands)
entries.what: a common product, churned from yogurt or doogh; used in chicken dishes and in the butter tea of the highlands.

entries.heading: Gjalpë (butter)
entries.what: butter eaten with bread at breakfast, used for frying rice (kabuni) and in pastries such as papare and kungullur (pumpkin pastry)

entries.heading: Karag (կարագ; butter)
entries.what: Traditional butter churned from matsun, plus butter used in cooking and as a flavouring. Armenian Wikipedia's article on butter is a general article.

entries.heading: Manteiga (butter, industrial)
entries.what: butter made by local dairy firms; named producers are Lactiangol and Aldeia Nova.

entries.heading: Butter (manteca)
entries.what: the fat of cream, churned and kneaded. Part of the classic breakfast of bread with butter and jam; medialunas "de manteca" are common, and Buenos Aires mainly orders "de grasa" or "de manteca", while Mar del Plata uses "dulces" or "saladas"

entries.heading: Butter
entries.what: butter in Austrian cooking, including alpine pastures, where butter and cheese are made on the Almen (Sennereien)

entries.heading: Butter (industrial)
entries.what: Butter produced in the national dairy industry. Australians consume roughly 3.8 kg per person a year (Wikipedia figure).

entries.heading: Kərə yağı (butter)
entries.what: butter made by churning fresh or fermented ayran or cream. Hand-made butter, sea-salt butter and butter with sugar are shown on the article.

entries.heading: Mlado maslo / maslo (butter; puter, maslac, posvojenica)
entries.what: Fresh churned butter is called "mlado maslo" in Bosnia and Herzegovina. "Maslo" refers to the clarified, melted-and-set form, a granular, anhydrous milk fat with a strong flavour, stored cool and dark (traditionally in a cellar).

entries.heading: Butter (home-churned, historical)
entries.what: A participant in a Barbados qualitative study recalled that people once churned their own butter at home.

entries.heading: Makhan / butter (মাখন)
entries.what: butter made by churning cream; the Banglapedia entry says it is used fresh or after ripening (going sour); average composition 82% fat, 0.4% protein, 15% water, 2% salt, plus vitamins A and D.

entries.heading: Butter (solid or liquid)
entries.what: Butter listed as one of the best-known dairy products of Burkina Faso, sold in solid and liquid forms.

entries.heading: Amavuta (Kirundi; butter)
entries.what: a household-made Burundian milk product named in the review abstract as one of the milk products.

entries.heading: Butter (in a Christmas cassava pie)
entries.what: Butter is one of the ingredients of Christmas cassava pie, a traditional holiday dish made with grated cassava, eggs, salt and sugar.

entries.heading: Butter (served with boiled salted codfish and potatoes)
entries.what: Boiled salted codfish and potatoes served with a hard-boiled egg and butter, or with an olive oil sauce.

entries.heading: Mantequilla (butter, eaten at breakfast)
entries.what: Butter is a common breakfast spread with bread, especially the marraqueta roll, often with jam.

entries.heading: Manteiga (industrial butter)
entries.what: Water-in-fat emulsion of about 83% fat, made from cream by churning. Types: acidic (traditional) and sweet butter; salted or unsalted.

entries.heading: Mar (butter)
entries.what: The main household and cooperative dairy product in Bhutan. 1,727.46 MT of butter was processed nationally in 2023 (NSB figures cited by Rai et al. 2025).

entries.heading: Butter (johnny cakes and table use)
entries.what: butter spread on johnny cakes, a Kriol breakfast food

entries.heading: Butter
entries.what: named by Dairy Farmers of Canada as a dairy category; the 2021 "Buttergate" controversy concerned butter texture.

entries.heading: Nebam (butter, lumps or clarified)
entries.what: Butter, either in lumps (en motte) or clarified; the Fula article mentions Fulani calabashes used for butter and milk storage.

entries.heading: Butter (Anken, Anke; Swiss grades)
entries.what: Swiss butter; the dialect name is Anken or Anke. Swiss rules define four grades: Vorzugsbutter (at least 82% fat, fresh cream, sold unstored), Kochbutter (frozen Vorzugsbutter, stored up to nine months), Käsereibutter, and Bratbutter (clari

entries.heading: Butter (mantequilla)
entries.what: Butter used in Colombian breads and pan de queso and bollos; produced on farms in Boyacá.

entries.heading: Mantequilla (butter)
entries.what: Butter is in high demand and is also an ingredient in natilla and some Costa Rican cooking.

entries.heading: Butter (manteiga; eaten at breakfast)
entries.what: Butter is eaten with the Cape Verdean sweet bean-flour cake (couscous-style) at breakfast, and sometimes drunk with coffee.

entries.heading: Butter (served with baked potatoes)
entries.what: Butter served as an accompaniment to foil-wrapped potatoes baked in charcoal.

entries.heading: Máslo (butter)
entries.what: Butter, roughly 80% milk fat; salt often added.

entries.heading: Butter (Süßrahmbutter, Sauerrahmbutter, Mildgesäuerte, Salzbutter, Kräuterbutter, Landbutter, Maibutter, Halligbutter)
entries.what: churned milk fat. Butter must have at least 80% milk fat (max 16% water, 2% non-fat milk solids). Reduced-fat versions are labelled Dreiviertelfettbutter (about 60–62%) or Halbfettbutter (about 39–41%).

entries.heading: Smør (butter)
entries.what: Danish butter, with a deep export history; Denmark was the world's largest butter exporter around 1900. Commercial butter about 80% fat, 15% water; traditional butter as low as 65% fat, about 30% water. Max 1.2% added salt in Denmark.

entries.heading: Või (butter)
entries.what: the butter family, including natural, flavoured and reconstituted types

entries.heading: Butter (zibda — local name not confirmed in sources)
entries.what: Butter used in Egyptian cooking; part of urban elite cooking historically.

entries.heading: Butter (trade and home use, Tigre pastoralists)
entries.what: Butter traded by Tigre-speaking pastoralists in the Eritrean lowlands and highlands.

entries.heading: Mantequilla (mantequilla; butter; Asturian artisanal butter)
entries.what: Butter made by churning cream, which separates the fat from buttermilk.

entries.heading: Voi (butter), including kirnuvoi (churned cultured butter)
entries.what: Most Finnish butter is now churned from unfermented cream (imelävoi, sweet-cream butter). Manufacturers add an aroma distillate from bacterially fermented whey, which gives hapatettu tykkivoi. Traditional kirnuvoi was churned from soured cr

entries.heading: Butter (table butter)
entries.what: churned cream or milk fat, eaten as a spread and used in cooking.

entries.heading: Smør (butter)
entries.what: Butter, used at meals and in baking. It appears in the Faroese breakfast and lunch examples in the iodine study. Nutrition per 100 g on MBM's page: about 81 g fat.

entries.heading: Beurre (beurre doux et beurre demi-sel)
entries.what: Butter made by churning cream; French fat rules: at least 82% fat for sweet butter, 80% for salted (demi-sel).

entries.heading: Butter (კარაქი)
entries.what: water-in-fat emulsion from milk cream; 60–80% fat; about 20–25 L milk per kg (historically a symbol of prosperity).

entries.heading: Norse-era butter (butter)
entries.what: Butter listed among the dairy foods of Norse farmers in Greenland.

entries.heading: Butter (mantequilla; used as a cooking fat)
entries.what: Butter used to coat baked bananas in the dessert/breakfast dish akwadu.

entries.heading: Butter (voútyro)
entries.what: butter served at the traditional Greek breakfast with bread, honey and jam.

entries.heading: Butter (Fulakunda)
entries.what: Butter prepared by Fulakunda women from cattle milk.

entries.heading: Butter (牛油)
entries.what: Butter spread on bread and served with buns and set meals in cha chaan teng.

entries.heading: Mantequilla (butter)
entries.what: butter, named as a local product, and used to dress boiled corn (elotes cocidos).

entries.heading: Maslac (butter)
entries.what: Butter made by churning sweet or sour cream. Industrial butter may contain up to 2% salt and may be coloured with natural colouring.

entries.heading: Maslo (clarified butter)
entries.what: Butter cooked gently until the water and milk solids separate out.

entries.heading: Vaj (butter)
entries.what: Butter from milk fat; Hungarian classes include teavaj (80% fat), szendvicsvaj (70%), and vajkrém (spread, ~40%).

entries.heading: Mentega (butter)
entries.what: Butter, the dairy product made by churning cream; spread on bread and biscuits, used in cooking and frying.

entries.heading: Butter (full cream butter, made from cream)
entries.what: Butter sold by the Isle of Man Creamery. Dairy butter is made with Isle of Man Salt Company products, according to the trade report.

entries.heading: Smjör (butter; including sheep's-milk butter)
entries.what: Butter, historically made from soured cream and kept unsalted. It was once a form of currency: rents for land and livestock were paid in butter.

entries.heading: Butter (زبدة)
entries.what: butter used extensively; in the Levant mainly for desserts; churned from yoghurt in traditional goatskin churns (see jameed)

entries.heading: Butter (バター, batā) and fermented butter (発酵バター)
entries.what: Butter made from cream: fat globules are churned until they clump, then worked and pressed; most Japanese butter is non-fermented. Fermented butter is churned from cream fermented with lactic bacteria; it is growing in Japan. Home salted bu

entries.heading: Sary may (сары май)
entries.what: Clarified butter, used like butter for dipping bread. Listed among Kyrgyz traditional foods.

entries.heading: Butter (май)
entries.what: Butter eaten with bread, often with jam or kaymak.

entries.heading: Butter (fresh)
entries.what: Butter made on farms and sold alongside fresh milk and cream. Butter and margarine are the preferred cooking fats in modern Cambodian cooking.

entries.heading: 버터 (butter)
entries.what: Butter sold industrially in Korea. Old Korean name 수유 (酥油), also 빠다 in North Korean usage. The 서울우유 product list includes butter.

entries.heading: Butter (zibda; used in sweets)
entries.what: Butter used in Kuwaiti sweets, such as asida and ghraiba cookies.

entries.heading: Sary may (сары май; butter)
entries.what: Kazakh butter, made from old milk and often stored in a leather bag.

entries.heading: Sviestas (butter)
entries.what: a fat emulsion of at least 80% milk fat, with a sour taste and a smooth spreadable texture, pale yellow in colour.

entries.heading: Butter (Botter; Bauerebotter, Molkereisbotter, pasteurised, demi-sel, concentrated)
entries.what: Butter made from milk fat and water (water content max 16%). Types: farm butter (Bauerebotter), dairy butter (Molkereisbotter), pasteurised butter, lightly salted demi-sel (2–5% salt), and concentrated butter (up to 99% fat). Buttermilk is

entries.heading: Sviests (butter)
entries.what: Butter, a standard dairy product in Latvian cooking.

entries.heading: Butter (as a topping and in Libyan dishes)
entries.what: butter used as a topping on dishes; melted butter poured around asida.

entries.heading: Butter (general cooking fat)
entries.what: Traditionally used as a cooking fat alongside animal fat before olive oil began to replace it.

entries.heading: Butter (beurre; eaten as a table spread)
entries.what: Butter is listed among Monégasque cuisine's common staples, served alongside honey and jam at the table.

entries.heading: Butter (unt)
entries.what: fat from cream churned until it separates from the buttermilk; often salted; coloured yellow with annatto or carotene in commercial versions.

entries.heading: Butter (maslac; масло; путер)
entries.what: butter from sweet or sour cream, a fat product also used in Montenegrin dishes; English Wikipedia lists butter under Montenegrin dairy and notes cicvara uses butter.

entries.heading: Butter (eaten with bread)
entries.what: butter eaten on bread, mentioned alongside cheese in the Malian cuisine article.

entries.heading: Butter (ထောပတ် htaw pat)
entries.what: butter from milk fat; Myanmar terms include sweet (unsalted) butter and buttermilk (ထောပတ်ရည်).

entries.heading: Butter (beurre) served with dried dates
entries.what: Butter served as a dip for dried dates in Mauritanian typical dishes.

entries.heading: Butter (beurre)
entries.what: butter is a dairy product in the Niger household milk survey; wassalé, a semolina dish, is made grilled with butter or oil.

entries.heading: Roomboter (butter)
entries.what: Churned cream; in the Netherlands the name boter is legally protected and requires at least 80% milk fat, so margarine cannot be called boter.

entries.heading: Smør (butter)
entries.what: butter from cream, which was first a way to preserve milk. In Norwegian tradition the cream is usually soured before churning. Its colour depends on the feed: summer grazing gives a natural yellow, winter dry feed gives a pale butter; old p

entries.heading: Butter (नौनी; nauni, makhan)
entries.what: Butter, the fat skimmed from churned dahi (and the source for ghee). Known as नौनी in Nepali.

entries.heading: Butter
entries.what: Churned milk fat, sold as a table butter (Anchor, Westgold) and used as an ingredient.

entries.heading: Butter (as a garnish on harees)
entries.what: Butter poured over harees, an alternative to ghee or added on top.

entries.heading: Mantequilla (butter, used as flavouring in bollo)
entries.what: Butter used as a flavouring and as a filling option for corn-dough bollos (such as bollo preñado).

entries.heading: Mantequilla (butter)
entries.what: Butter from pasteurised cream; in Peru it is sold as butter with a legal definition (INACAL NTP 202.024.2021): a fat product derived only from milk, a water-in-oil emulsion, for cooking, baking and spreading. Industrial versions can be fort

entries.heading: Butter (Magnolia Inc.; butter and margarine)
entries.what: Butter made by Magnolia, a Philippine dairy company, which the company's Wikipedia page describes as manufacturing "butter, margarine and processed cheese" and, at its Aurora Boulevard plant, "ice cream, milk, butter, margarine and processe

entries.heading: Makhan (white butter; makhan = butter)
entries.what: Butter. The Sindhi cuisine article uses "makhan (butter)" for the butter eaten with Sindhi busri bread and chulho; Punjabi farmers ate parathas with freshly churned butter and buttermilk.

entries.heading: Masło (butter)
entries.what: Butter made from pasteurised cream. Grades: ekstra, delikatesowe, wyborowe, stołowe, śmietankowe.

entries.heading: Mantequilla (butter)
entries.what: Butter, named among the local dairy products.

entries.heading: Butter (home-made, traditional)
entries.what: butter made at home in traditional Palestinian households; the clarified form is samneh (see entry above).

entries.heading: Manteiga (butter)
entries.what: Butter eaten with bread at breakfast in Portugal. Lactogal makes butter under the Primor brand.

entries.heading: Butter (زبدة; zubda)
entries.what: Fat churned from cream or soured milk. Used in Qatari sweets and savoury dishes.

entries.heading: Unt (butter)
entries.what: A milk-fat product made by churning smântână (sour cream).

entries.heading: Butter (maslac; puter)
entries.what: butter served with bread at breakfast in Serbia; mentioned in a historical account of Serbian food.

entries.heading: Sliv. maslo (сливочное масло, butter)
entries.what: Russian butter, with GOST grades by fat (traditional 82.5%, amateur 80%, peasant 72.5%, sandwich 61%, tea 50%); Vologda butter is a regional fresh-cream variant.

entries.heading: Butter (cow butter, amavuta y'inka)
entries.what: butter made from cow milk, listed as a Rwandan milk-derived product.

entries.heading: Butter (زبدة; zubda)
entries.what: Butter used in Saudi sweets and breakfast dishes, with dates and bread.

entries.heading: Ma'soub (butter, bread and banana breakfast)
entries.what: A breakfast dish from Mecca and Jazan; bread, butter, bananas and honey are mashed together, served with cream or cheese.

entries.heading: Zibda (butter) (الزبدة; butter)
entries.what: butter, named in the dairy list of the Arabic Wikipedia Sudanese cuisine article.

entries.heading: Smör (butter)
entries.what: Swedish butter, a dairy fat made by churning cream; classed as salted, unsalted or clarified. Historically a cash item and tax payment; margarine has taken market share since the late 1800s.

entries.heading: Maslo (butter)
entries.what: Fat made by churning cream, mostly milk fat.

entries.heading: Maslo (butter)
entries.what: Butter is a common fat in Slovak cooking; animal fats and butter were used instead of cooking oils.

entries.heading: Butter (local name not found)
entries.what: Butter used in Somali porridge and dishes.

entries.heading: Mantequilla (butter)
entries.what: A yellowish dairy fat eaten on bread or used in cooking; shrimp are sometimes cooked in it.

entries.heading: Butter (zibdeh)
entries.what: Butter used in baking and sweets, and as a major fat in traditional sweets.

entries.heading: Butter (butter; local name not found)
entries.what: butter named in Eswatini Dairy Board farmer training.

entries.heading: Gibde (gibdé; butter; fursa in Sudan)
entries.what: The butter separated when soured milk is churned in the rouaba process; the buttermilk is then drunk.

entries.heading: Butter (เนย)
entries.what: fat from churned cream or milk. The Thai word เนย is derived from Tamil nei, per the Thai ghee article.

entries.heading: Butter (roghan; Tajik равған)
entries.what: butter used in breakfast with non (bread) and in fatir ravghani, a flaky flatbread made with butter or lard.

entries.heading: Tereyağı (butter, general)
entries.what: Turkish butter, used in cooking and at breakfast.

entries.heading: Butter (all kinds)
entries.what: butter, eaten on bread and with starchy foods; also listed as a fat.

entries.heading: Butter (sweet-cream and US "European-style" cultured)
entries.what: Fat churned from cream; sweet-cream butter dominates the US, cultured butter is marketed as "European-style".

entries.heading: Bơ (butter)
entries.what: Butter introduced under French influence; used in French-Vietnamese fusion cooking and bread.

entries.heading: Butter (imported)
entries.what: Butter, appearing in a food-category list used in the trade analysis of Vanuatu imports.

entries.heading: Butter (churned in a gourd)
entries.what: butter made by shaking milk in a gourd shell container. The wild-plant paper says the dried cucurbit shell (qaraa) is used to hold livestock milk and to shake it into butter.

entries.heading: Iogurt (yoghurt; mostly imported, with some made at Casa Raubert)
entries.what: Yoghurt sold in Andorra. Most is imported: the Tridge trade table gives 797,860 (volume) and USD 2,876,331 for 2023, and 702,077 and USD 2,114,915 for 2022, under HS code 040320. Casa Raubert also makes yoghurt "from only the creamiest milk

entries.heading: Iogurte (yoghurt, industrial)
entries.what: packaged yoghurt made by local dairies; the report says urban consumers in Luanda are increasingly buying it.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (yogur)
entries.what: fermented milk product sold in full-fat and skimmed versions. A 2024 Argentine perspective paper reports that 53% of households buy both skim and whole yoghurt, and that full-fat is the predominant choice where only one type is bought; skim

entries.heading: Joghurt (yoghurt, incl. Trinkjoghurt)
entries.what: fermented milk with thermophilic cultures; drinking yoghurt (Trinkjoghurt) is made without added water

entries.heading: Yoghurt (industrial)
entries.what: Yoghurt and yoghurt products produced by the national dairy industry. Australians eat roughly 7.1 kg per person a year (Wikipedia figure).

entries.heading: Yoghurt (Mattas gårdsmejeri)
entries.what: Organic yoghurt made by the Mattas family farm dairy in Sund, northern Åland, without additives or preservatives. It won gold at the Swedish craft food championships.

entries.heading: Qatıq (yoghurt, sour milk)
entries.what: a thick fermented milk, classed as yoghurt; keeps 2–3 days cool; base for ayran, dovğa, doğramac, and many sauces.

entries.heading: Jogurt (yoghurt)
entries.what: Yoghurt, named in the Bosnian dairy list. Balkan yoghurt production dates back to the 7th century per en.wiki Yogurt.

entries.heading: Yoghurt
entries.what: Yoghurt is named among the animal-product foods that people in a Barbados qualitative study identified as part of their diet.

entries.heading: Doi (dahi; plain yoghurt; "curd") (দই; "yogurt")
entries.what: the everyday fermented milk of Bangladesh, eaten plain, with puffed or flattened rice, and used to marinate meat and to cook fish (Catla). Northern doi is often made from evaporated milk and tastes more intense, similar to kheer.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (Belgian market, production)
entries.what: Standard yoghurt sold in Belgium since about 1950, when it was a niche product. Consumption reportedly rose by about 10% a year from 1950 to 1980.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (local and industrial, including flavoured)
entries.what: Yoghurt sold locally in several versions: plain, sweetened, and flavoured with moringa or pineapple.

entries.heading: Pendidan (yoghurt) and latchiiri / dakkere
entries.what: pendidan is the Fulfulde word for yoghurt; latchiiri or dakkere is a meal eaten by almost all Fulani communities, made from fermented milk yoghurt with corn couscous.

entries.heading: Iogurte (batido; drinkable yoghurt not covered)
entries.what: In Brazil the most consumed yoghurt is the batido type with strawberry pulp. Consumption is rising but still modest compared with richer countries; bought mostly for taste.

entries.heading: Dahi (yoghurt)
entries.what: Yoghurt, called dahi or dhai, is the base for butter and for datshi. Cooperatives and small processors also make yoghurt in small quantities.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (yogurt)
entries.what: named by Dairy Farmers of Canada as a dairy category; in a 2023 national survey of 4,045 Canadian adults, yogurt was among the most eaten fermented foods, along with cheese and sour cream.

entries.heading: Kosam / pendidan (fermented milk, yoghurt; Fulfulde)
entries.what: Fulfulde term used for curdled milk and yoghurt; the English Fula article says "kossam" is the general term for both fresh milk (miraɗam) and yoghurt, which in Fulfulde is pendidan. French Wikipedia renders kosam as "lait caillé".

entries.heading: Joghurt (yoghurt) and Sauermilch (legal naming)
entries.what: Yoghurt is eaten daily, often with muesli. In Switzerland a product may be called Joghurt only if it contains at least 10 million colony-forming units of micro-organisms per gram; otherwise it must be labelled Sauermilch. Four fat grades: w

entries.heading: Yoghurt (yogur)
entries.what: Yoghurt made by small farms and sold locally in Boyacá; also industrial yoghurt.

entries.heading: Yogur (yoghurt)
entries.what: The fastest-growing dairy product in the country. Variants include natural, fruit, with seeds, Greek, dietary and vegan.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (natural, eaten with bulgur)
entries.what: Natural yoghurt, a staple eaten with bulgur and used as the base for tzatziki-type dishes.

entries.heading: Commercial yoghurt (Cypriot retail brands; cow, sheep or goat milk)
entries.what: Yoghurt sold in Cypriot shops. A milk-species test on a small set of Cyprus commercial products found one of four yoghurt brands adulterated.

entries.heading: Jogurt (yoghurt), incl. Opočno and fruit yoghurt
entries.what: Fermented dairy product; Czech legal name "jogurt" is restricted to products without heat treatment or preservatives (decree 77/2003 Sb.).

entries.heading: Joghurt (Naturjoghurt, Joghurt mild, Sahnejoghurt, Fruchtjoghurt, Trinkjoghurt)
entries.what: milk thickened by lactic acid bacteria. Legal tiers under the Milcherzeugnisverordnung: skim up to 0.5% fat; low-fat 1.5–1.8%; Joghurt at least 3.5%; Sahnejoghurt at least 10%; Greek-style strained up to about 10%. Fruit yoghurt is about 80

entries.heading: Jogurt (yoghurt)
entries.what: thick, usually flavoured fermented milk with more dry matter than other sour milks

entries.heading: Yoghurt (plain)
entries.what: plain yoghurt eaten with dates at iftar and given to infants as complementary food.

entries.heading: Plain yoghurt (rug-o in Tigrinya; urgo in Amharic)
entries.what: Plain fresh yoghurt served as a side with Eritrean and Ethiopian dishes.

entries.heading: Yogur (yogur; pasteurised and live)
entries.what: Yoghurt made by fermenting milk with live cultures.

entries.heading: Jogurtti (yoghurt; jugurtti; jukurtti)
entries.what: Fermented milk or milk-and-cream mix. The name comes from Turkish yoghurt. Thickness and creaminess depend on its fat content.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (English "yogurt")
entries.what: Recorded only once in FSM top-five dairy lists, in Chuuk (1 child).

entries.heading: Yoghurt (joghurt)
entries.what: Yoghurt sold in the Faroes. MBM has made it since the 1980s; the iodine study tested plain and fruity yoghurt. Sold in several flavours, and a lactose-free, skimmed version exists (see below).

entries.heading: Yaourt (yogurt; ferme, brassé, à boire, bifidus)
entries.what: French yogurt, legally reserved for milk fermented by Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus at a minimum count of 10 million bacteria per gram; variants: set (ferme), stirred (brassé), drinking, bifidus (not called yaourt)

entries.heading: Yoghurt (historic, Guernsey Dairy)
entries.what: The Guernsey Dairy once made yoghurt, but production was discontinued during the production manager's nearly 40 years at the Dairy. No current yoghurt product is listed.

entries.heading: FanYogo (yoghurt)
entries.what: Fan Milk's yoghurt brand in Ghana, sold in strawberry, mango and passion-fruit flavours, and strawberry banana.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (yogurt; local name not given)
entries.what: A yoghurt that Gambian mothers and grandmothers name among the animal-source foods for young children, alongside fish, milk and meat.

entries.heading: Pendidan (pendidan, yoghurt; Fulfulde)
entries.what: The Fulfulde word for yoghurt. The Fula article says "kossam" is the general term for milk, covering both fresh milk (miraɗam) and yoghurt (pendidan).

entries.heading: Jogurt (yoghurt)
entries.what: Yoghurt as a general product. The Croatian article gives no local varieties.

entries.heading: Joghurt (yoghurt)
entries.what: Yoghurt with 5% fat; the Hungarian standard form.

entries.heading: Yoghurt
entries.what: Listed among dairy staples served with bread in Gaelic Ireland; no detail on how it was made.

entries.heading: Dahi / curd (दही; dahi, dohi, thayir)
entries.what: Set curd eaten widely across India. Curd rice and buttermilk are southern staples; raita or plain curd is common in the north. About 7–9% of milk goes to direct dahi consumption.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (yogurt; made by Dairy Industries Jamaica, DIJL)
entries.what: Yoghurt made by Dairy Industries Jamaica Limited (DIJL), sold for local and regional markets.

entries.heading: Yogurt (ヨーグルト)
entries.what: Fermented milk in Japan, sold in several forms: plain, hard, soft, drinkable, frozen and powdered; plant-based versions also exist. Japan has no separate yogurt standard; by law it is 発酵乳 (fermented milk).

entries.heading: Yoghurt
entries.what: Plain, flavoured and strawberry or vanilla yoghurt. The fastest-growing dairy category, per market analysis.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (commercial samples)
entries.what: Yoghurt sold commercially in Kuwait, included in a study of aflatoxin M1 in commercial milk and dairy products.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (laban)
entries.what: The everyday yoghurt of Lebanon, commonly consumed by all ages. Yoghurt is central to Lebanese cooking, including as the base of labneh, kishk and shanklish.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (Joghurt)
entries.what: Yoghurt produced by the national dairy and also listed among common foods in Liechtenstein.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (commercial)
entries.what: packaged yoghurt that is part of Basotho children's diets in Maseru.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (Yaourt, Yaourt Funny, Yaourt bio, Yaourt 0%, Yaourt satiné, Yaourt à la grecque)
entries.what: Luxlait's "Yaourts du Luxembourg": plain yoghurt in several flavours, Funny (for children), organic, 0% fat, and a rich "satiné" version. The Greek-style yoghurt ("à la grecque", with cherry flavour listed) is also in the milk-desserts cate

entries.heading: Jogurts (yoghurt)
entries.what: Yoghurt, made by culturing milk with lactic acid bacteria.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (local name not given in sources read)
entries.what: yoghurt sold in Libyan markets, sampled as a separate category.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (Danone brand, Morocco)
entries.what: Danone yoghurt made in Morocco by Centrale Danone.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (iaurt)
entries.what: milk fermented by lactobacilli into a gel with a slightly sour taste; the Romanian word also appears as lapte prins and chișleag.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (jogurt; jogurt)
entries.what: thick fermented milk, eaten plain and in cold dishes (e.g. cold yoghurt with kačamak or potatoes in Montenegro).

entries.heading: Yoghurt (yaourt)
entries.what: Locally produced and homemade yoghurt sold at street stalls and markets; cited as a common source of calcium.

entries.heading: Jogurt (јогурт; yoghurt)
entries.what: Yoghurt as sold and made in North Macedonia; the Macedonian article itself gives only general information.

entries.heading: Tarag (тараг; yoghurt)
entries.what: The traditional Mongolian yoghurt, a sour fermented milk and a staple of the white foods. Sheep and goat milk suit it well; yak tarag is dense and prized.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (industrial, eaten in Martinique)
entries.what: Yoghurt as a packaged food group in the Martinique and Guadeloupe diet. No local variant is named in the source.

entries.heading: Yaourt nature (Tiviski, plain yoghurt)
entries.what: Plain yoghurt in the Tiviski dairy range.

entries.heading: Everyday yoghurt (plain yoghurt, 1 kg tub)
entries.what: Namibia Dairies' everyday yoghurt, sold in 1 kg tubs; the homepage shows it on promotion at Shoprite-Checkers at N$36.99.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (consumed; not produced in rural areas)
entries.what: Yoghurt is eaten, especially by urban and pluri-ethnic adolescents, according to the questionnaire.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (yaourt; tona for the Tuareg thick yoghurt)
entries.what: yoghurt is listed as a food in Nigerien cuisine and used as a base for millet dishes and drinks.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (roeryoghurt; standyoghurt; Griekse yoghurt)
entries.what: Dutch yoghurt in its main styles: roeryoghurt (stirred, the most widely produced type in the Netherlands), standyoghurt (set in its pot), and Griekse yoghurt (strained, thicker, a milder form of hangop).

entries.heading: Yoghurt (yoghurt, jogurt)
entries.what: pasteurised milk set by Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus. Plain yoghurt is an ingredient in many dishes; sweetened, fruit and flavoured versions are eaten on their own; also sold with grain mixes as snacks.

entries.heading: Dahi (दही; curd / yoghurt)
entries.what: Set (cultured) milk, the everyday fermented milk of Nepal. It is also the base for butter, ghee and several dahi-based drinks.

entries.heading: Yogur (industrial yogurt and drinkable yogurt; Gloria and Chugur)
entries.what: Industrial yogurts in fruit and Greek styles, lactose-free probiotic versions, and drinkable yogurts sold under Gloria brands (Yomost, Yogurello) alongside Chugur products in Cajamarca.

entries.heading: Dahi (yoghurt)
entries.what: Set yoghurt, the staple of Pakistani cooking. Consumers prefer thick, creamy dahi (market research snippet only, unconfirmed).

entries.heading: Jogurt (yoghurt; jogurt naturalny, jogurt pitny)
entries.what: Yoghurt made by fermentation of milk with live cultures. Types: jogurt naturalny (plain, no flavouring), jogurt pitny (drinking, lower viscosity), jogurt smakowy (flavoured). Also called mleko bułgarskie.

entries.heading: Yogur (yoghurt)
entries.what: Yoghurt, named among the local dairy products.

entries.heading: Iogurte (industrial yoghurt)
entries.what: Yoghurt produced by Portuguese dairies, including Lactogal (brand Adágio) at its Oliveira de Azeméis and Vila do Conde plants.

entries.heading: Yogur (yoghurt, including Greek-style)
entries.what: Yoghurt is sold by the industry. Greek-style yoghurt is named as the most visible example of the industry's move toward protein products.

entries.heading: Iaurt (yoghurt)
entries.what: Milk fermented by lactobacilli into a gel-like, slightly sour product.

entries.heading: Jogurt (јогурт; yogurt)
entries.what: standard yogurt; served with burek and other baked goods in the Balkans, and listed in Serbian cuisine as a salad/appetizer base; yogurt is a staple across Southeastern Europe and the Balkans.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (йогурт)
entries.what: Yoghurt made with Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus; the Russian article's definition requires at least 10^7 CFU streptococci per g at end of shelf life.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (processed)
entries.what: yoghurt listed among processed milk products in Rwanda.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (زبادي style; plain, fruited, Greek-style)
entries.what: Full-fat, fruited and Greek-style plain yoghurts are sold in Saudi Arabia; the Saudi dental study tested them as commercial products.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (natural, fruit, drinking yoghurt, low-sugar, lactose-free, greek-style)
entries.what: Swedish yoghurt sold in natural, fruit, berry, vanilla and honey flavours, and as low-sugar, low-fat, organic, lactose-free, drinking yoghurt and cooking yoghurt. Greek-style (strained) is also sold.

entries.heading: Jogurt (yoghurt)
entries.what: Dairy product made by bacterial fermentation of milk.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (yoghurt, industrial; Michi and Rudisa & Nuprocess)
entries.what: Yoghurt produced by the commercial dairies Michi and Rudisa & Nuprocess from the early 2000s, alongside fresh milk and cheese.

entries.heading: Yogur (yoghurt)
entries.what: Yoghurt eaten at breakfast and mid-morning snacks in El Salvador.

entries.heading: Yogurt (laban, yoghurt)
entries.what: The base of many Syrian dishes and drinks.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (yoghurt; local name not found)
entries.what: a fermented milk product named in Eswatini Dairy Board farmer training.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (yogurt; yoghurt, plain)
entries.what: Plain yoghurt sold in vending sites in urban Turkmenistan, listed among the traditional beverages.

entries.heading: Yoğurt (yoghurt, general)
entries.what: the basic Turkish yoghurt, served with kebab, köfte, meze, mantı, pilav; the name is from Ottoman Turkish "yugurt/yoğurt", and Turkish usage is recorded from the 11th century (Dīwān Lughāt al-Turk).

entries.heading: Yoghurt (all types)
entries.what: fermented milk products, all types listed in the TT food list.

entries.heading: Dahi (curd, fresh homemade yoghurt)
entries.what: traditional set curd.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (йогурт; yogurt)
entries.what: Fermented with Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus. Drinking (stirred), dessert and bio-yogurts are described as especially popular in Ukraine recently; fruit fillers are common.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (commercial and artisanal)
entries.what: Sold widely in Uganda, both supermarket and market-vendor products.

entries.heading: Yogur (yogurt, incl. lactose-free, drinkable and "semi" lines)
entries.what: Yoghurt is a standard Uruguayan dairy product sold in supermarkets and by the cooperative and by private producers. The Colonial/Granja Pocha company offers lactose-free yoghurt (named as Uruguay's first such line), a "Yodrink" drinkable li

entries.heading: Sữa chua (yoghurt; sữa chua đặc, yaourt)
entries.what: Yoghurt sold industrially and made at home; eaten plain or with fruit as a snack.

entries.heading: Yoghurt (laban-style soured yoghurt, shafut ingredient)
entries.what: yoghurt, a shafut ingredient alongside hakeen. Also listed among milk products tested in Yemen for aflatoxin.

entries.heading: Commercial yoghurt (yogurt, sold in shops)
entries.what: Shop-bought yoghurt, used by caregivers in a Gauteng qualitative study; the households that bought it did not make yoghurt at home.

entries.heading: Ice cream (frozen milk dessert; milk source not stated)
entries.what: Ice cream is listed as a common dessert in Antiguan meals, alongside cake, apple pie, and gelatin.

entries.heading: Akullore (ice cream)
entries.what: ice cream, eaten in summer and winter

entries.heading: Ice cream (helado)
entries.what: Argentine ice cream in many flavours, including dulce de leche, close to Italian gelato. Ice cream parlours are popular in Buenos Aires. Argentina has a high consumption rate (about 6.0 L per person per year), and artisanal ice cream is mad

entries.heading: Ice cream (Australia)
entries.what: Ice cream, which Australians and New Zealanders eat among the most in the world (about 18 litres per person per year, per the Wikipedia article).

entries.heading: Ice cream (imported and processed)
entries.what: Ice cream is named as a comfort food by younger adults in a Barbados study, who preferred imported and processed foods such as ice cream.

entries.heading: Ice cream (branded and locally made; probiotic trial)
entries.what: branded and locally made ice creams sold in Bangladesh; a 2025 study in Kushtia City compared them; a 2024–25 sample study in the south-west included chocolate and vanilla ice cream from commercial and traditional outlets.

entries.heading: Roomijs (cream ice cream)
entries.what: Cream ice cream; in several European countries it must contain at least 5% milk fat, and "roomijs" is a protected term under Dutch law. Melkijs is the 2.5% milk-fat type.

entries.heading: Sorvete (ice cream; picolé)
entries.what: Frozen dessert made from a dairy base (milk or cream) with fruit or other flavourings. Brazil uses sorbet for the water-based version. Forms: cup, cone (casquinha), stick (picolé).

entries.heading: Ice cream (Bahamian ice cream)
entries.what: A frozen dessert the source describes as popular in the Bahamas, including in fruit flavours.

entries.heading: Ice cream (small-scale)
entries.what: Ice cream is processed in small quantities alongside yoghurt, hard cheese and Gouda-type cheese by dairy cooperatives and farmer groups.

entries.heading: Ice cream (марожанае; marozhanae)
entries.what: A frozen dairy dessert. The Belarusian-language Wikipedia shows a cornflower ice cream (валошкавы пламбір) as a Belarusian example.

entries.heading: Ice cream (Canadian standard)
entries.what: under Canadian food rules, "ice cream" must have at least 10% milk fat and at least 180 g of solids per litre; products with added cocoa, chocolate syrup, fruit, nuts or confections may have 8% milk fat. "Ice cream mix" is the pasteurised u

entries.heading: Helado de leche (ice cream)
entries.what: The most popular ice creams are milk-based. Other kinds include water-based nieves and yogurt flavours. Flavours include crema, dulce de leche, natilla with strawberry or fruit, tiramisu, cheesecake, Irish cream and arroz con leche. Italian

entries.heading: Zmrzlina (ice cream)
entries.what: Czech law sorts frozen creams: mléčné (min. 2.5% milk fat, no vegetable fat), smetanové (min. 8% milk fat), and others with vegetable fat, water, fruit or sorbet.

entries.heading: Jäätis (ice cream)
entries.what: ice cream, usually from milk or cream, sugar and flavourings; the word also covers sorbet and fruit ice

entries.heading: Ice cream (frozen milk dessert)
entries.what: Ice cream served as topping on rozz be-laban and as a scoop in fakhfakhina (per Egyptian cuisine page).

entries.heading: Ice cream
entries.what: ice cream is one of the dairy foods sold in Ethiopia that have been tested for Listeria.

entries.heading: Jäätelö (ice cream, milk-based by Finnish law)
entries.what: Finnish ice cream. Under a decree in force 1956–2007 the name jäätelö was limited to milk-based products. Kermajäätelö needs at least 8% milk fat (customarily about 12%); maitojäätelö at least 2.5%; kasvirasvajäätelö uses skimmed milk and v

entries.heading: Ice cream (English; "ice milk" also recorded)
entries.what: Among the top five dairy foods in all four FSM states: most recorded in Chuuk (8 children, the top dairy item there), and in the top five in Kosrae (11), Pohnpei (10) and Yap (20). "Ice milk" is listed separately in Kosrae (18 children).

entries.heading: Ice cream (Guernsey ice cream)
entries.what: Ice cream made from Guernsey milk and cream, sold by the Guernsey Dairy.

entries.heading: Ice cream (other names: ice cream)
entries.what: A frozen dessert of milk or cream, sugar and flavourings.

entries.heading: Ice cream (Murphy's)
entries.what: Artisan ice cream from Dingle, Co. Kerry, founded 2000; flavours include brown bread and sea salt.

entries.heading: Ice cream (Strauss; Tilon, Exodus, Witman brands)
entries.what: Ice cream made by the Strauss Group, which added ice cream products in the 1950s; Strauss ice cream introduced in 1949, Tilon and Exodus made at a leased factory in Acre from 1962, Witman acquired in 1979. Strauss ice creams are now sold un

entries.heading: Ís (ice cream; Kjörís, Hveragerði)
entries.what: Ice cream made by Kjörís, a family company in Hveragerði with about 160 product types, plus some imported brands. It began with packaged nougat, chocolate and vanilla ice cream.

entries.heading: Ice cream (Jamaican flavours)
entries.what: Ice cream sold in many flavours, including coffee, pistachio, coconut and mango. Grapenut and rum-and-raisin are called popular desserts.

entries.heading: Ice cream (アイスクリーム, aisukurīmu; アイスミルク; ラクトアイス)
entries.what: Japan sorts frozen milk desserts by milk content. アイスクリーム needs milk solids of at least 15.0% by weight, with milk fat at least 8.0%. アイスミルク needs milk solids at least 10.0% and milk fat at least 3.0%. ラクトアイス needs milk solids at least 3.0%

entries.heading: Ice cream (Taesongsan Ice Cream Factory, 태성산 아이스크림 공장)
entries.what: An ice cream manufacturing plant at the foot of Taesŏngsan, a mountain in Taesong-guyok, Pyongyang, opened in 2022 on Kim Jong Un's order.

entries.heading: Ice cream
entries.what: Ice cream is one of Lebanon's dairy outputs, at 6.25% of potential output (Lebanese Dairy Board, 2016). No Lebanese brand or product page was confirmed in this pass.

entries.heading: Saldējums (ice cream)
entries.what: Ice cream made from milk or milk components.

entries.heading: Ice cream
entries.what: ice cream sold in Libyan markets.

entries.heading: Ice cream (înghețată; Moldovan local name not confirmed)
entries.what: packaged industrial ice cream sold at market vending sites in Chișinău.

entries.heading: Ice cream (crème glacée)
entries.what: Locally produced ice cream, cited as a dairy source of calcium.

entries.heading: Ice cream (commercial)
entries.what: ice cream, a food item in the CHL intake analysis and part of the "dairy other than milk" class

entries.heading: Ice cream (glace; in biscuit manioc)
entries.what: Ice cream is an ingredient of biscuit manioc, a Mauritian dessert of flavoured manioc biscuit cookies mixed with fresh fruit and ice cream. The Mauritian cuisine article names it; no ice cream type is given.

entries.heading: Roomijs (ice cream; melkijs variant)
entries.what: Consumer ice cream; roomijs is a protected term requiring a minimum milk fat (8% until 2009, now 5%). Melkijs has about 2.5% fat. Eggs can be added but then the product cannot be called roomijs. Classic dessert dame blanche (vanilla ice cre

entries.heading: Ice cream (Tip Top, Kāpiti)
entries.what: Commercial ice cream brands in NZ.

entries.heading: Helados de crema (ice cream; helado de lúcuma and other flavours)
entries.what: Peruvian ice cream in common flavours (lúcuma, chocolate, vanilla, strawberry) and exotic ones (camu camu, guaraná). D'Onofrio is a leading brand (owned by Nestlé per the article).

entries.heading: Helado (ice cream), including codfish ice cream
entries.what: Ice cream is served on the island, and the Wikipedia cuisine article mentions codfish ice cream at a Lares ice cream parlour.

entries.heading: Gelado (ice cream)
entries.what: The Portuguese term for dairy ice cream, based on milk or cream with sugar and flavours. Sorvete in Portugal is a dairy-free fruit sorbet.

entries.heading: Ice cream (English)
entries.what: Ice cream, consumed in the household survey.

entries.heading: Sladoled (ice cream)
entries.what: Icy dessert made from milk or cream, sugar and additions (mainly fruit and flavourings).

entries.heading: Zmrzlina (zmrzlina; mrazený krém; ice cream)
entries.what: a frozen product of a mix made from milk, cream, sugar and flavourings; the article says the mix is often made with dried milk, guar gum and stabilisers, and that cheap cream products use vegetable fats.

entries.heading: Ice cream (frozen milk dessert)
entries.what: Ice cream made by small and medium companies that reconstitute powdered milk.

entries.heading: Ice cream (ice cream; local name not found)
entries.what: ice cream named in Eswatini Dairy Board farmer training.

entries.heading: Ice cream (homemade and commercial)
entries.what: frozen dessert, sold on hot days, including homemade flavours.

entries.heading: Ice cream (imported; sold and eaten, not made locally as far as sources show)
entries.what: ice cream, listed among foods eaten in a Tuvalu dietary survey and among the imported-food patterns.

entries.heading: Ice cream (Bakhresa Group)
entries.what: ice cream made by Bakhresa Group, a Tanzanian industrial group.

entries.heading: Helado (ice cream)
entries.what: Ice cream sold by Conaprole as a national product line. Not described further in opened sources.

entries.heading: Muzqaymoq (muzqaymoq; ice cream)
entries.what: Ice cream. The atlas lists Uzbek name muzqaymoq. The Uzbek article gives a frozen sweet made from eggs, cream or fruit.

entries.heading: Ice cream (industrial)
entries.what: ice cream sold in Taizz Governorate, from local industries or imports.

entries.heading: Leite em pó (milk powder, imported)
entries.what: the main dairy import of Angola and the main raw input for local reconstituted milk and other dairy goods. Between 2019 and 2025 Angola imported about 295,000 t of dairy products, worth US$856 million (CIF), with milk powder the leading pro

entries.heading: Powdered milk (leche en polvo)
entries.what: milk dehydrated for human food, in whole, partly skimmed and skimmed classes.

entries.heading: Milk powder (skim and whole)
entries.what: Skim and whole milk powder made for export. Australia exported over 13,000 tonnes in fiscal year 2020–21, worth about AUD 83 million.

entries.heading: Leite em pó (powdered milk; Ninho)
entries.what: Dehydrated milk, about 90% of mass removed.

entries.heading: Milk powder (reconstituted, imported)
entries.what: Powdered milk that many households buy instead of fresh milk. In a 2025 survey of dairy farmers in Thimphu, Paro and Haa, farmers in Paro and Thimphu said they prefer powdered milk; farmers in Haa mostly drink their own dairy products.

entries.heading: Milk powder (powdered milk)
entries.what: powdered milk, which Indigenous Canadians commonly consume today, a habit linked to colonial-era rations. Canadian powdered milk must have added vitamin D, enough to give 300–400 IU per reasonable daily intake.

entries.heading: Leche en polvo (powdered milk, Colún)
entries.what: Powdered milk sold in tins and bags. The Colún article says the company began distributing "leche en polvo en latas, bolsas" after its early butter production.

entries.heading: Leche en polvo (milk powder)
entries.what: Powdered milk made in Costa Rica.

entries.heading: Mælkepulver / tørmælk (milk powder)
entries.what: dried milk (milk with water removed), named in the Danish milk article.

entries.heading: Piimapulber (milk powder)
entries.what: milk dried to a powder; types cream powder (>=42% fat), whole milk powder (26–42%), reduced-fat (1.5–26%), skim (up to 1.5%)

entries.heading: Powdered milk (reconstituted)
entries.what: dried milk used as the everyday milk in refugee camps when fresh milk is unavailable.

entries.heading: Maitojauhe (milk powder)
entries.what: Dried milk used in the food industry, in households and as animal feed. Powder-based products include sauce and soup mixes, custard powders, infant formula powders, porridge powders, coffee-cream powder and cocoa milk powder.

entries.heading: Milk powder (in fishcakes and cold cuts)
entries.what: Milk powder used as an ingredient in Faroese fishcakes and cold cuts. It is not a standalone product.

entries.heading: Powdered milk (leche en polvo)
entries.what: powdered milk sold and used in Guatemala, mainly imported; Nicaragua is named as the main source.

entries.heading: Leche en polvo (milk powder, Ceteco)
entries.what: milk powder made, packed and distributed by the Honduran company Ceteco, a Lacthosa brand, described as a leading Honduran dairy-powder producer.

entries.heading: Tejpor (milk powder)
entries.what: Powdered milk; whole-milk powder 26% fat, skim-milk powder none.

entries.heading: Milk powder (dried milk, BEO)
entries.what: Dried milk powder sold under the Kerrygold company's BEO brand; a dairy powder facility in Ireland is studied in a 2026 paper.

entries.heading: Milk powder (Dairygold, Mallow)
entries.what: Milk powder made at Dairygold's factory in Mallow, Co. Cork. Butter, cheese and milk powder together make up 70% of Dairygold's annual revenue, per the company page.

entries.heading: Milk powder (skim, buffalo-based) (दूध पाउडर)
entries.what: Skim milk powder, developed in Amul's Anand programme and scaled up under Operation Flood; domestic output rose from 22,000 to 140,000 t by 1989.

entries.heading: Milk powder (powdered milk; DIJL, Everyday Milk Powder)
entries.what: Powdered milk made by DIJL. DIJL has a co-manufacturing deal with Nestlé to produce the Everyday Milk Powder.

entries.heading: Powdered milk
entries.what: Milk powder sold as a drinking milk and in formula-type products. The Euromonitor category covers it.

entries.heading: Milk powder (imported, reconstituted and dried)
entries.what: Imported dried milk, sold and traded in the islands for reconstitution. Local dairy production is too small to supply the market.

entries.heading: 분유 (milk powder; skim powder; infant formula base)
entries.what: Milk powder made in Korea, including skim-milk powder (탈지분유, made by Seoul Milk from 1971) and infant formula (조제분유).

entries.heading: Milk powder (dried milk)
entries.what: Powdered milk is listed as one of the milk products sampled in Kuwait for aflatoxin M1 contamination.

entries.heading: Milk powder (whole and skim, reconstituted)
entries.what: Imported whole and skim milk powder, reconstituted for domestic processing.

entries.heading: Milk powder
entries.what: Powdered milk dominates Sri Lankan consumption (172 g to 345 g per person per month over 1990/91 to 2019). Local production meets about 45% of domestic need; large imports (97,263 MT in 2020, 79,471 MT in 2025).

entries.heading: Piena pulveris (milk powder)
entries.what: Dried milk product.

entries.heading: Milk powder (full-cream and skimmed)
entries.what: full-cream and skimmed milk powder sold in Libya.

entries.heading: Ronono vovoka (powdered milk)
entries.what: Powdered milk, named as a product in the Malagasy Wikipedia.

entries.heading: Milk powder (Nicaragua as a source)
entries.what: Nicaragua named as one of the main sources of powdered milk that Guatemala imports. This is one paper's statement, not a Nicaraguan product description.

entries.heading: Melkpoeder (milk powder)
entries.what: Milk with water removed to a dry powder; base for solid block milk and condensed milk.

entries.heading: Tørrmelk (milk powder)
entries.what: milk dehydrated to powder, made from whole or skimmed milk. Whole-milk powder goes rancid after the bag is opened; skimmed powder keeps for a long time. Instant versions dissolve easily.

entries.heading: Milk powder (dried milk, imported; reconstituted)
entries.what: Dried cow's milk sold in local supermarkets, used mainly to add calcium and to make milk drinks. Reported in a PNG prison diet study as available in supermarkets, and suggested as a way to add calcium to the diet.

entries.heading: Mleko w proszku (milk powder)
entries.what: Cow's milk dried to about 2% moisture, whole, standardised or skimmed.

entries.heading: Leche en polvo (milk powder)
entries.what: Dried milk, a main value-added dairy export.

entries.heading: Milk powder (imported)
entries.what: powdered milk listed among milk products imported into Rwanda.

entries.heading: Milk powder (powdered milk, used in cooking)
entries.what: Powdered milk is used as an ingredient in Saudi dishes and sweets, sold as full-cream powder.

entries.heading: Mjölkpulver (torrmjölk, milk powder)
entries.what: Dried whole milk, skimmed milk, whey, or buttermilk powder; dissolved at about 125 g per litre.

entries.heading: Milk powder (imported; reconstituted)
entries.what: The main form of dairy imported into Senegal, used by industrial and semi-industrial firms and to reconstitute milk and yoghurt.

entries.heading: Powdered milk (imported)
entries.what: Imported dried milk, and cartons imported from Kenya, used in towns for tea and coffee and for infant feeding.

entries.heading: Powdered milk (full cream and skimmed)
entries.what: reconstituted drinking milk made from dried milk, full cream and low-fat.

entries.heading: Milk powder (cow, whole fat and fat-free)
entries.what: powdered whole-fat and fat-free cow's milk, listed among dairy foods in a Tanzanian diet study.

entries.heading: Milk powder (dried whole milk and nonfat dry milk)
entries.what: Dehydrated milk for long shelf life and transport.

entries.heading: Leche en polvo (milk powder, whole and skimmed)
entries.what: Powdered whole and skimmed milk, made and sold by Conaprole and listed in Uruguayan gastronomy.

entries.heading: Sữa bột and reconstituted milk (milk powder)
entries.what: Milk powder, mostly imported as raw material and reconstituted into liquid milk; also sold as infant products.

entries.heading: Ghee (samneh / samn, clarified butter)
entries.what: Clarified butter, called samneh in the infobox of the Wikipedia article. Used for cooking and in desserts, and as a preserved food in Bedouin cooking.

entries.heading: Ghee (desi ghee; Kochi / Kuchi-supplied)
entries.what: clarified butter, poured over plain rice with yogurt, and used in festival sweets.

entries.heading: Butterschmalz (clarified butter)
entries.what: clarified butter, heated to remove water and milk proteins

entries.heading: Sarı yağ (ghee, clarified butter)
entries.what: clarified butter, also called sarı yağ ("yellow fat") or qhi in Azerbaijani; the Azerbaijani article is a copy of the general ghee article.

entries.heading: Ghee (سمن; samn)
entries.what: clarified butter used as a cooking fat, added to harees in Bahraini cooking.

entries.heading: Butterschmalz (clarified butter; Schmalzbutter; Geklärte Butter)
entries.what: almost pure milk fat, with water, milk protein and milk sugar removed. Solid at room temperature; smoke point about 205 °C.

entries.heading: Ghee (subag; samneh; Somali/Afar "butter oil")
entries.what: Clarified butter eaten in Djibouti as a breakfast fat with lahoh flatbread, honey and tea; also one of the ingredients of xalwo (halva).

entries.heading: Klaret smør (clarified butter)
entries.what: butter heated and cooled so water and casein separate, leaving nearly pure milk fat; tolerates higher frying heat.

entries.heading: Samna / samneh baladi (سمنة بلدي; samna baladi; ghee)
entries.what: Clarified butter, used generously in Egyptian feteer pies and in sawabe' Zeinab (per Egyptian cuisine page). A 2024 study describes traditional samna as a clarified fermented Egyptian butter.

entries.heading: Kirkastettu voi (clarified butter, ghee)
entries.what: Clarified butter with the whey protein removed; tolerates higher frying temperatures.

entries.heading: Vajzsír / derített vaj (clarified butter)
entries.what: Clarified butter, heated and filtered to remove water and solids; stable for frying.

entries.heading: Ghee (घी; ghṛta; desi ghee)
entries.what: The most consumed value-added dairy product in India, and central to rituals and Ayurveda.

entries.heading: Burro chiarificato (clarified butter, Italian name for ghee)
entries.what: clarified butter, with a caramel note from prolonged boiling.

entries.heading: Samneh / ghee (سمنة; samneh)
entries.what: clarified butter, a preserved food central to Bedouin cuisine (named alongside jameed)

entries.heading: Ghee (clarified butter, northern Kenya; local name not given)
entries.what: clarified butter fed to young children in pastoral communities of northern Kenya, mixed into other foods because mothers believe it is "good for their health".

entries.heading: 버터기름 / 정제버터 (clarified butter; ghee-type)
entries.what: Clarified butter separated from butter, very high in fat. The Korean article lists 기 (ghee) and the old term 버터기름 as traditional forms.

entries.heading: Ghee (samn; clarified butter)
entries.what: Clarified butter used as an ingredient in Kuwaiti cooking, including the sweet asida.

entries.heading: Samneh (سمنة; ghee, clarified butter)
entries.what: Clarified butter used in Lebanese sweets and pastries.

entries.heading: Ghee (buffalo ghee, cow ghee)
entries.what: Listed among Sri Lankan oils and fats as cow ghee and buffalo ghee.

entries.heading: Clarified butter (butter oil)
entries.what: butter with the water and milk solids removed, so it keeps longer.

entries.heading: Ghee (clarified butter, Malaysian Indian homes)
entries.what: Clarified butter still widely used for cooking in Malaysian Indian homes.

entries.heading: Geklaarde boter (clarified butter, ghee-type)
entries.what: Melted butter with solids and water removed. Higher smoke point, used in cooking. Ghee is a form of clarified butter, mainly used in Indian cuisine.

entries.heading: Ghee (घिउ / घ्यू; ghyu, gheu)
entries.what: Clarified butter, used as a cooking fat, in butter tea, in puddings, sweets and halwa, served with rice in Madhesi meals.

entries.heading: Ghee (samn; Arabic سمن)
entries.what: Clarified butter served on harees, with qabuli, and used as an ingredient in Omani sweets and halwa.

entries.heading: Ghee (desi ghee; clarified butter)
entries.what: Clarified butter, widely used in Pakistani cooking, noted for its high smoke point.

entries.heading: Masło klarowane (clarified butter, ghee-like)
entries.what: Clarified butter: cooked butter with the water and milk solids removed, leaving golden fat. Ghee is the Indian and Pakistani form, not claimed as Polish in the source.

entries.heading: Samneh (سمنة, samneh baladi; clarified butter / ghee)
entries.what: butter clarified into a shelf-stable fat; used for frying and cooking, for kibbeh, in Mfarakeh, Qadha, and Gaza's qidra rice dish (where it smothers the farasheeh bread layer), and in knafeh (Nablus method: pan coated with clarified butter)

entries.heading: Ghee (سمن; samn)
entries.what: Butterfat cleared of water and milk solids. Used as a cooking fat and a garnish in Qatari dishes.

entries.heading: Ghee
entries.what: ghee produced from cow milk and consumed locally and exported.

entries.heading: Ghee (samn; clarified butter)
entries.what: Clarified butter used across Saudi cooking; the Saudi cuisine article calls ghee one of the main ingredients, with wheat, dates, meat and vegetables.

entries.heading: Samn / samin (ghee) (السمن; ghee)
entries.what: ghee, named in the dairy list of the Arabic Wikipedia Sudanese cuisine article.

entries.heading: Ghee (klarifierat smör, ghi)
entries.what: Clarified butter made of pure butterfat, described in the Swedish article as a milk product; used mainly in Afghan, Pakistani and North Indian cooking.

entries.heading: Ghee (subag)
entries.what: Clarified butter, called subag, used widely in Somali breakfasts and dishes and as a traded good.

entries.heading: Ghee (samneh, samin)
entries.what: Clarified butter; the fat is kept after the milk solids are skimmed.

entries.heading: Sary yag (clarified camel milk butter, ghee)
entries.what: Clarified butter made from camel milk, one of the Turkmen fats (with fat-tail and sesame oil).

entries.heading: Sadeyağ (clarified butter, general)
entries.what: butter oil that is at least 99% milk fat under the Turkish Food Codex.

entries.heading: Ghee (clarified butter)
entries.what: milk fat cooked to remove water and solids, used for cooking and in Hindu ritual.

entries.heading: Samli (ghee)
entries.what: the Swahili name for ghee.

entries.heading: Toplene maslo / pryazhene maslo (топлене масло; пряжене масло; clarified butter)
entries.what: Clarified butter, nearly pure milk fat (at least 99%), called пряжене or топлене масло in Ukrainian and linked to ghee.

entries.heading: Ghee (artisanal sample, Uganda)
entries.what: An artisanal Ugandan ghee sampled for a 16S microbiome study of African fermented dairy products.

entries.heading: Ghee
entries.what: Clarified butter cooked until the water and solids are removed.

entries.heading: Samn / semn (سمن) (clarified butter; ghee)
entries.what: Clarified butter called semn (سمن) in Yemen. Wikipedia says it is the fat of choice in pastries, while ghee is the fat for savoury dishes.

entries.heading: Nata (cream, creme de leite)
entries.what: cream sold for cooking and for the table. The report says it has strong demand, linked to Portuguese cooking influence.

entries.heading: Cream (crema de leche, chantilly and pastry cream)
entries.what: fresh cream whipped into chantilly, widely used on desserts and cakes; pastry cream (crema pastelera) used as a filling for pastries such as medialunas. Also cream as a filling in curanto (Patagonia) per the English article.

entries.heading: Cream (room, slagroom, zure room, crème fraîche)
entries.what: Dutch/Belgian cream categories: room (at least 10% fat), dubbele room 45%, volle room 35%, koffieroom 15%; slagroom (whipping cream, at least 30% fat); zure room (sour cream, about 20% fat, acidified); crème fraîche (about 35% fat); halfroo

entries.heading: Cream
entries.what: Cream listed among dairy products in the country.

entries.heading: Creme de leite
entries.what: Cream with about 20% fat; the most consumed milk-fat product in Brazil. Fresh cream (creme de leite fresco) is about 35% fat, pasteurised before sale.

entries.heading: Nata
entries.what: High-fat dairy product, especially in the southern states; sold solid and refrigerated there. Used to make butter.

entries.heading: Cream (Parmalat Botswana)
entries.what: Cream listed among Parmalat Botswana's products.

entries.heading: Cream (fresh and whipping)
entries.what: named by Dairy Farmers of Canada as a dairy category; also used in moose milk, eggnog and sucre à la crème.

entries.heading: Cream (crema de leche, Colún)
entries.what: A cream product in Colún's range; the Colún product list has a "Cremas" category.

entries.heading: Natas (postre de natas; cream and milk-skin dessert)
entries.what: "Postre de natas", a milk-based Colombian pudding made with natas (the cream skin from heated milk). Fresas con crema is a separate cream dessert from the same Bogotá list.

entries.heading: Crema de leche (cream)
entries.what: Fresh cream, associated with natilla and with dairy products introduced in the colonial period.

entries.heading: Sahne / Rahm (cream, Schlagsahne)
entries.what: the fat-rich phase of milk; Schlagsahne is the whipping cream.

entries.heading: Fløde (cream)
entries.what: Danish cream; used in hjerter i flødesovs, rødgrød med fløde, fløderand; whipping cream (piskefløde) about 38% fat.

entries.heading: Cream (qishta in dishes)
entries.what: Cream used as an ingredient in Egyptian festive and sweet dishes.

entries.heading: Cream (separated and churned)
entries.what: fat layer skimmed by hand or scoop from milk stored overnight. Used alone or mixed with yoghurt for churning butter. Also separated by cream separators in the North Shoa study.

entries.heading: Cream (English "cream", dairy; not coconut)
entries.what: Recorded in the top five dairy foods of Chuuk (4 children). The paper's food-group method puts coconut products in the fruit group, so this item is treated as dairy.

entries.heading: Cream (rjómi / rómi)
entries.what: Cream, one of the dairy products tested for iodine. Sold by MBM as whipping cream (38%), cooking cream (18%), and UHT cream; see the entries below.

entries.heading: Kaimaki (kaïmáki; milk skin, cream)
entries.what: the fatty, foamy skin that forms on boiled milk (Greek Wikipedia disambiguation) and also a cream spread. English Wikipedia describes it as a soft cream cheese spread on bread or used in cooking and sweets.

entries.heading: Vrhnje (cream)
entries.what: Cream skimmed from milk fat in Croatia. Sold at 12%, 20% or 30% milk fat.

entries.heading: Tejszín (cream)
entries.what: Cream separated from raw milk; whipping cream 30% fat, coffee cream 16%.

entries.heading: Khameh (خامه; cream)
entries.what: Persian word for cream, named as the thinner product close to sar-e-shir.

entries.heading: Rjómi (cream; whipped cream)
entries.what: Cream whipped and used as a topping on sponge cakes served at birthdays, weddings and family gatherings.

entries.heading: Panna (cream, fresh)
entries.what: fat separated from milk; used for butter, desserts and sauces.

entries.heading: Cream (クリーム, kurīmu; 生クリーム)
entries.what: Milk with non-fat components removed, leaving milk fat. Also sold as cream powder (keeps the milk fat, lacks other milk components) and clotted cream in Codex.

entries.heading: Cream
entries.what: Cream is used in Cambodian desserts, and as a fresh cream product in farm lines.

entries.heading: 크림 (cream)
entries.what: Cream sold by Korean dairies (생크림 and similar). The 서울우유 product list includes cream.

entries.heading: Cream (Rahm, Sahne; butter-making cream)
entries.what: Fresh cream produced by the national dairy. Butter-making cream (Butterungsrahm) was historically the main product, sold as a semi-finished item to industrial processors in Switzerland.

entries.heading: Krējums (cream)
entries.what: Cream, used in cooking and in some soups and desserts.

entries.heading: Cream (jowhara filling)
entries.what: Cream used as the filling of jowhara, a Fes pastry made with fried waraq, cream and toasted almonds.

entries.heading: Cream (မလိုင် malaing)
entries.what: cream from the milk fat; the Burmese term is malaing, also used for malai (cream).

entries.heading: Zöökhii (зөөхий; cream)
entries.what: The simplest cream, skimmed from naturally curdled milk; the base for tsagaan tos (white butter).

entries.heading: Cream (crème) served with dried dates
entries.what: Cream served as a dip for dried dates in Mauritanian typical dishes.

entries.heading: Crema de leche (crema)
entries.what: fresh cream named among the dairy products of the Pacific region. Plain crema is also served on pipián, a traditional dish, in the same article.

entries.heading: Fløte (cream)
entries.what: the fatty part of milk, separated from cow's milk, pasteurised but not homogenised. Norwegian types: kremfløte 38 % fat (whippable); matfløte 20 % (not whippable); kaffefløte 9 or 12–13 % (for coffee and tea); fløtebase 15 % with gelatin, u

entries.heading: Cream
entries.what: Fresh cream sold as Anchor cream, and UHT (long-life) cream for foodservice.

entries.heading: Śmietanka and kremówka (cream; whipped cream)
entries.what: Sweet cream (śmietanka, double cream) and whipped cream, used in soups, cabbage dishes, cakes and desserts. Kremówka is a cream-filled pastry, a less common version of napoleonka filled with whipped cream instead of custard.

entries.heading: Natas (cream)
entries.what: Cream (natas) used in Portuguese cooking, for example in natas do Céu and bacalhau com natas, and in cream-based pastries; the Lactogal plants make cream.

entries.heading: Crema de leche (milk cream)
entries.what: Fresh milk cream sold in the country.

entries.heading: Cream
entries.what: Cream is served with a Saudi breakfast dish (Ma'soub) and is listed as an ingredient in the traditional dish paper.

entries.heading: Cream (industrial, Uganda)
entries.what: Cream sold by a processor in western Uganda, listed alongside cheese.

entries.heading: Cream (heavy, light and whipping cream; US standards)
entries.what: The higher-fat layer of milk; US standardised cream products.

entries.heading: Cream (fresh, industrial or imported)
entries.what: cream sold among the industrial dairy products of Taizz Governorate. Not the same as the clotted qishta cream above.

name: Kefir
names: also นมเปรี้ยวคีเฟอร์

entries.heading: Kefir (կեֆիր)
entries.what: A fermented milk drink. The word is of North Caucasian origin and it is very popular in the North Caucasus. Armenian Wikipedia gives the Armenian name կեֆիր ([ˈkɛfir]).

entries.heading: Kefir (kéfir de leche; milk kefir)
entries.what: one of the fermented-milk categories of the Argentine Food Code (CAA). The Code reserves the word kefir for products that meet its definition.

entries.heading: Kefir
entries.what: fermented milk drink made with kefir grains (a mix of bacteria and yeasts)

entries.heading: Kefir
entries.what: Fermented drink made with kefir grains, from the Caucasus (North Caucasian origin of the name). Listed as a non-alcoholic beverage in the Bosnian cuisine article.

entries.heading: Kefir (кефір; kefir)
entries.what: A fermented milk drink made with kefir grains, widely drunk in the former Soviet Union and Central and Eastern Europe.

entries.heading: Kefir (as consumed in Canada)
entries.what: kefir was tried by 53% of Canadians surveyed in 2023, though only 6% of those who had tried it drink it daily. It was consumed mostly for perceived health benefits.

entries.heading: Kefír (kefir)
entries.what: Fermented milk drink listed among Czech/Slovak fermented milk products, with a Caucasian origin per the source.

entries.heading: Kefir (incl. Kefir mild, Sahnekefir)
entries.what: fermented milk drink. Industrial "Kefir mild" uses a defined mix of bacteria and yeasts for consistent taste. Sahnekefir is a cream variant with fruit added. Starter is kefir grains (Kefirknollen) or powdered starter (Kefirferment).

entries.heading: Keefir (kefir; kefiir)
entries.what: drink fermented by bacteria and yeasts; sour, slightly fizzy

entries.heading: Kefiiri (kefir)
entries.what: A kefir from the Caucasus and Tibet, bought ready-made in Finnish shops. Thickness is roughly that of yoghurt; it is sour and slightly alcoholic (0–2%).

entries.heading: Kefir (კეფირი)
entries.what: fermented drink with kefir grains; attributed to the Karachay and Balkar peoples and the Elbrus area; widespread in the post-Soviet space.

entries.heading: Kefir (Greek commercial kefir)
entries.what: commercial kefir sold in Greece. A 2026 study sampled 32 kefir products from eight regions (Koufalia, Kilkis, Drama, Thrace, Katerini, Larissa, Volos, Attica) and found the bacteria are mostly Bacillota, with Streptococcus thermophilus and

entries.heading: Kefir (kefir; Vindija kefir)
entries.what: a kefir sold in Croatia under the Vindija brand.

entries.heading: Kefir
entries.what: Fermented milk drink with about 1% alcohol and some carbonation; jelly-like texture.

entries.heading: Kefir (Glenisk)
entries.what: Glenisk kefir, sold as a new product by Glenisk Organic Irish Dairy.

entries.heading: Kefir (кефир)
entries.what: Fermented milk drink listed among Kyrgyz dairy foods.

entries.heading: Kefyras (kefir)
entries.what: a fermented drink made mostly from milk, with kefir grains, the lactic and yeast mix that gives it a little carbonation and alcohol. Used widely in Eastern and Central Europe and the Caucasus.

entries.heading: Kefir (natural and flavoured)
entries.what: Kefir sold by Luxlait in natural and flavoured versions; the page says it originates in the mountains of the northern Caucasus.

entries.heading: Kefīrs (kefir)
entries.what: Kefir, consumed with hot meals and also used in soups.

entries.heading: Kefir (chefir)
entries.what: fermented milk drink from kefir grains (a symbiosis of bacteria and yeasts), originating in the Caucasus.

entries.heading: Kefir
entries.what: Kefir listed among non-alcoholic drinks in Macedonian cuisine.

entries.heading: Kefir (drink made in the Netherlands)
entries.what: Fermented milk drink. Traditional kefir uses grains; factory "mild" kefir uses a bacteria and yeast blend and little alcohol.

entries.heading: Kefir (Norwegian kefir)
entries.what: one of the oldest soured-milk types, a nordic kind of yoghurt, made with kefir grains. Norwegian kefir is usually cow-milk based.

entries.heading: Kefir
entries.what: A fermented milk drink made with kefir grains, a symbiotic mix of lactic streptococci, lactobacilli and lactose-fermenting yeasts, producing lactic acid and alcohol. Grains are 5–35 mm and held together by kefiran. Also sold as biokefir (wi

entries.heading: Kefir (chefir)
entries.what: A fermented drink made with kefir grains, a symbiotic mix of lactic bacteria and yeasts; originally from the Caucasus.

entries.heading: Kefir (кефир)
entries.what: a commonly consumed dairy beverage in Serbia that often accompanies savory pastries (per the Serbian cuisine page).

entries.heading: Kefir (кефир)
entries.what: Sour, lightly alcoholic fermented milk drink made with kefir grains; the Russian word for the drink.

entries.heading: Kefir (Arla kefir)
entries.what: Kefir is a soured milk drink made with kefir grains. Arla launched a kefir in Sweden in 1978 at 3% fat; Norrmejerier makes one from northern milk at 2.5% fat.

entries.heading: Kefir (milk kefir)
entries.what: Fermented milk drink made with kefir grains (dozens of bacteria and yeasts).

entries.heading: Kefir (คีเฟอร์, also นมเปรี้ยวคีเฟอร์)
entries.what: a sour milk that resembles yoghurt, per the Thai Wikipedia article. Phukamyao uses goat-milk kefir as its culture.

entries.heading: Kephyr (kefir)
entries.what: Fermented milk drink made with kefir grains. Sold in urban Turkmenistan as a traditional beverage.

entries.heading: Kefir
entries.what: a kefir drink made with kefir grains (bacteria and yeasts), with Turkish use in the eastern Anatolian region.

entries.heading: Kefir (кефір)
entries.what: Fermented milk drink made with kefir grains, a symbiotic mix of bacteria and yeasts. Listed in the English Wikipedia lists of fermented milk as associated with Russia, Ukraine and Belarus.

entries.heading: Kefir (US)
entries.what: Milk fermented with kefir grains; spread to the US by the early 21st century.

entries.heading: Kefir (kefir)
entries.what: A fermented milk drink cultured with kefir grains. The atlas lists it as a dairy drink in Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan.

entries.heading: Leite condensado (sweetened condensed milk)
entries.what: sweetened condensed milk, made locally by Gulkys and also imported. The report says it is among the cheaper, long-keeping dairy products, favoured in rural areas.

entries.heading: Sweetened condensed milk (leche condensada o concentrada con azúcar)
entries.what: a syrupy product from partly dehydrated pasteurised whole milk, with added nutritive sweeteners, defined in the Food Code.

entries.heading: Sweetened condensed milk
entries.what: Condensed milk, made industrially. Nestlé built what the article calls the world's largest condensed milk plant at Dennington, Victoria, in 1911.

entries.heading: Condensed milk
entries.what: named by Shahnaz et al. 2004 as very popular in Bangladesh, among the non-traditional products that grew only in recent years.

entries.heading: Leite condensado
entries.what: Milk with water partly removed, usually with added sugar. Base for brigadeiro and pudim de leite condensado.

entries.heading: Condensed milk (sweetened)
entries.what: milk concentrated with sugar; the first Canadian condensery was built at Truro, Nova Scotia, in 1871. Brands named in the article (Eagle Brand, Carnation, La Lechera, Nestlé) are not tied to Canada in the text.

entries.heading: Condensed milk (sweetened and evaporated; Anglo-Swiss, Nestlé)
entries.what: A concentrated milk product developed in Switzerland. Anglo-Swiss Condensed Milk Company founded 1866 at Cham; Nestlé added condensed milk in 1878, and Henri Nestlé is called one of its main creators.

entries.heading: Kondenzované mléko (condensed milk; salko)
entries.what: Milk with part of its water evaporated; Czech names zahuštěné or kondenzované mléko, colloquially salko.

entries.heading: Kondenspiim (condensed milk; magustatud / magustamata)
entries.what: milk with part of its water removed; sweetened form has added sucrose

entries.heading: Kondensoitu maito (condensed milk; sweetened condensed milk)
entries.what: Thick, sticky, very sweet concentrated milk, often used in desserts and baking. Sold mostly sweetened; unsweetened versions also exist.

entries.heading: Condensed milk (sweetened)
entries.what: milk with water removed, usually sweetened, sold in tins.

entries.heading: Condensed milk (煉奶)
entries.what: Sweetened thick milk used in toast, coffee, salad pork ribs, cha jau, and as a topping on Hong Kong-style French toast.

entries.heading: Susu kental manis (sweetened condensed milk)
entries.what: Cow's milk with its water removed and sugar added. Very sweet, keeps about a year unopened. Used in cakes, sweet desserts and iced drinks.

entries.heading: Latte condensato (sweetened condensed milk)
entries.what: milk concentrated by evaporation, now usually sweetened.

entries.heading: Condensed milk (factory-made, sweetened)
entries.what: Milk condensed and sweetened in a factory. Jamaica has had a condensed milk factory since 1940.

entries.heading: Condensed milk (練乳, rennyū)
entries.what: Milk concentrated by evaporation, sold sweetened (加糖, commonly called コンデンスミルク) or unsweetened (無糖, called エバミルク). Japanese law recognises four types: unsweetened, sweetened, and skim versions of each.

entries.heading: Sweetened condensed milk
entries.what: Sweetened condensed milk is a common product in Cambodia, used in coffee and eaten on bread.

entries.heading: 연유 (sweetened condensed milk)
entries.what: Condensed milk, mostly sold sweetened (가당연유). Used in Korean desserts such as 빙수 and in coffee.

entries.heading: Condensed milk (сгущённое молоко; sgushchyonka)
entries.what: Factory condensed milk; exports rose 2.2 times in 2025.

entries.heading: Kondensētais piens (condensed milk)
entries.what: Condensed milk product.

entries.heading: Sweetened condensed milk (in tea, coffee, juices)
entries.what: sweetened condensed milk, the standard sweetener and milk for Myanmar drinks.

entries.heading: Sweetened condensed milk (susu pekat) and evaporated milk, as used in drinks
entries.what: Condensed and evaporated milk are the main dairy ingredients in Malaysian sweet milk drinks and desserts.

entries.heading: Gecondenseerde melk (sweetened condensed milk; evaporated milk)
entries.what: Cow's milk with part of the water removed and sugar added, which preserves it. Popular in the Middle East; diluted for coffee.

entries.heading: Kondensert melk (condensed milk; Viking Melk unsweetened)
