entries.what: milk with about half the water removed by vacuum evaporation, so it is thick and sweet (sweetened versions); the unsweetened version is sold in Norway as Viking Melk. Sterile and canned, keeps for years unopened; 3–4 weeks once open if cove

entries.heading: Leche condensada azucarada (sweetened condensed milk; leche condensada)
entries.what: Milk concentrated with added sugar, sold in tins; distinct from evaporated milk, which is not sweetened. Peru exports it, mostly to the United States, Chile, Puerto Rico and Bolivia.

entries.heading: Mleko skondensowane (sweetened condensed milk)
entries.what: Milk with about 60% of its water removed, usually sweetened with sugar.

entries.heading: Leche condensada (condensed milk)
entries.what: Condensed milk is listed as an import.

entries.heading: Kondenserad mjölk (condensed milk, sweetened and unsweetened)
entries.what: Milk reduced by water removal to about 25% of its volume, brown and syrupy. The sweetened version (40–45% sugar) keeps without sterilisation; the unsweetened version (called evaporated milk in English) needs sterilisation.

entries.heading: Sweetened condensed milk (นมข้นหวาน)
entries.what: milk with water removed and sugar added. It is the main sweetener in Thai milk tea and nom yen, and is poured over pathongko as a dip.

entries.heading: Condensed milk (sweetened condensed milk)
entries.what: sweetened, thickened canned milk, used as a sweetener and an ingredient.

entries.heading: Condensed milk (згущене молоко)
entries.what: Mass-produced in the Soviet food industry; served with tvorog and used in desserts.

entries.heading: Sweetened condensed milk (Eagle Brand)
entries.what: Milk with about 60% water removed and sugar added, so it keeps without refrigeration.

entries.heading: Quyultirilgan sut (condensed milk; evaporated and sweetened)
entries.what: Cow milk from which part of the water is removed, with other processing. In Russia it is usually sweetened with sugar. Used in tea and coffee, as a cream or sauce, and in breads, biscuits, ice cream and sweets.

entries.heading: Buttermilch (buttermilk)
entries.what: the liquid left after churning butter; usually under 1 % fat

entries.heading: Karnemelk (buttermilk, drinkable)
entries.what: Low-fat, sour, drinkable dairy product (informally botermelk). Sold in Belgium, but much less familiar there than in the Netherlands.

entries.heading: Buttermilk (name in Belarusian not confirmed)
entries.what: Buttermilk used as a liquid in polivka soup, added to the stock after thickening with flour and water.

entries.heading: Podmáslí (buttermilk; also cmar)
entries.what: A mildly sour dairy product of about 0.5% fat.

entries.heading: Buttermilch (buttermilk, incl. Trinkbuttermilch and Buttermilchpulver)
entries.what: the liquid left after churning butter from cream, usually under 1% fat. Also sold cultured (soured with lactic bacteria), mixed with skim milk as Sauermilch or Trinksauermilch, whipped, flavoured with fruit, or dried as powder.

entries.heading: Kærnemælk (buttermilk)
entries.what: originally the liquid left after churning cream into butter; today most is made from skimmed milk soured with culture. About 0.5% fat, sour taste. Main ingredient of koldskål. Can be labelled "gammeldags" if churn-made (since 1990).

entries.heading: Pett (buttermilk; võipiim, petipiim)
entries.what: the liquid left after churning butter; about 91–92% water

entries.heading: Kirnupiimä (buttermilk)
entries.what: The liquid left when soured cream is churned into butter. Modern dairies add skimmed piimä to lower the fat content.

entries.heading: Babeurre (buttermilk)
entries.what: The liquid left after churning cream into butter; in France it is also a name used for lait ribot.

entries.heading: Do (დო; buttermilk)
entries.what: the liquid left after churning butter from cream.

entries.heading: Buttermilk (Guernsey buttermilk)
entries.what: The liquid left after churning butter. It was drunk by country people in the 1830s and is sold as a Guernsey Dairy product today.

entries.heading: Író (buttermilk)
entries.what: Sour liquid left after butter churning, about 0.3–2.0% fat; sweet buttermilk must be used within hours.

entries.heading: Buttermilk (traditional and cultured)
entries.what: Traditional buttermilk is the liquid left after churning butter from soured cream; in Ireland it was a main drink of the rural poor after potatoes became their staple and was used for porridge. Modern cultured buttermilk is sold as a produc

entries.heading: Buttermilk
entries.what: Buttermilk listed among the Isle of Man Creamery's products.

entries.heading: Buttermilk (Maasai)
entries.what: a commonly drunk milk product of the Maasai; the leftover liquid when butter is churned.

entries.heading: Pasukos (buttermilk)
entries.what: the liquid left after churning butter from cream; sour, thin and widely eaten in Lithuania, mostly with boiled potatoes.

entries.heading: Buttermilk (lapte bătut)
entries.what: the liquid left after churning butter; a lactic-acid fermented drink with fine casein curds.

entries.heading: Buttermilk (ထောပတ်ရည်)
entries.what: the liquid left after churning butter.

entries.heading: Karnemelk (karnemelk; botermelk informally)
entries.what: A sour, low-fat, drinkable dairy product. Traditionally the liquid left after churning soured cream into butter. Drunk year-round in the Netherlands, most in summer, though its popularity has declined.

entries.heading: Kjernemelk (buttermilk; also kinnemelk, saup)
entries.what: the thin liquid left after butter has separated from cream in churning. Tangy when the cream was soured. Used in baking, soups and sauces. Hardly sold commercially now because butter is usually made from unsoured cream and soured afterwards

entries.heading: Chaas (buttermilk; chhach, chaach)
entries.what: A curd-based drink. Plain (with salt), spiced (masala) or sweet (sweet chaas is lassi).

entries.heading: Maślanka (buttermilk, fermented milk drink)
entries.what: A fermented milk drink. Originally the by-product of butter-making, formed when fat particles separated from sour cream. Now also a sold product, flavoured or blended.

entries.heading: Lapte bătut (buttermilk)
entries.what: A fermented dairy product made as a by-product of butter production.

entries.heading: Mlaćenica (млаћеница; buttermilk)
entries.what: thin liquid left after churning butter from cream (traditional); now mostly cultured milk like yogurt, drunk and used in cooking and marinades; common in the Balkans.

entries.heading: Pakhta (пахта, buttermilk)
entries.what: Liquid left after churning butter; drunk fresh or fermented; used in baking, porridges, diet cheeses and as a partial sour cream substitute.

entries.heading: Kärnmjölk (buttermilk)
entries.what: The liquid left after churning butter from cream; under 1% fat, slightly sour and somewhat thick, thinner than filmjölk. Rich in phospholipids, so used as an emulsifier in cooking and baking.

entries.heading: Pinjenec (buttermilk)
entries.what: Liquid left after churning butter; slightly sour drink, also used in bread and sauces.

entries.heading: Buttermilk (Slovak name not given in source)
entries.what: A product made from processing milk, listed in Slovak cuisine.

entries.heading: Cultured buttermilk (buttermilk, US commercial)
entries.what: Pasteurised, homogenised milk thickened and soured by lactic bacteria; the commercial US product dates from the 1920s and was used in baking and as a drink.

entries.heading: Hakeen / laban (buttermilk, soured milk)
entries.what: traditional buttermilk, hakeen in the Wikipedia article. Laban in the flatbread review is described as soured milk. Enjoyed almost daily in some villages where it is most available.

entries.heading: Sauerrahm (sour cream)
entries.what: cream fermented with lactic acid bacteria; "Sauerrahm" is the Austrian term for saure Sahne

entries.heading: Sour cream (Mattas gårdsmejeri; sour cream with potatoes)
entries.what: Sour cream from the Mattas farm dairy, which took silver at the Finnish craft food championships. Also served as a topping on waffle-pan fried Åland potatoes (with whitefish roe) at a food truck, Våffelrakan.

entries.heading: Pavlaka (cream; sour cream; kisela pavlaka, slatka pavlaka)
entries.what: A "vrsta mliječne kreme" (a kind of milk cream). Contains up to 30% fat. Sweet pavlaka (skimmed before souring, 24% fat) is used for whipping, ice cream, parfaits and sauces; sour pavlaka (10–20% fat) is skimmed when acidity has developed.

entries.heading: Smetana (сметана) — sour cream
entries.what: sour cream, traditional in Central, Eastern and Southeastern Europe; Bulgarian form given as заквасена сметана (zakvasena smetana)

entries.heading: Sour cream (смятана; smyatana)
entries.what: Fermented cream, used in cooking and as a garnish. Accompanies cold khaladnik soup and tomato-onion and radish salads, and enriches soups and porridges.

entries.heading: Sour cream
entries.what: named in the 2023 national survey of Canadian adults among fermented foods, reported as eaten at least monthly by many respondents.

entries.heading: Smetana (cream)
entries.what: Cream used in soups, sauces and dishes.

entries.heading: Zakysaná smetana (sour cream)
entries.what: Cream fermented by lactic acid bacteria; name suggests it was originally skimmed off soured milk.

entries.heading: Hapukoor (sour cream; koor)
entries.what: cream fermented with lactic acid bacteria; thicker with higher fat

entries.heading: Sour cream (súrrómi)
entries.what: Soured cream sold by MBM as "Súrrómi" in three fat levels: 36% for firm cooking, 18% for dressings and dips, 9% as a lighter option. Nutrition per 100 g: 9 g fat, 2.9 g protein at the 9% grade.

entries.heading: Sour cream (served with baked bananas)
entries.what: sour cream served as an accompaniment to baked bananas.

entries.heading: Kiselo vrhnje (sour cream)
entries.what: Sour cream used in Croatian cooking, especially in the north.

entries.heading: Tejföl (sour cream)
entries.what: Sour cream, with 16% fat in the Hungarian standard, used as a topping and in many dishes.

entries.heading: Sour cream
entries.what: Sour cream served in kibbutz-style meals and, in Russian immigrant meals, with herring, boiled potatoes and dark bread.

entries.heading: Sýrður rjómi (sour cream)
entries.what: Cream fermented with lactic acid bacteria, thicker and sourer than fresh cream. The Icelandic article illustrates it with potato skins and chili sauce.

entries.heading: Smetana (сметана)
entries.what: Sour cream listed among Kyrgyz dairy foods (with kajmak).

entries.heading: Sour cream (industrial)
entries.what: Dairy Khoury's 500 g sour cream, described as a fermented milk cream made with lactic acid bacteria and mildly sour.

entries.heading: Grietinė (sour cream)
entries.what: a soured cream product with a sour, cultured taste, from thick to creamy, white to cream in colour. Used in sauces, dressings, doughs and stews, and eaten by itself in some cultures as a sauce substitute or to add flavour.

entries.heading: Skābais krējums (sour cream)
entries.what: Sour cream used on cottage cheese, potato pancakes, dumplings and mushroom sauce. Latvia mainly makes 25% fat sour cream, with 18%, 15% and 12% versions also sold; farm-style cream is about 40% fat.

entries.heading: Sour cream (smântână; Moldovan local name not confirmed)
entries.what: the fat that rises to the top of unhomogenised milk; in Romanian shops, the fermented version is sold as smântână de consum.

entries.heading: Homemade sour cream (pavlaka)
entries.what: cream skimmed from the top of milk, sold sweet or sour; English Wikipedia lists "homemade sour cream" under Montenegrin dairy.

entries.heading: Zure room (sour cream)
entries.what: Cream soured with lactic bacteria. About 10% milk fat in the Netherlands. Used in cold dishes, unlike the richer crème fraîche (35% or more) used warm.

entries.heading: Rømme (sour cream)
entries.what: cream or a mix of whole milk and cream that is soured. Ordinary rømme is 18–20 % fat; seterrømme (from the summer dairy farm) is 35 % fat. The 18–20 % version is sold as "Lettrømme", an imprecise name.

entries.heading: Śmietana (sour cream)
entries.what: A dairy product made from sweet cream (śmietanka), soured by lactic cultures. Also called śmietana kwaśna or ukwaszona. Standard fat examples 12% and 18%.

entries.heading: Smântână (smântână; sour cream)
entries.what: Romanian sour cream, a thick cream that is used as a condiment and a base in cooking.

entries.heading: Smetana (сметана, sour cream)
entries.what: Russian sour cream, fat content roughly 10–30% (up to 58% in some); served with borscht, shchi, pelmeni, blini.

entries.heading: Gräddfil (sour cream)
entries.what: A Swedish soured cream of about 12% fat, homogenised, pasteurised and soured with a culture. Introduced in Sweden in the early 1950s, based on Central and Eastern European smetana.

entries.heading: Smetana (cream / sour cream)
entries.what: Cream; sour cream (kisla smetana) is cream fermented with lactic acid bacteria; sweet cream (sladka smetana) is unfermented.

entries.heading: Smetana (сметана; sour cream)
entries.what: Sour cream, called smetana across Central, Eastern and Southeastern Europe and Central Asia. Stirred into borscht and soups, served with varenyky and pelmeni, used as salad dressing.

entries.heading: Sour cream (US)
entries.what: Cream fermented with lactic acid bacteria to sour and thicken it.

entries.heading: Susu masam (susu kerbau masam; sour buffalo milk)
entries.what: A rare traditional product from Kuala Berang, Terengganu, made from fermented buffalo milk. The milk is fermented until it largely solidifies.

entries.heading: Laban (buttermilk / drinking yoghurt)
entries.what: A sour fermented milk drink, the core Emirati dairy drink. Laban is also the Arabic word for yoghurt in the Levant and Iraq. In the Arabian Peninsula it means buttermilk.

entries.heading: Kiselo mlijeko (sour milk)
entries.what: Sour milk named in the Bosnian cuisine article, used as an alternative to pavlaka in Kljukuša.

entries.heading: Laban (لبن; laban / لبن رائب)
entries.what: a salty, thin drink made from fermented milk, served as a popular drink in Bahrain, including during meals.

entries.heading: Sour milk (spontaneously fermented cow milk, Abidjan and Korhogo)
entries.what: Naturally fermented milk sold by vendors in Abidjan and Korhogo; the paper names it as the sour milk of Abidjan. No local name is given in the source.

entries.heading: Leche agria (sour fermented milk)
entries.what: Milk fermented with Lactobacillus, texture close to yogurt or kefir but with a different taste. Eaten on its own with salt or sugar, or with cola syrup. It is also used for ice cream, tortillas, biscochos and batters, and drained in cloth t

entries.heading: Surmælk (sour milk, 1.5% fat)
entries.what: Danish sour milk product at 1.5% fat, named in the milk-types list.

entries.heading: Hapupiim (sour milk)
entries.what: a fermented milk drink soured by lactic acid bacteria; pH about 4.0–5.0

entries.heading: Leben (laban)
entries.what: A yogurt listed in Israel among the fresh, high-quality dairy products available there.

entries.heading: Laban / leben (لبن; liben, lben, laban zabady, raib)
entries.what: A sour fermented milk common across Iraq and the wider Middle East and North Africa. Eaten plain or with spices, and the same word is used for a chilled drink made from yoghurt and water, sometimes salted or flavoured with dried mint.

entries.heading: Súrmjólk (sour milk)
entries.what: Sour milk made from whole milk and soured with lactic acid bacteria. A staple of Icelandic food culture.

entries.heading: Laban (لبن; leben, buttermilk/yoghurt drink)
entries.what: A sour fermented milk drink listed among Kuwaiti beverages, described as buttermilk. Kuwaiti laban is a regular table drink.

entries.heading: Laban (Libyan traditional fermented milk; Latin spelling as in source; Arabic script not sourced)
entries.what: traditional fermented milk made in Libya and Tunisia, and across the Middle East and North Africa; a Libyan study isolated lactic acid bacteria from it.

entries.heading: Lben (leben, laban, liben; لبن in Arabic script)
entries.what: A soured fermented milk drink, sold as a beverage in Moroccan menus and in Morocco's dairy shops.

entries.heading: Sour milk (lapte acru)
entries.what: milk acidified by lactic-acid bacteria; eaten directly and used to make quark and sour-milk cheese.

entries.heading: Sour milk (kiselo mlijeko; kisjelo mlijeko; buttermilk)
entries.what: milk soured by bacteria (or occasionally by added acid); eaten on its own and with dishes.

entries.heading: Kiselo mleko (кисело млеко; sour milk, yoghurt-type)
entries.what: The everyday soured milk of North Macedonia, a yoghurt-type product listed among regional names of Balkan fermented milks.

entries.heading: Susu masam (sour milk, Terengganu)
entries.what: A traditional sour milk from Terengganu, sold in bamboo tubes.

entries.heading: Surmelk (sour milk, general term)
entries.what: any milk soured by lactic acid bacteria, which lowers sugar and raises acidity and thickness, and makes it keep longer. In Norway it is mostly a controlled, culture-based process today, not spontaneous as it used to be.

entries.heading: Laban (salty buttermilk drink; Arabic لبن / اللبن; other names: laban, liben, lben)
entries.what: A salty drink made from fermented milk mixed with buttermilk, with yoghurt added. Cardamom or pistachio is optional. Drunk with meals or as a refreshment at any time of day.

entries.heading: Leche agria (sour milk)
entries.what: A sour-milk drink listed under Bebidas (drinks).

entries.heading: Lapte acru (soured milk; sour milk)
entries.what: Milk that has soured through naturally occurring lactic bacteria, not through added starter cultures.

entries.heading: Kiselo mleko (киселo млеко; kiselo mlijeko)
entries.what: the everyday soured milk of Serbia; the Balkan review calls it the local name for yogurt in Serbia and North Macedonia; Serbia is among former-Yugoslav countries where it is bought or made at home.

entries.heading: Laban (لبن; buttermilk / plain fermented milk drink)
entries.what: The standard Saudi fermented milk drink, widely eaten. Wikipedia describes laban in the Arabian Peninsula as buttermilk; the Saudi dental study tested plain laban as a thin, acidic drink (pH about 4.5).

entries.heading: Kislo mleko (kislo mleko; sour milk)
entries.what: Soured milk, described as common in Slovenia and Croatia and in neighbouring countries.

entries.heading: Kyslé mlieko (sour milk; kyslé mlieko)
entries.what: Sour milk eaten as a staple, mainly with potatoes in winter and with žinčica alongside bryndzové halušky.

entries.heading: Laban (sour milk; churned in goatskin)
entries.what: Sour milk, described in the Tunisian cuisine article as the yoghurt or kefir equivalent; now also produced industrially.

entries.heading: Kysliak (кисляк; sour milk, samokysh)
entries.what: Cow's milk soured by the bacteria already in it, thicker than fresh milk with a pronounced sour taste. Alternative names: samokysh, samokys, kysle moloko, kvasne moloko. Used in drinks, cooking (some doughs), and cosmetics (hair and skin).

entries.heading: Arròs amb llet (rice pudding)
entries.what: Rice simmered slowly in sweetened milk with lemon peel, dusted with vanilla. Listed among Andorran desserts on the official recipe index; named by a small number of respondents in the 2017 survey.

entries.heading: Arroz con leche
entries.what: rice cooked in milk, a colonial-era dish that persisted in the Región Central y Pampeana.

entries.heading: Milchreis (milk rice)
entries.what: round-grain rice simmered slowly in milk until creamy; also called Dicker Reis or Reisbrei

entries.heading: Rijstebrij / rijstpap (rice pudding)
entries.what: Rice cooked gently in milk with sugar until the grains are soft. In Flanders and the southern Netherlands it is called rijst(e)pap; the Dutch article places it in the Belgische keuken category.

entries.heading: Arroz con leche
entries.what: Sweetened rice cooked in milk; a common Colombian dessert and an Andean dairy dessert.

entries.heading: Arroz con leche (rice pudding)
entries.what: Rice pudding, listed as a traditional Costa Rican dessert and as an ice cream flavour.

entries.heading: Arroz con leche
entries.what: Spanish-style rice pudding, listed in Cuban cuisine.

entries.heading: Milchreis (rice pudding; Condéreis; Reisbrei)
entries.what: rice cooked in milk, served warm or cold, as a main meal or dessert. Also called "dicker Reis" or "Reisbrei".

entries.heading: Arroz con leche (arroz con dulce; Dominican rice pudding)
entries.what: A rice pudding flavoured with cinnamon, cloves, raisins and nutmeg, one of the most popular desserts in the Dominican Republic.

entries.heading: Arroz con leche (rice pudding)
entries.what: rice pudding of cooked rice, milk, cinnamon or nutmeg and raisins; one of the most common home and restaurant desserts.

entries.heading: Arroz con leche (arroz con leche; Asturian "arroz con lleche", Galician "arroz con leite", Basque "arroz-esne")
entries.what: A rice pudding of milk, rice and sugar, cooked slowly over low heat, flavoured with orange peel in Spain.

entries.heading: Riz au lait (rice pudding, gâteau de riz)
entries.what: Rice cooked in milk with vanilla, citrus zest and butter, served warm or cold; in France it changed from a soup to a dessert in the 19th century.

entries.heading: Rizogalo (rice pudding)
entries.what: a Greek dessert, rice pudding. The Greek cuisine article links to "rice pudding".

entries.heading: Arroz con leche (Guatemalan version)
entries.what: rice pudding; in Guatemala it is listed among desserts and hot drinks.

entries.heading: Arroz con leche
entries.what: rice pudding cooked in milk. The English article cites a version "made to Spanish recipes" with anise seed, star anise and raisins, attributed to Nicaragua, El Salvador and Costa Rica.

entries.heading: Arroz con leche (rice pudding)
entries.what: Rice cooked in milk and sugar; listed among Panamanian desserts.

entries.heading: Arroz con leche (arroz con leche peruano; quinua con leche; arroz zambito)
entries.what: A rice pudding eaten warm or cold, often with mazamorra morada. The Peruvian version is made with evaporated and condensed milk. Related versions: quinua con leche (quinoa in place of rice), and arroz zambito (a street version sweetened wit

entries.heading: Arroz con leche (rice pudding)
entries.what: Rice pudding made with milk.

entries.heading: Riz au lait (rice pudding, Sicalait)
entries.what: rice pudding made with milk. A world-record version was made at the Miel Vert fair, with milk supplied by Sicalait.

entries.heading: Orez cu lapte (rice pudding)
entries.what: A rice pudding made with milk, listed as a Romanian dessert.

entries.heading: Arroz con leche (rice pudding)
entries.what: Rice pudding, called the country's typical dessert, flavoured with anise, star anise or raisins.

entries.heading: Rice pudding (rezz bil halib)
entries.what: Rice cooked in milk or water, flavoured with cinnamon and sugar.

entries.heading: Sütlaç (rice pudding)
entries.what: a Turkish rice pudding made of rice, milk and sugar, with more than 20 variants (starch, caramel, lemon, chocolate, date, baked fırın sütlaç and regional versions such as Rize and Gaziantep).

entries.heading: Arroz con leche (rice pudding)
entries.what: Rice pudding, sold by Colonial in three flavours alongside flan, gelatins and puddings.

entries.heading: Whey (dairy by-product)
entries.what: named in Afghan dairy lists; no description.

entries.heading: Mohi (whey)
entries.what: The liquid left after butter is churned out of dahi. It is gently heated in making datshi.

entries.heading: Syrovátka (whey)
entries.what: A yellowish-white liquid left when milk curdles.

entries.heading: Vadak (whey)
entries.what: the liquid left after casein clots and is strained out; 8–10 litres of whey per kilogram of cheese; older Estonian name juustuvesi ("cheese water")

entries.heading: Aguat (whey; baduu in Oromo)
entries.what: liquid left after milk has curdled and been strained for cheese (cottage cheese, ayib). In Oromo, the same liquid is called baduu.

entries.heading: Lactosérum (whey, petit-lait)
entries.what: The liquid left after cheese curd is formed, about 94% water with lactose and protein; used in drinks, infant formula, bakery and animal feed.

entries.heading: Sirutka (whey)
entries.what: The liquid left after milk curdles.

entries.heading: Whey
entries.what: Whey given to children as a soft food in traditional Irish diets.

entries.heading: Mysa (whey, including fermented whey)
entries.what: The liquid left after making skyr, soured and used to preserve and pickle meat and fish.

entries.heading: Išrūgos (whey)
entries.what: the liquid left after curd or cheese is made from milk. Named in the Lithuanian dairy classification.

entries.heading: Sūkalas (whey)
entries.what: The liquid separated from curd during cheese or curd production.

entries.heading: Whey (zer)
entries.what: the liquid left after milk is curdled for cheese; in Romania, traditionally made into urdă.

entries.heading: Surutka (сурутка; whey) and cvik (цвик)
entries.what: Liquid left after milk coagulates in cheese or casein production; Macedonian terms сурутка and цвик.

entries.heading: Sharasü (шар сүү; yellow milk, whey)
entries.what: The yellow liquid left after curds separate, used as the base for chagaa and aarts; the sources also call it yellow whey.

entries.heading: Wei (whey)
entries.what: The liquid left after curdling milk with rennet in cheese making, greenish-yellow and slightly sour. Used in drinks (e.g. Rivella), as a food ingredient, in baby food, and for protein supplements.

entries.heading: Myse (whey; valle)
entries.what: the liquid left when milk curdles, containing most of the water, salts, lactose, whey protein and some fat. Sour whey is made by chemical precipitation; sweet whey by rennet coagulation. Historically a waste product in Norway; now used in f

entries.heading: Mohi (मोही; mahi, Nepali buttermilk)
entries.what: The liquid left after butter is churned from dahi. Nepali name मोही; the Nepali article also lists छच्छिका, मट्ठा, मही and छाई as related terms.

entries.heading: Suero lácteo (whey; by-product)
entries.what: Liquid whey left after cheese and other dairy production. Peru generates large annual volumes, mostly discarded; a 2025 review lists fermented beverages, ricotta, confectionery, biogas and protein ingredients as low-cost uses.

entries.heading: Suero (whey)
entries.what: The liquid left when milk is curdled. It is a common ingredient in sopa paraguaya and is released when queso Paraguay is cut.

entries.heading: Zer (whey)
entries.what: The liquid drained off when curd is made; in Romania it is produced when making urdă.

entries.heading: Surutka (сурутка; whey)
entries.what: liquid left after milk is curdled for cheese; contains lactose, minerals and some fat.

entries.heading: Sirotka (whey)
entries.what: Liquid by-product of cheese making; sweet and sour whey.

entries.heading: Umlaza (whey)
entries.what: the watery whey that separates from amasi during fermentation.

entries.heading: Suero (suero; "suero de leche" in Lara, Trujillo)
entries.what: A creamy, acidified and salted milk product used with breakfast and lunch in Lara state; the source warns it is not the same as true whey (suero de leche).

entries.heading: Goat milk (leche de cabra)
entries.what: goat milk has its own forms in the Food Code: whole, partly skimmed and skimmed, including UHT (UAT) versions, with bacterial limits for goat milk at reception.

entries.heading: Goat milk (Red Maradi, West African Dwarf and West Long-Legged goats, northern Benin)
entries.what: milk from three indigenous goat breeds kept in northern Benin; the study says goat milk is an underused resource, with the national goat population large but milk output low.

entries.heading: Kozí mléko (goat milk)
entries.what: Goat milk, produced mostly on small farms for household use or direct sale.

entries.heading: Ziegenmilch (goat milk)
entries.what: goat milk from dairy breeds such as Bunte Deutsche Edelziege, Weiße Deutsche Edelziege and Thüringer Waldziege. Most German goat milk goes to cheese; the article names no other German goat milk product.

entries.heading: Goat milk for processing (leche de cabra)
entries.what: Goat milk that Dominican processors are buying; demand for fresh and aged goat cheese is growing, and processors want to develop aged goat cheeses.

entries.heading: Goat milk (fresh, soured, boiled, yoghurt)
entries.what: local goat milk, drunk by 97.8% of households in Garda Marta (Southern Ethiopia).

entries.heading: Vuohenmaito (goat milk; kutunmaito)
entries.what: Goat milk, which tastes fairly similar to cow's milk. In 2013, world goat milk production was 18.0 million tonnes, about 2.4% of all milk. Largest producers: India, Bangladesh, Sudan and Pakistan; in Europe, Greece, France and Spain.

entries.heading: Susu kambing (goat milk; Etawah)
entries.what: Goat milk, described as best when fresh and raw. It has a distinctive smell from caproic acid, which certain feed reduces.

entries.heading: Goat milk (बकरी का दूध)
entries.what: About 4% of India's milk, the third-largest source.

entries.heading: Kaplamjólk (goat milk)
entries.what: Goat milk said to resemble breast milk in composition and to cause less intolerance than cow's milk. Sometimes given to infants who cannot tolerate cow's milk.

entries.heading: Latte di capra (goat milk)
entries.what: goat milk, mainly used for traditional cheese in Apulia (Caprino, Cacioricotta) and Gargano.

entries.heading: Goat milk
entries.what: Goat milk sold as a drinking milk, listed among Cambodian drinking-milk products.

entries.heading: Geitemelk (goat milk)
entries.what: milk from the domestic goat (Capra aegagrus hircus), with higher fat and solids content than cow milk and smaller casein micelles. In Norway goats breed when days shorten in October–November and milk production stops until kidding in early

entries.heading: Leche de cabra (goat milk, and goat yoghurt)
entries.what: Goat milk and goat yoghurt from a company that started as a small family production.

entries.heading: Goat milk
entries.what: goat milk exists in Rwanda but is minor in the national dairy picture.

entries.heading: Goat milk (fresh goat milk)
entries.what: Goat milk is produced on commercial farms in Saudi Arabia; the Al-Kharj dairy survey included goat farms alongside cattle and camel farms. Traditional use of goat milk is not confirmed by the opened sources.

entries.heading: Goat milk (unfortified, fed to young children)
entries.what: Goat milk given as the main milk to some young children in Somalia.

entries.heading: Goat milk (นมแพะ)
entries.what: milk from goats on small Thai farms. The Thai milk article mentions goat milk only as an alternative for people who lack lactase.

entries.heading: Goat milk (dairy goat sector)
entries.what: milk from dairy goats, a small, low-input, small-scale sector.

entries.heading: Goat milk (козяче молоко)
entries.what: Close to cow milk but with more protein, fat and calcium, and smaller fat globules; acidity about 17–19 °T; less heat-stable than cow milk.

entries.heading: Sữa dê (goat milk)
entries.what: Milk from goats kept by smallholders; goats are increasing in number and dairy goats are 2–5% of the national herd.

entries.heading: Fresh goat milk (Socotra)
entries.what: raw milk from the semi-feral goats of Socotra island, the main milk source for Socotri herders.

entries.heading: Chaka (chakka, chakida; strained yogurt / soft curd)
entries.what: a thick, strained, sour dairy product eaten in Afghan cooking. Named in the Afghan dairy section and in the diaspora study among dishes that remain.

entries.heading: Labneh (لبنة, labne; other names: strained yogurt cheese)
entries.what: a soft cheese made by straining yogurt; dried, rolled and oil-stored forms are also made.

entries.heading: Labneh (לבנה; labaneh)
entries.what: A salted strained yogurt, thicker than Greek yogurt, eaten as a dip, mezze or sandwich filling; the Israeli list describes it as a soft, creamy, tangy spreadable cheese served with herbs and olives.

entries.heading: Labneh (لبنة; labneh, strained yogurt)
entries.what: Yogurt strained through cloth or a bag to remove the whey; the texture is between yogurt and cheese.

entries.heading: Labneh (لبنة, labaneh; labaneh malboudeh; labaneh Jarashiyyeh)
entries.what: A strained yogurt, thicker than Greek yogurt and salted, eaten as a mezze dish, sandwich filling or breakfast dip. Jordan's variant, labaneh Jarashiyyeh (from Jerash), is described in Wikipedia's Jordanian cuisine article as creamy yogurt t

entries.heading: Suzma (сүзмө)
entries.what: the strained curd of ayran, drained in a cloth bag and used as the base for kurut; eaten fresh as a spread or made into balls.

entries.heading: Labneh (لبنة; labaneh, labni, labne)
entries.what: Yogurt drained of whey through cloth until thick and spreadable; salted; served with olive oil, herbs, bread or mezze. Wikipedia calls it "yogurt cheese" in some usage.

entries.heading: Labneh (لبنة, strained yogurt cheese) in Saudi camel-milk products
entries.what: Named among camel-milk products on sale in Saudi Arabia (with yogurt, laban, cream, ice cream, and aqit) in a 2026 consumer study.

entries.heading: Labneh (labaneh malboudeh for the dried version)
entries.what: A strained yogurt, tarter than cream, with a cheese-like consistency, served in mezze and sandwiches. Listed in the Syrian cuisine article.

entries.heading: Suzma / chakka (сузьма; süzme, suzma; чака, chaka, chakka)
entries.what: A strained yogurt eaten across Tajik, Afghan, Uzbek and other Central Asian cuisines; when further dried it becomes qurut.

entries.heading: Suzma (Chakka / Süzma / Süzbe)
entries.what: A thick, strained soft curd made from qatiq (local fermented milk). Also called chakka in English Wikipedia. Wikipedia's Strained yogurt article says chak(k)a or süzme is eaten across Uzbek and other Central Asian and Iranian-Turkic cuisine

entries.heading: Labneh (labaneh; strained yoghurt)
entries.what: Strained yoghurt, salted and strained longer than ordinary strained yoghurt, to a soft, cheese-like consistency. Wikipedia places it in "the countries of the Levant, Egypt, and the Arabian Peninsula".

entries.heading: Strained yoghurt (στραγγιστό γιαούρτι; Cypriot strained yoghurt)
entries.what: Strained yoghurt, widely used in Cypriot cooking both as a recipe ingredient and eaten on its own or as a side to a dish. Strained yoghurt in 10%, 5% and 0% fat versions ranked among the most-liked dairy products in a Cypriot adult survey.

entries.heading: Labneh (לבנה; labna, lebni in Arabic)
entries.what: Yogurt strained of its whey until it reaches a soft-cheese texture, then salted. Common Levantine mezze and sandwich filling.

entries.heading: Yogurt greco (strained yoghurt; Italian name yogurt colato)
entries.what: thick, creamy white yoghurt strained three times to reduce whey, lactose and fat; often sweetened with fruit or honey.

entries.heading: Labneh (لبنة; labaneh, labni; labaneh jarashiyyeh / لبنه جرشيّه)
entries.what: thick, salted strained yoghurt, eaten at breakfast and as a mezze; jarashiyyeh is a very thick version spread on flatbread as a sandwich filling (Jordanian name, from Jerash)

entries.heading: Süzbe / suzma (сүзбе; chak(k)a, süzme)
entries.what: Strained yoghurt from qatyq, eaten in Kazakh and wider Turkic and Iranian cuisines.

entries.heading: Labneh (لبنة; labneh makbouseh, labaneh biz-zayt, labneh Ambaris excluded here)
entries.what: A strained yoghurt, thick and spreadable, tangy and mildly acidic; central to the Lebanese diet.

entries.heading: Labneh (لبنة, labaneh; labneh balls: mkaabaleh / mdahbaleh / labneh tabat)
entries.what: yoghurt drained until thick and soft, eaten as breakfast spread with olive oil, za'atar or dried mint, or in sandwiches. Called "an essential ingredient to the Palestinian pantry" by one source.

entries.heading: Suzma (сузьма)
entries.what: Salted curd-like product from strained katyk or sour cream; looks like cottage cheese, used in sauces, soups, and for kurut.

entries.heading: Labneh (لبنة, labaneh; also labneh biz-zayt and labaneh malboudeh as variants)
entries.what: Yogurt drained through cloth until soft and spreadable, then salted; thicker and tarter than Greek yogurt.

entries.heading: Süzme (süzme; strained yoghurt)
entries.what: Named in English Wikipedia among traditional dairy products served at a ribbon-cutting ceremony for new housing.

entries.heading: Süzme yoğurt (strained yoghurt, labneh-type)
entries.what: a thick yoghurt strained in cloth bags to remove whey; also called labneh, kese yoğurdu, torba yoğurdu.

entries.heading: Suzma (chak(k)a, süzme; Uzbek Latin "suzma")
entries.what: Qatiq drained through a cloth bag, leaving a thick, spreadable product. Eaten across Uzbek, Tajik, Tatar, Afghan and other Central Asian cuisines.

entries.heading: Goat cheese (Woolwich Dairy and Montchevre, Ontario and Quebec goat dairies)
entries.what: goat cheese made by two producers that Saputo acquired, per the Saputo article's citation titles: "Saputo buys goat cheesemaker Woolwich Dairy" and "Saputo completes acquisition of Montchevre Goat Cheese".

entries.heading: Chilean goat cheese (queso de cabra)
entries.what: Goat cheese made artisanally in rural zones of Chile, mainly in the Valle del Limarí area (Coquimbo Region, north-central Chile), per the Spanish Wikipedia article on goat cheese.

entries.heading: Ziegenkäse (goat cheese)
entries.what: cheese made from goat milk. In Germany, a cheese declared as Ziegenkäse must be 100% goat milk (Käseverordnung, §14, 8). Varieties run from fresh and soft through mould-ripened to hard, with flavours from mild and creamy to strongly aromati

entries.heading: Gedeost (goat cheese)
entries.what: the Danish term for goat cheese.

entries.heading: Goat cheese (queso de cabra; fresh and aged)
entries.what: Goat cheese whose demand is growing in the Dominican Republic; processors buy goat milk and plants want to develop aged goat cheeses.

entries.heading: Kutunjuusto (vuohenjuusto; goat cheese)
entries.what: A Finnish goat cheese, made in places such as Häme.

entries.heading: Kecskesajt (kecskesajt; goat cheese)
entries.what: any cheese made from goat's milk; the Hungarian article says many kinds of kecskesajt are made in Hungary, and some are blended with cow's milk into csemegesajtok (gourmet cheeses).

entries.heading: Caprino (Caprino di Urbino)
entries.what: A goat cheese in the Marche, named as Caprino di Urbino in one list; the regional traditional list names "caprino" generally.

entries.heading: Caprino (Abruzzo)
entries.what: a goat's-milk cheese recognised as a traditional product of Abruzzo.

entries.heading: Caprino (goat cheese, Molise row)
entries.what: A goat cheese listed in the Molise row of the national table of traditional products.

entries.heading: Caprino (goat's milk, family name; PAT in Basilicata)
entries.what: A family of creamy cheeses, soft or semi-hard, traditionally made from goat's milk in several Italian regions. Cow's milk has replaced goat's milk in many versions; caprino sold today is usually cow's milk unless the label says otherwise.

entries.heading: Caprino (goat cheese, raw paste)
entries.what: A goat cheese listed among Sardinian cheeses.

entries.heading: Caprino
entries.what: a goat's-milk cheese; fresco (soft, aged only days) and stagionato (aged 20–40 days or more, saltier and tangier).

entries.heading: Fromage de chèvre (Tiviski goat cheese, unnamed)
Queso de cabra (Peruvian goat cheese)
entries.what: Goat cheese made in small artisanal dairies in northern Peru (Cajamarca's Chugur sells one; Piura is the main goat region).

entries.heading: Getost (goat cheese)
entries.what: The Swedish name for goat cheese generally; the Swedish article notes the caprylic flavour and cites organic and artificial rind forms.

entries.heading: Goat cheese (fromage de chèvre; no local name found)
entries.what: Goat's milk cheese on sale in Senegal, in supermarkets and mini-markets in cities and tourist areas, and supplied to hotels and restaurants.

entries.heading: Queso de cabra (Falcón)
entries.what: Goat cheese listed among the local foods of Falcón state.

entries.heading: Fresh cow's milk (cow milk, self-sufficient supply)
entries.what: Fresh cow's milk produced on the island, which the sources describe as one of the few farm products Barbados does not have to import.

entries.heading: Milk, fresh (حليب; cow milk)
entries.what: liquid milk, used as a drink and in tea and some sweets in Bahrain. Low-fat milk is the advice given in national dietary guidance.

entries.heading: Fresh cow's milk (whole, reduced-fat and lactose-free)
entries.what: Commercial fresh milk widely consumed in Cyprus. Whole (3% fat), reduced-fat (1.5%) and lactose-free milk were among the most-liked dairy products.

entries.heading: Milk, fresh (cattle; drunk with grains)
entries.what: Milk eaten as a staple with grain-based food by the Fulakunda, a Fula sub-group living in the Guinea-Bissau area.

entries.heading: Susu sapi (fresh cow's milk)
entries.what: Cow's milk, which in the early 20th century began gaining popularity as a drink in Indonesia. Whole milk is defined as at least 3.25% milk fat and 8.25% non-fat solids.

entries.heading: Cow milk (गाय का दूध)
entries.what: About 47% of milk in 2017–18 (cross-bred 26%, indigenous 10%, non-descript 10%, exotic 1%); exotic cow yields about 11.5 kg/day, indigenous about 3.7 kg/day.

entries.heading: Fresh cow's milk
entries.what: Fresh milk sold from small farms near Phnom Penh, in Takeo and in Preah Vihear province.

entries.heading: Fènè (fènè; sour milk, cow milk)
entries.what: a traditional Malian sour milk, described as a fermented cow-milk product sold in Mali and among the most studied Malian dairy products.

entries.heading: Fresh cow's milk (နွားနို့)
entries.what: cow's milk, which the Burmese-language page says people of all ages commonly drink.

entries.heading: Nono (Fulani fermented milk)
entries.what: a fermented milk product made in Nigeria and West Africa, especially in Fulani settlements.

entries.heading: Nono (nono; cow milk, spontaneously fermented)
entries.what: A spontaneously fermented cow's milk, the main Fulani/Hausa dairy drink of northern Nigeria, sold by milkmaids in calabashes and markets.

entries.heading: Kumelk (cow milk, drinking milk types)
entries.what: the most drunk milk in the western world. Norwegian sweet milk: whole 3.8 % fat, lettmelk 0.7–1.5 %, extra light 0.5–0.7 %, skimmed 0.1 %, flavoured (chocolate, strawberry); also lactose-free and lactose-reduced milk, organic milk and long-

entries.heading: Fresh cow's milk (lait de vache frais; local dairy in Tahiti)
entries.what: Fresh cow's milk produced locally and drunk, reported in the mid-1960s to mid-1970s mainly in Tahiti and, less often, Raiatea in the Society Islands. Not reported in other archipelagos.

entries.heading: Leche fresca (fresh cow's milk)
entries.what: Ordinary fresh milk sold in Puerto Rico; the industry article names it among the products the island's farms supply.

entries.heading: Fresh cow's milk (Baladna)
entries.what: Fresh cow's milk and processed dairy sold in Qatar by the national dairy company Baladna.

entries.heading: Fresh cow's milk (raw and heat-treated)
entries.what: Full-fat fresh milk sold in Saudi Arabia (tested as Almarai full-fat fresh milk). Raw milk is also sold directly from farms.

entries.heading: Fresh cow's milk (lait de vache, raw; Mahoran local name not found)
entries.what: the only milk produced on Mayotte; about 22% of the bovine herd is kept for milk

entries.heading: Qeymar (قيمر; geimar, kaymak)
entries.what: A creamy dairy product, similar to clotted cream, made across the Balkans, Turkey, Iran and Central Asia; listed in the Arabic Iraqi cuisine article's Dairy section.

entries.heading: Kajmak (also skorup in Montenegro)
entries.what: Creamy, slightly sour dairy product. Traditional in the Balkans; in Montenegro around Durmitor and Sinjavina.

entries.heading: Kajmak (kajmak / skorup)
entries.what: a creamy, sour, ripened milk-fat product used at breakfast and in sandwiches and dishes (for example, Karađorđeva šnicla and urnebes)

entries.heading: Qishta / gishta (clotted cream, milk skin)
entries.what: Cream used as a filling in desserts, notably in Levantine halawet el jibn and in qatayef.

entries.heading: Qaimak / qaymaq (clotted cream; Persian sarshir; Afghan "khame" in one paper)
entries.what: a creamy layer skimmed from simmered milk; thinner in Afghanistan than the Turkish kaymak.

entries.heading: Kajmak / ajkë / maza (kaymak, skimmed boiled-milk cream)
entries.what: rich cream with about 60% milk fat, eaten at breakfast and as a dessert, or as an appetiser or condiment; Albanians call it ajkë, maza or kajmak, and consider it a national dish

entries.heading: Kaymak (kaymak; cream skimmed from boiled milk)
entries.what: a thick cream skimmed from the surface of slowly boiled milk. The English article's infobox lists Azerbaijan among the places where it is made, with Afghanistan and Kyrgyzstan.

entries.heading: Kajmak (kajmak; kaymak, kajmaku in other languages)
entries.what: A soft, creamy dairy product with a mildly sour taste, about 60% milk fat, made by fermenting the fat that separates from cooked milk. Bosnian wiki describes it as an aged and young form; young is milder, aged is sharper and yellowish.

entries.heading: Kaymak (каймак)
entries.what: a creamy, clotted-cream-like product with about 60% milk fat, pale yellow, sweet-sour; called a national meal by Bulgarians along with Bosnians, Montenegrins, Serbs and Albanians (en.wikipedia)

entries.heading: Clotted cream (Cornish clotted cream; Devon clotted cream)
entries.what: thick, very high-fat cream served with scones and jam in a cream tea; a product of South West England.

entries.heading: Kajmak (kajmak, kaymak; fermented fat cream)
entries.what: a fermented cream made from the fat skimmed off boiled raw milk; used as a spread and as an ingredient, for example in basa pomješa from Lika (see the cheese file).

entries.heading: Qaymaq / kaymak (қаймақ; qaymoq)
entries.what: Thick cream skimmed from boiled milk; served with tea or bread; very high fat (about 60%).

entries.heading: Kajmak (skorup) (кајмак; скорупа/скоруп in Montenegro; kaymak)
entries.what: a creamy, sour, buttery product made from the fat that forms on boiled and cooled milk; sits between cheese and butter. In Montenegro the name skorup is common and it is a national meal.

entries.heading: Kajmak (кајмак; kaymak, cream-like dairy)
entries.what: A thick, creamy dairy food with about 60% milk fat and a slightly sour taste; in the Balkans it can be salted and ripened into a butter-like product.

entries.heading: Kajmak (sweet cooked milk-sugar spread/mass)
entries.what: A very sweet, thick, chewy mass made from milk or cream cooked with sugar. Different from Turkish kajmak (a buffalo-milk cream).

entries.heading: Kajmak (кајмак; stari/zreli kajmak; also called kaymak)
entries.what: thick, creamy, about 60% milk fat; eaten at breakfast with bread (lepinja s kajmakom), in pljeskavica and Karađorđeva šnicla; in western Serbia it is a traditional household product sold at open markets.

entries.heading: Kaymak (qaymoq; Tajik қаймоқ)
entries.what: rich high-fat clotted cream served in the appetizer spread and at breakfast with bread.

entries.heading: Kaymak (clotted cream)
entries.what: a thick clotted cream about 60% milk fat, served with desserts (künefe, kadayıf, katmer) and for breakfast; Afyon is named as a buffalo kaymak centre.

entries.heading: Qaymoq (qaymoq; cream)
entries.what: Cream, traditionally skimmed from milk. Today made at 10%, 20% or 35% fat, pasteurised and sold in jars or cartons. Most of it is turned into butter, sour cream and ice cream.

entries.heading: Feta (φέτα; Greek name only in local script)
entries.what: The protected brined white cheese of mainland Greece; its PDO area includes Macedonia and Thrace, so the region is inside it.

entries.heading: Feta (Φέτα)
entries.what: Greece's national brined cheese, made across mainland Greece and Lesbos, including Central Macedonia. Stored in brine and sold in blocks.

entries.heading: Feta (Φέτα; Feta)
entries.what: Greece's best-known PDO cheese, brined in a tub.

entries.heading: Feta (Φέτα), Epirus artisanal example
entries.what: Greece's best-known brined sheep-milk cheese. Epirus is in the mainland PDO area.

entries.heading: Feta (φέτα)
entries.what: The Greek PDO brined white cheese; protected area is mainland Greece plus Lesbos Prefecture.

entries.heading: Feta (Φέτα)
entries.what: The best-known Greek white brined cheese

entries.heading: Feta (Φέτα, ΠΟΠ)
entries.what: the PDO cheese of Greece, made from sheep (or mixed sheep and goat) milk, matured in brine.

entries.heading: Φέτα (Feta; PDO; mainland Greece)
entries.what: Greece's best-known brined cheese, protected by a PDO that covers mainland Greece and Lesbos.

entries.heading: Feta (Φέτα; PDO)
entries.what: Greece's best-known brined cheese, protected as PDO across mainland Greece and Lesbos; Peloponnese is one of the PDO areas.

entries.heading: Feta (Φέτα; Π.Ο.Π. Mainland Greece and Lesbos)
entries.what: Greece's best-known brined white cheese. It is the most widely sold Greek cheese, protected by PDO status.

entries.heading: Feta (فيتا)
entries.what: Named as one of the cheeses in Iraqi cuisine and as a common filling for burek.

entries.heading: Feta
entries.what: a brined white cheese made in Kenya by several dairies.

entries.heading: Feta (made in Mexico)
entries.what: A Greek-style brined cheese also made in Mexico.

entries.heading: Feta (Omaruru cheese)
entries.what: One of the cheeses made by Tinkie Cornelissen in Omaruru.

entries.heading: Feta (feta cheese; local name not found)
entries.what: a feta cheese named as one of the products in Eswatini Dairy Board farmer training.

entries.heading: Feta (Phukamyao)
entries.what: feta made by the Phukamyao goat farm, added after its fresh products.

entries.heading: Lattella (milk, Berglandmilch)
entries.what: a product in the Berglandmilch milk range

entries.heading: Milk (fresh/raw; miraɗam in Fulfulde)
entries.what: Fresh milk is the basis of Peul diet and one of the most common drinks, drunk throughout the day with sweet mint tea.

entries.heading: Mléko (fresh, pasteurised, UHT, flavoured milk)
entries.what: Raw, pasteurised, UHT (long-life), and flavoured milk (e.g. chocolate, ochucené).

entries.heading: Trinkmilch (raw, Vorzugsmilch, pasteurised, ESL, UHT, sterilised; cow milk)
entries.what: legal drinking milk types. Rohmilch (raw) 3.5–5.0% fat, sold only from the farm; Vorzugsmilch (raw quality, filtered and packaged for retail) 3.5–4.0%; Vollmilch at least 3.5%; fettarme 1.5–2.7%; Magermilch up to 0.5%.

entries.heading: Piim (milk; piim)
entries.what: the basic dairy drink; the Estonian word covers both raw and processed milk

entries.heading: Milk (mjólk; cow's milk, whole/semi-skimmed/low-fat/skimmed)
entries.what: Everyday drinking and cooking milk, sold in four fat grades: whole "Mjólk" (about 3.5% fat), "Millummjólk" (about 1.5%), "Lættimjólk" (about 0.5%) and "Soltimjólk" (about 0.1%).

entries.heading: 우유 (milk; pasteurised, homogenised, UHT, sterilised)
entries.what: Ordinary drinking milk in Korea (흰우유, 저지방우유, 무지방우유, 멸균우유). Also called 소젖, 쇠젖, or 타락 in older usage.

entries.heading: Milk (Trinkmilch, Frischmilch, incl. organic)
entries.what: Ordinary drinking milk, consumed as a beverage by many Liechtensteiners. Liechtenstein's milk output is large relative to its size.

entries.heading: Piens (milk)
entries.what: Milk served at breakfast, usually light.

entries.heading: Milk (fresh, heat-treated or unspecified, consumed in Martinique)
entries.what: Milk as the largest dairy subgroup in the diet model for Guadeloupe and Martinique.

entries.heading: Mleko (fresh, pasteurised and UHT milk)
entries.what: Cow's milk as a daily drink. Historically a daily drink in the Middle Ages; in modern Poland sold as heat-treated milk.

entries.heading: Milk (leite), fresh/UHT/pasteurised, cow — industrial
entries.what: Everyday cow's milk sold in Portugal, mostly industrial. The Lactogal page lists UHT milk and pasteurised milk, with brands including Mimosa, Vigor, Matinal, Serra Dourada and Milhafre.

entries.heading: Milk (mleko; fresh and pasteurised)
entries.what: milk served with breakfast; small producers sell raw and pasteurised milk and process it into kajmak and cheese.

entries.heading: Mlieko (milk; fresh and sour)
entries.what: Fresh and sour milk were among the main beverages and a winter staple.

entries.heading: Milk (fresh/raw, cow and mixed)
entries.what: Raw milk produced nationally, and the base for all Syrian dairy products.

entries.heading: Milk (type not stated)
entries.what: "milk" is on the survey food list for Tuvalu alongside eggs, biscuits and sweetened drinks.

name: Donor human milk
names: นมแม่บริจาค

entries.heading: Donor human milk (pasteurised, milk banks)
entries.what: Pasteurised donor human milk, given to preterm and vulnerable babies in hospitals. Australian milk banks rely on voluntary donors. The Australian Red Cross Lifeblood milk bank is one, and it is regulated.

entries.heading: Leite humano doado (donor human milk)
entries.what: Donated breast milk collected, analysed, stored and distributed by milk banks; banks also do research and counselling.

entries.heading: Donor human milk (human milk bank, Southwest China)
entries.what: Donor milk is collected, pasteurised and distributed by a human milk bank (HMB). Southwest China's first HMB (First Affiliated Hospital of Army Medical University, Chongqing) follows the Chinese group standard T/CNSS2020-003 (Establishment

entries.heading: Frauenmilch (donor human milk)
entries.what: milk given to a baby by a woman other than its mother, mainly preterm babies whose mothers do not have enough milk. Donor milk banks (Frauenmilchbanken) collect, test, store and distribute it.

entries.heading: Donor human milk (UK milk banks)
entries.what: donor human milk processed by milk banks for premature and sick infants in the UK.

entries.heading: Latte umano donato (donor human milk)
entries.what: human donor milk collected and pasteurised in milk banks.

entries.heading: Donor human milk (human milk bank, planned)
entries.what: Mongolia's first human milk bank is planned for Amgalan Maternity Hospital in Ulaanbaatar, to supply pasteurised donor milk to sick and preterm babies; the Infant and Young Child Food Act (2017) provides for mothers' milk banks.

entries.heading: Leche humana donada (donor human milk; INMP milk bank)
entries.what: Donated breast milk collected and given to premature and sick newborns. The Lima bank (INMP, Cercado de Lima) started in 2010 with Spanish and Valencia support; five banks are operating (INMP, San Bartolomé, Huancayo, Cusco, Cayetano Heredi

entries.heading: Donor human milk (community milk exchange, Tabuk, Kalinga)
entries.what: A community human-milk exchange run by the Abundant Grace of God Maternity Center (AGGMC), a midwife-run clinic in Tabuk City, Kalinga, central Luzon. Donating mothers are screened for hepatitis B and HIV before milk is shared.

entries.heading: Donor human milk (Polish milk banks)
entries.what: Pooled human milk donated and distributed by hospital-based non-profit milk banks for preterm and ill infants.

entries.heading: Donor human milk (Palestinian Territories)
entries.what: donor human milk is treated as the next best option when a mother's own milk is unavailable. In an online survey of 80 mothers in the Palestinian Territories and Israel, objective knowledge of donor milk averaged 3.4 of 6, and religion was

entries.heading: Donor human milk (донорское молоко, молочные банки)
entries.what: Donor human milk for premature or ill infants; Russia has two milk banks (Moscow 2014, Ufa 2017), both closed-mode (only mothers of children treated at the same hospital donate and receive). Peer milk sharing networks: "Молочная мама" (2013

entries.heading: Donor human milk
entries.what: Donor human milk banking is discussed in Saudi Arabia; a 2026 survey of mothers found many support human milk banks, but religious milk-kinship concerns were the main barrier.

entries.heading: Donor human milk (นมแม่บริจาค)
entries.what: pasteurised donor milk for preterm and sick infants.

entries.heading: Donor human milk (human milk bank, Haydom)
entries.what: donor milk for infants from a human milk bank; the 2026 study asks women at Haydom Lutheran Hospital about such a bank and does not say a bank is running.

entries.heading: Dulce de leche (dulce de leche; manjar and arequipe in other countries)
entries.what: a thick, caramel-coloured spread made from milk and sugar, eaten on bread, in cakes and alfajores, with ice cream, and as a filling. Argentina is a principal home of it.

entries.heading: Manjar blanco (manjar blanco)
entries.what: A thick, cream-coloured spread made by slowly cooking milk with sugar until it thickens, similar in method to sweetened condensed milk but usually thicker.

entries.heading: Manjar (dulce de leche; manjar blanco in neighbouring countries)
entries.what: A milk-and-sugar confection cooked until thick and golden, used in Chile as a filling and topping. Chile's name for dulce de leche. Used in alfajores, cuchuflíes, empolvados, brazo de reina, with panqueques, and on cakes and crepes.

entries.heading: Manjar blanco (milk sweet, term used in Chile)
entries.what: Milk-based sweet; the page says the term is used in Peru, Ecuador, Chile and Bolivia. Chilean use of the term is only mentioned in passing; Chilean recipe not given.

entries.heading: Manjar blanco (Colombian rice version)
entries.what: A thick, creamy milk-based sweet; in Colombia made with milk, rice and sugar, a traditional Christmas dish eaten with natilla, buñuelos and hojuelas.

entries.heading: Dulce de leche
entries.what: Milk-and-sugar caramel sweet, listed among Cuban sweets.

entries.heading: Dulce de leche (Dominican name for caramelised milk sweet)
entries.what: Milk and sugar cooked and stirred until thick and golden. The name is also used in the Dominican Republic.

entries.heading: Dulce de leche (in alfajores and other sweets)
entries.what: caramelised sweetened milk. Used in Ecuador as a filling, for example in alfajores.

entries.heading: Manjar blanco
entries.what: a dessert of milk thickened with cornstarch, light yellow to beige, served in small glasses with cinnamon. Used in pastry and bakery since the colonial era.

entries.heading: Dulce de leche / manjar (dulces de leche; manjar)
entries.what: milk cooked with sugar until thick and brown, listed among Nicaraguan milk-based desserts. "Manjar" is listed beside it under the same heading.

entries.heading: Manjar blanco (manjar; sweet filling)
entries.what: A milk-based sweet; on the Panama pages it is a sweet filling for empanadas, equated there with dulce de leche.

entries.heading: Manjar blanco (manjarblanco; manjar; in Peru also a filling)
entries.what: A thick, cream-to-caramel-coloured milk-and-sugar spread, used in alfajores, tejas, King Kong and other sweets and eaten by itself. In Peru it is a national sweet; the name is shared across Latin America, and Peruvian usage is the one descr

entries.heading: Dulce de leche (milk caramel sweet)
entries.what: A sweet spread made from milk, known as "candy made of milk". It fills cakes, is spread on toast, and is eaten with kokitos or buttered mosquitos.

entries.heading: Manjar de leche (white milk pudding; manjar blanco)
entries.what: A thick, sweet milk pudding or custard made with milk, cornstarch, sugar and vanilla; also used as a filling for plantain empanadas.

entries.heading: Dulce de leche (Salvadoran version)
entries.what: A Salvadoran sweet with a soft, crumbly, almost crystallised texture.

entries.heading: Dulce de leche (dulce de leche; doce de leche in Portuguese)
entries.what: A thick, caramel-brown spread of milk and sugar. Uruguay calls it the country's most representative dairy product; its origin is disputed with Argentina, and the two countries proposed it jointly to UNESCO in 2003 as Río de la Plata intangi

entries.heading: Dudh cha (দুধ চা; milk tea)
entries.what: milk tea as a common drink.

entries.heading: Ngaja (milk tea)
entries.what: A popular milk-based tea in Bhutan.

entries.heading: Shai bi-laban (شاي بلبن; milk tea)
entries.what: Tea served with milk, a variant of the national drink.

entries.heading: Milk tea (Turkana and general Kenyan use)
entries.what: black tea bought from towns and brewed with milk; described as a staple for Turkana who buy tea from the towns. Samburu also serve tea with a lot of sugar and milk when possible.

entries.heading: Süt qoşılğan chai / chai bo'shir (milk tea)
entries.what: Spiced tea brewed with milk, sugar and spices such as cardamom and cinnamon. The atlas gives the Kyrgyz name "Süt qoşılğan chai (Kir)".

entries.heading: Milk tea (Kazakh tea with milk)
entries.what: Kazakh tea is strong black tea served with milk or cream.

entries.heading: Milk tea (local name not given in source)
entries.what: milk tea served hot and sweetened in Libya.

entries.heading: Milk tea (chiya)
entries.what: Tea usually taken with milk and sugar; one of the most common non-alcoholic drinks in Nepal.

entries.heading: Doodh pati chai (milk tea)
entries.what: Tea boiled in full-cream milk with sugar and sometimes spices (cardamom, ginger, cinnamon, cloves, saffron).

entries.heading: Shirchoy (ширчой, milk tea)
entries.what: black tea brewed with milk and butter; the Russian-language name for Tajik milk tea.

entries.heading: Milk tea (Kazakh-style, Dashoguz region)
entries.what: Green tea drunk with milk, Kazakh-style, mainly in the Dashoguz region. Milk is added partly to mask the salty taste of local water.

entries.heading: Milk tea (chai ya maziwa)
entries.what: tea with milk, listed as a dairy food item in a Tanzanian diet study.

entries.heading: Shirchoy (shirchay, shurchay; salty milk tea)
entries.what: A hot breakfast drink made from tea and milk, with salt. Served in cups on the breakfast table; traditional for festive occasions.

entries.heading: Trà sữa (milk tea)
entries.what: Black or other tea with milk and sweetener, sold in Vietnamese milk-tea shops; a Vietnamese market for milk-tea franchises is cited.

entries.heading: Fresh milk (cow, sheep, goat, camel by region)
entries.what: plain milk used in tea, desserts and drinks; warm milk drunk with pastries and cakes (Pashtun cuisine).

entries.heading: Fresh milk (leche)
entries.what: the staple milk of Argentina; consumption is about 240 litres per person per year.

entries.heading: Fresh milk (süd)
entries.what: plain milk drunk daily, at breakfast and as a snack, and with lunch and dinner.

entries.heading: Leche (fresh and boiled cow milk, Altiplano)
entries.what: Fresh milk is part of the Altiplano Indigenous diet and is usually boiled before drinking. Raw milk is also consumed.

entries.heading: Fresh milk (pasteurised, local dairies)
entries.what: Fresh milk sold by Botswana dairy companies Clover Botswana and Delta Dairies.

entries.heading: Fresh milk (цэльнае малако; tselnaye malako)
entries.what: Whole cow's milk, drunk and used in cooking. Consumption was under 100 litres per person per year as whole milk.

entries.heading: Fresh milk (breakfast and morning drinks; Mennonite milk)
entries.what: plain milk served at breakfast, with cereal, and as a base for morning drinks such as Milo, Ovaltine and cocoa

entries.heading: Lait (fresh / raw milk drinking)
entries.what: Milk drunk every morning in the north, sometimes at the end of the day, often mixed with coffee; drunk widely in all forms.

entries.heading: Maito (fresh milk)
entries.what: Milk served with meals and used as a recipe ingredient; common in the Finnish diet.

entries.heading: Miraɗam (fresh milk; kossam as general term)
entries.what: Fresh milk in Fulfulde; the general term for milk in Fula is kossam.

entries.heading: Fresh milk (lait)
entries.what: milk from household herds, a major source of cash and nutrition for rural and pastoral households.

entries.heading: Fresh milk (pasteurised and raw)
entries.what: Whole and reduced-fat drinking milk sold in bottles and cartons, with fat-percentage varieties. Fonterra's Anchor is the main brand named.

entries.heading: Leche (cow's milk, fresh and pasteurised)
entries.what: The everyday milk of Paraguay. It is the main breakfast drink and is served in school snack programmes.

entries.heading: Topfen
entries.what: Austrian name for quark-style curd cheese, used mainly in baking.

entries.heading: Tvarog (тварог; fresh curd cheese)
entries.what: The main fresh white dairy food in Belarusian cuisine, eaten in large quantities and used in desserts and savoury dishes.

entries.heading: Fresh curd cheese (imported; cottage and plain curd cheese)
entries.what: a fresh, unripened curd cheese traded into Belize as an import, listed under HS code 040610 (fresh cheese including whey cheese and curd)

entries.heading: Tvaroh (cottage cheese, quark)
entries.what: the Czech fresh curd, the base for tvarůžky and many dishes.

entries.heading: Quark (Speisequark)
entries.what: Curd made from coagulated milk protein, drained of whey; the basic German fresh cheese.

entries.heading: Kvark (quark; Danish "kvark")
entries.what: a fresh dairy product, a Central European tradition that Danish sources list as kvark; natural and flavoured (vanilla) versions.

entries.heading: Túró (quark)
entries.what: túró is the Hungarian term for quark, the fresh, unripened curd cheese; it is central to many Hungarian sweet and savoury dishes.

entries.heading: Cottage cheese, industrial (tvorog; творог)
entries.what: Factory cottage cheese made by the Emil dairy in East Kazakhstan.

entries.heading: Tvorog (творог) — listed here for completeness; a fresh curd, not generally treated as a cheese in Russia
entries.what: Soft white fermented dairy product; sold fat-free to 23%; a staple of the post-Soviet kitchen.

entries.heading: Tvaroh (tvaroh; Slovak "quark / farmer's cheese")
entries.what: a fresh curd cheese used in many traditional Slovak dishes, including tvarohové rezance (cottage-cheese noodles), štedrák (Christmas cake layers) and zlaté halušky (semolina dumplings).

entries.heading: Tvorog (cottage cheese; Uzbek "tvorog")
entries.what: A soft white fresh curd made by fermenting milk and draining the whey. The Central Atlas gives Tvorog as the Uzbek (and Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Tajik) name for a solid, white dairy product made by fermenting milk and removing the whey.

entries.heading: Topfen (quark, curd cheese in Austrian/Bavarian usage)
entries.what: the Austrian and Bavarian word for quark; the German disambiguation page lists it as a dairy product (Milchprodukt) and not a cheese

entries.heading: Tvarog (тварог; tvorog, fresh curd)
entries.what: A high-protein fresh curd, the most common of Belarus's high-protein dairy products, widely used in cooking. Sweet curd snacks (сыркі) with sugar or cocoa, and savoury ones with salt, are packed in bricks of 50–500 g.

entries.heading: Tvaroh (dried or fresh curd)
entries.what: Commonly called cheese in Czechia; technically an unripe cheese from skimmed cow or goat milk.

entries.heading: Túró (túró; quark)
entries.what: Soft, white, slightly sour curd made from curds of soured aludttej.

entries.heading: Quark (fresh curd)
entries.what: A fresh curd product made by the national dairy.

entries.heading: Tvorog (творог; quark, cottage cheese)
entries.what: Drier, firmer relative of quark; a staple for families and children in Ukraine and Russia. Eaten with sour cream, jam, sugar or condensed milk.

entries.heading: Ayran (salted diluted yoghurt drink)
entries.what: a cold, salted yoghurt-and-water drink served with meals, especially in hot weather; sold industrially in 5-litre packs.

entries.heading: Ayran (Uyghur salted yoghurt drink)
entries.what: Salty yoghurt-based drink found in Uyghur communities, popular in Turkey as well.

entries.heading: Airan (ayran; airan)
entries.what: a yoghurt-based drink, usually drunk cold and salted; sometimes carbonated or flavoured with mint

entries.heading: Ayran
entries.what: A cold, salty yogurt drink made by mixing yogurt with iced water, often flavoured with mint, black pepper, lime juice or cucumber. It is found across Central Asia, the Balkans and the Middle East; the Wikipedia article lists it under Israel

entries.heading: Ayran (айран)
entries.what: Cold, salty yoghurt drink made from yoghurt, water and salt, sometimes with mint or carbonation. Listed on the Kyrgyz cuisine page as a traditional drink.

entries.heading: Ayran (айран)
entries.what: Cold salted yoghurt drink from Turkic and Iranic peoples; ancient across Central Asia (mentioned in the 11th-century Dīwān Lughāt al-Turk).

entries.heading: Ayran (aayran; the Dairy Khoury drink "Iran")
entries.what: A chilled, fresh fermented milk drink. Candia sells "Ayran Frais" in 1 L and 250 ml packs, with a 0% version. Dairy Khoury sells a drink named "IRAN" that it describes as a yoghurt drink diluted with pure water and a pinch of salt; the name

entries.heading: Ayran
entries.what: A cold, savoury yoghurt drink made by mixing yoghurt with chilled water and salt, sometimes with mint or carbonation.

entries.heading: Ayran
entries.what: A cold, salted yogurt drink.

entries.heading: Ayran (ayran; airan)
entries.what: A savoury yoghurt-based drink made by mixing yoghurt with water and salt. Sold as a traditional drink in urban Turkmenistan.

entries.heading: Ayran
entries.what: a chilled, salted or unsalted yoghurt drink, the national drink of Türkiye, made with yoghurt, water and sometimes salt; also in the Balkans, Caucasus, Iran, Central Asia.

entries.heading: Ayron (ayran; Cyrillic Айран in other-language interwiki)
entries.what: A drink made from qatiq. It is the liquid left after the fat is churned out of qatiq.

entries.heading: Camel milk (fresh, raw and pasteurised; camel milk products)
entries.what: Camel milk drunk fresh, a Bedouin staple beside meat, and a commercial product in the UAE. Recent UAE studies sampled both raw and pasteurised camel milk, from farms and from market shelves.

entries.heading: Camel milk (fresh)
entries.what: milk from camels kept in the mountains of northern and southern Afghanistan (Meiji); Pakistani and Afghan camels have high yields, up to 30 litres a day.

entries.heading: Camel milk (Australian camel dairies)
entries.what: Camel dairy farming in Australia. Camels were introduced in the 1840s; the feral population now exceeds 600,000. Australia's first camel dairies opened in 2014.

entries.heading: Camel milk (fresh, raw, drunk from a shared bowl)
entries.what: the staple milk of Sahrawi nomads, drunk fresh; also called the "white blood" of the badiya (desert).

entries.heading: Camel milk
entries.what: Camel milk sold packaged in plastic bottles in Israel, shown in a photo caption on the Camel milk article.

entries.heading: Camel milk (ऊँट का दूध)
entries.what: Camel milk is consumed in Rajasthan. A study of about 2,000 people from the Raica community in north-west Rajasthan found regular consumption linked to very low diabetes prevalence (0.4% versus 5.5%).

entries.heading: Camel milk (Malian production)
entries.what: camel milk is part of Mali's milk production, with Mali cited as one of the larger camel-milk producers.

entries.heading: Camel milk (general; no Pakistani product found)
entries.what: Milk from camels kept in Pakistan; the Wikipedia article says Pakistani and Afghan camels are supposed to yield up to 30 litres a day.

entries.heading: Camel milk (raw and pasteurised)
entries.what: Camel milk is drunk fresh in Saudi Arabia, both pasteurised (retail) and unpasteurised (raw, bought direct from farms). A 2025 survey of 2,176 adults found that taste, religious belief and tradition shaped consumption.

entries.heading: Camel milk (N'Djamena supply)
entries.what: Camel milk, one of three supply chains feeding N'Djamena (with cow fresh milk and sour milk); it does not compete with cow milk and is consumed mainly by people from the northern pastoral regions.

entries.heading: Camel milk (US camel dairy)
entries.what: Camel milk produced in the US as an alternative to cow dairy.

entries.heading: Camel milk (Taizz)
entries.what: camel milk sold by a small group of producers in the Taizz assessment area.

entries.heading: Hytteost (cottage cheese)
entries.what: the Danish term for cottage cheese.

entries.heading: Kodujuust (teraline kohupiim; "cottage cheese")
entries.what: a large-grained cottage cheese, between kohupiim and cheese in structure, fat content typically 0–9%.

entries.heading: Cottage cheese (Glenisk)
entries.what: Cottage cheese, listed among the Glenisk organic range.

entries.heading: Cottage cheese (גבינת קוטג', gvinat kotej)
entries.what: A fresh curd cheese named in the Israeli cuisine article and in the Israeli cheese navbox.

entries.heading: Kotasæla (cottage cheese)
entries.what: A mild, unripened, milk-white curd cheese, sometimes sold flavoured (pineapple, garlic).

entries.heading: Cottage cheese (Luxlait Cottage Cheese)
entries.what: Fresh cheese cut into grains and coated in crème fraîche, sold by Luxlait as "une recette de tradition".

entries.heading: Biezpiens (cottage cheese; biezpiens)
entries.what: the everyday fresh cheese of Latvia. It is eaten with sour cream and herbs at breakfast, in salads and in desserts, and traditionally with boiled potatoes, lightly salted herring, spring onions and sour cream at lunch.

entries.heading: Keso (cottage cheese)
entries.what: A grainy, mildly flavoured fresh cheese; lower-fat versions are 4% fat or less. Keso was registered as a trademark in 1958 by Mjölkcentralen, later Arla; Arla has owned it since 2000, and the name is used generically in Sweden.

entries.heading: Cottage cheese (Phukamyao)
entries.what: fresh cottage cheese made by the same farm, named with its yoghurt and chèvre from June 2016.

entries.heading: Chekize (cottage cheese, per the Central Asian food atlas)
entries.what: a solid, white dairy product made by fermenting milk and removing the whey.

entries.heading: Syr / domashnii syr (cottage cheese, quark-style)
entries.what: the everyday Ukrainian curd cheese (сир, домашній сир); used in varenyky, syrnyky, syrna paska and nalysnyky. The List of cheeses also lists "Syr" as a firm quark-style cheese.

entries.heading: Cottage cheese
entries.what: A mild, lumpy fresh cheese with a creamy dressing.

entries.heading: Chekize (чекизе; tvorog)
entries.what: A solid, white dairy product made by fermenting milk and removing the whey. Listed under Turkmen name "Chekize" next to tvorog.

entries.heading: Cuajada (curd)
entries.what: A milk curd eaten in Colombia, typically with melado (panela syrup); used in arepas (Bogotá, Boyacá), desserts, soup, and bizcocho.

entries.heading: Cuajada (Guanacaste)
entries.what: A tender cheese of Guanacaste, eaten with corn tortillas or used in leche dormida (a traditional drink/dessert). The name "cuajada" also appears as a cheese in El Salvador and Honduras.

entries.heading: Cuajada (Ecuador)
entries.what: a milk curd. In Ecuador it is named as the alternate name for the Loja dessert miel con quesillo, and listed among coastal and Galápagos dishes.

entries.heading: Cuajada (Honduran cuajada)
entries.what: a milk curd from Spain that the Wikipedia article says is also popular in parts of Latin America, including Honduras.

entries.heading: Cuajada
entries.what: A soft, creamy milk curd from northern Mexico. Closer to a curd than a pressed cheese.

entries.heading: Cuajada (soft curd cheese, Salvadoran)
entries.what: an egg-shaped, smooth, pudding-like soft cheese and a staple at many Salvadoran tables. It keeps some whey and is not pressed into a solid wheel. Retail listing as queso cuajada at $3.25 in the 2026 elsalvador.com article.

entries.heading: Cuajada (coalhada; fermented milk)
entries.what: a fermented-milk category in the Argentine Food Code, defined next to yoghurt and kefir.

entries.heading: Coalhada
entries.what: The solid part of coagulated milk (whey is the liquid). Eaten in Brazil as the base of labneh, which Lebanese immigrants brought to Brazil.

entries.heading: Cuajada (cuajada con melao; cuajada curd)
entries.what: A soft milk curd, eaten as a dessert or used as filling; in Colombia often served with melado (thick panela syrup).

entries.heading: Cuajada (fresh milk curd)
entries.what: A milk curd served as a dessert with honey and walnuts or sugar, or for breakfast with fruit or honey. Popular in northern Costa Rica.

entries.heading: Cuajada (cuajada; traditionally sheep, now often cow)
entries.what: A soft set curd dessert, eaten sweet, with sugar or honey and walnuts, raisins or fruit on top.

entries.heading: Cuajada (fresh curd)
entries.what: a fresh, mild milk curd eaten in Honduras as in other Central American countries; cuajada is named for Honduras in the English Wikipedia article.

entries.heading: Cuajada (sopa de cuajada o queso)
entries.what: a soup made with cuajada (curd) or cheese, which the Spanish article calls very popular in Nicaragua. The article notes the soup can be made with different ingredients.

entries.heading: Cuajada (Salvadoran curd)
entries.what: A fresh curd eaten at lunch in El Salvador, with milk as its base.

entries.heading: Cuajada (Venezuelan milk curd)
entries.what: A milk curd made with rennet or plant extracts; popular in Venezuela as well as Colombia and Central America.

entries.heading: Halloumi
entries.what: An unripened brined white cheese served grilled or fried.

entries.heading: Halloumi (Χαλλούμι, Turkish Hellim; also Halloumi/Hellim)
entries.what: The Cypriot national cheese, with an elastic texture and a high melting point, so it can be fried or grilled without melting. Also eaten cold, often with watermelon, and grated when aged.

entries.heading: Halloumi (חלומי)
entries.what: Cypriot brined cheese, made locally in Israel and eaten fried or grilled.

entries.heading: Halloumi (حلوم)
entries.what: Named as one of the cheeses characteristic of Iraqi cuisine, with no further description in the sources opened.

entries.heading: Halloumi (حلوم, hallum)
entries.what: A semi-soft white cheese, "not quite as salty, crumbly and dry as feta" (Jordanian cuisine article). Wikipedia calls it a semi-hard, unripened brined cheese from Cyprus.

entries.heading: Halloumi
entries.what: a Cypriot-style cheese listed as made in Kenya.

entries.heading: Halloumi (Lebanese halloum; حلوم, ḥalūm, ḥalloum)
entries.what: A white brined cheese that is sold fresh or aged, and is grilled or fried. Made in Lebanon as a traditional cheese; the Lebanese review says it is widely consumed there.

entries.heading: Halloumi (حلوم; ḥalūm; Hellim; Halloumi)
entries.what: A brined cheese from the East Mediterranean. Wikipedia lists it in Category:Palestinian cheeses and in Lebanese cuisine; the article itself is centred on Cyprus.

entries.heading: Halloumi (Halloumi; Cypriot cheese, sold under the Baladna brand in Qatar)
entries.what: A brined cheese originating in Cyprus, sold in Qatar under the Baladna brand as "Halloumi Cheese" and "Halloumi Cheese Low Fat".

entries.heading: Halloumi (حلوم / جبنة حلومي; also hallum)
