entries.what: A brined, pressed, scalded cheese listed in the Syrian cuisine article and the Syrian cheese category. Its origin is given as Cyprus, with the name traced to Arabic and Coptic.

entries.heading: Hellim (Cyprus cheese fried in Turkey)
entries.what: Made in Cyprus; common to fry in Turkey.

entries.heading: Säuglingsnahrung (infant formula)
entries.what: in Germany, ready-made products are split into Pre-Nahrung (formerly adapted milk formula), whose only carbohydrate is lactose and which is close to breast milk, and 1-Nahrung (formerly partly adapted), which also contains sucrose. Preterm

entries.heading: Infant formula (imported / aid supply)
entries.what: formula given to infants alongside breast milk in the camps.

entries.heading: Äidinmaidonkorvike (infant formula; äidinmaidonvastike)
entries.what: A food for infants in the first months, used when breastfeeding is not possible or not enough. It is meant to meet all of the infant's nutritional needs until complementary food is introduced. The name is recommended by the Institute for th

entries.heading: Infant formula (imported, "formula milk")
entries.what: Commercially made infant formula that mothers buy and give to babies. It is used when breast milk is insufficient.

entries.heading: Infant formula (commercial)
entries.what: commercial formula milk fed to infants in Maseru.

entries.heading: Infant formula (powder, ready-to-feed and growing-up)
entries.what: infant formula, ready-to-feed baby milk and growing-up formula (fortified milk powder) sold in Libya.

entries.heading: Morsmelkerstatning (infant formula)
entries.what: a food product that replaces or supplements breastfeeding; it aims to imitate human milk. Sold as powder (to be mixed with water) or ready-mixed liquid.

entries.heading: Infant formula (milk-based)
entries.what: Milk-based formula powders for infants and toddlers, including a2 Platinum, made under contract for The a2 Milk Company.

entries.heading: Modersmjölksersättning (infant formula, made by Semper)
entries.what: Infant formula sold in Sweden; Semper AB, a Swedish food company, lists it among its products with baby food and milk powder.

entries.heading: Infant formula (US milk-based)
entries.what: Milk-based formula that is the main infant feed in the US, mostly commercial.

entries.heading: Sữa công thức (infant formula; sữa bột trẻ em; Dielac)
entries.what: Formula milk made to imitate the composition of breast milk, for infants and young children under 12 months, sold as powder, concentrate or ready liquid. Vinamilk's Dielac brand is a Vietnamese example.

entries.heading: Qoroot (qurut, quroot, qurt; Dari/Pashto name not confirmed)
entries.what: a hard, very sour, salted curd cheese made from the leftover buttermilk of butter-making. Used whole, or dissolved into a liquid base; served melted as a sauce over kichri (mung-bean and rice dish) and in mantu-style sauces.

entries.heading: Qurut (qurut, dried curd; Azerbaijani)
entries.what: A dried, salted curd made from strained cultured milk, used as a seasoning and as a cheese-like ingredient.

entries.heading: Kurut (库尔特, kurt; kashk in Iran and Turkey; Uyghur)
entries.what: Uyghur cheese shared with Iran and Turkey as kashk; tangy and hard, chewed or grated.

entries.heading: Kurut (Курут; qurut, kurut, kurt)
entries.what: a traditional Kyrgyz staple of the herding year, a dry, salty, sour fermented-milk product sold as balls and used as a snack, a seasoning, or dissolved in water as a drink (suusunduk) or in winter and spring as katyk.

entries.heading: Qurut (Khowar/Wakhi: qurut; "qurutaab" dish)
entries.what: A dried salty dairy product used by Khowar and Wakhi women in Chitral. In the Chitral source it is listed as "Qurut (cheese)" and used in a dish where it is softened in water and served with flatbread and desi ghee.

entries.heading: Qurut (қурут; kurut, qurt, kurt)
entries.what: A dried, salted dairy product made from yogurt or buttermilk, eaten as a snack or dissolved in water as the base of qurutob, which the source calls Tajikistan's national dish.

entries.heading: Qurut (Qurt / Kurut / Qurut; kashk in Persian-Turkic usage)
entries.what: A dried, salty, sour curd sold in balls or chunks. The Uzbek name is qurut; the Central Atlas lists it as a dense, sour-milk dairy product. Wikipedia's Kashk article shows balls of it at Chorsu Bazaar, Tashkent.

entries.heading: Qurut (dried salty curd balls)
entries.what: dried, salty sour-milk product, widely used in the western Azerbaijani districts, Naxçıvan and Ağbaba; also dissolved for sauce.

entries.heading: Kurut (ყურუთი)
entries.what: dense, oblong, dried loaf of nadughi, corn flour, milk and kaimaghi (cream), in Adjarian cuisine. Also a dried product from boiled cream after butter removal (Achara), eaten with corn bread instead of cheese.

entries.heading: Qurt (құрт; kurut, qurut, aaruul)
entries.what: Hard, dried, salty balls or chunks of fermented dairy, a durable steppe food; in Kazakh cuisine described as dried cheese and whey rolled into balls, pressed sour cream dried until white and salty.

entries.heading: Kurut (курут)
entries.what: Salted, sun-dried balls of suzma; kept for up to a month. Russian Wikipedia classes it as a fermented dairy product, not a cheese.

entries.heading: Qurut (kurut; Tajik қурут)
entries.what: small, very hard, salty dried balls of strained yoghurt; the core of qurutob and eaten as a snack or with cold drinks.

entries.heading: Kurut (dried fermented milk)
entries.what: a sun-dried, salty fermented milk product shared across Central Asia and Türkiye; a bibliography entry in the English Kashk article calls it a "Turkish dried dairy by-product".

entries.heading: Qurut (qurt; Uzbek and Tajik qurut, Kyrgyz kurut, Kazakh qurt)
entries.what: A dried sour-milk product, made by drying strained yoghurt further into balls, strips or chunks. It is dissolved in water for dishes such as qurutob in Tajikistan. In Uzbekistan it is sold as balls at markets (Chorsu Bazaar, Tashkent).

entries.heading: Processed cheese (UAE factory: spreadable cream cheese, cheddar in jars, mozzarella)
entries.what: Industrial cheese made at a UAE factory: spreadable cream cheese and cheddar in jars, and mozzarella in shredded form and as mozzarella balls.

entries.heading: Queso Fundido (processed cheese; queso procesado)
entries.what: a cheese made from one or more cheese varieties, with or without other dairy products or spices; cheese is the main dairy ingredient.

entries.heading: Processed cheese (as recorded in children's diets)
entries.what: Processed cheese in the diet records of children aged 2–8 in the Children's Healthy Living study, whose sample includes American Samoa.

entries.heading: Processed cheese (Eesti Juustu Tootmise OÜ)
entries.what: processed cheese made in Estonia by Eesti Juustu Tootmise OÜ, Seljal, Pärnu County.

entries.heading: Processed cheese (English "processed cheese")
entries.what: A packaged cheese recorded in the top five dairy foods of Yap children (4 children). It is not in the top five for Chuuk, Kosrae or Pohnpei. The same item is in the top five in several other jurisdictions (American Samoa, Palau, CNMI, Guam,

entries.heading: Processed cheese
entries.what: Processed cheese was one of four milk and cheese products collected from Kuwaiti hospitals and tested for antibiotic residues (50 samples).

entries.heading: Processed cheese (Sri Lankan market brands)
entries.what: The most-sampled cheese type in a 2024 survey of cheeses on sale in Sri Lanka: 28 of 50 samples from seven brands. Local brands A, B, D, F and G, and imported brands C and E.

entries.heading: Processed cheese (American-style commercial; "processed cheese" class in the CHL intake data)
entries.what: a processed-cheese food class in the Children's Healthy Living dietary intake tables, grouped with dairy other than milk

entries.heading: Eden (processed cheese; Eden cheese)
entries.what: A Philippine brand of processed cheese, first launched in the Philippines in 1981 by Kraft Foods Philippines. Varieties include Original, Singles, Cheddar, Melt Sarap (a quick-melt cheese food) and a seasonal Queso de Bola flavour.

entries.heading: Ser topiony (processed cheese)
entries.what: A cheese-derived product made by melting cheese with melting agents. Long shelf life is its main benefit.

entries.heading: Smältost (processed cheese)
entries.what: Swedish processed cheese, made from ground hard cheese and emulsifying salts; flavoured variants include shellfish, ham, smoked reindeer or mushroom.

entries.heading: Quesillo (Argentine quesillo, Noroeste)
entries.what: an artisanal fresh cheese of the Noroeste, made by spinning an acidified curd, traditionally by women; added to the Código Alimentario Argentino in 2017.

entries.heading: Quesillo (quesillo; queso; Spanish)
entries.what: A cheese served in Bolivian valley cooking, paired with motes (dried, boiled grains). The source describes cheese as a major protein source in those valleys.

entries.heading: Quesillo
entries.what: A cheese the Spanish Wikipedia article says is popular in "zones of Chile and Mexico with different culinary uses". Chile appears in the category "Quesos de Chile" and in the English navbox "Chilean cheeses".

entries.heading: Quesillo (Colombia)
entries.what: A double-cream cheese wrapped in plantain leaf, originally from the Tolima department, best known from Guamo.

entries.heading: Quesillo (Loja dessert)
entries.what: in Loja Province, miel con quesillo, a dessert with honey and a curd also called cuajada, per the English Wikipedia Ecuadorian cuisine article.

entries.heading: Quesillo (quesillo hondureño)
entries.what: a lightly salted cheese that melts easily; used in tortilla con quesillo, where two tortillas are pressed around it, pan-fried and served with tomato sauce, sometimes with mashed beans.

entries.heading: Oaxaca cheese (queso Oaxaca, quesillo)
entries.what: A stringy white cheese originating in Oaxaca, now made across Mexico; adapted from mozzarella brought by the Spanish; sold as balls or strands.

entries.heading: Quesillo (quesillo; Nicaraguan dish, cheese wrapped in tortilla)
entries.what: A soft, mozzarella-like cheese served wrapped in a thick corn tortilla, topped with pickled onion and a sauce of sour cream or liquid cheese with vinegar. Its form is usually square, though braid, circle or rectangle shapes also occur.

entries.heading: Quesillo (Peruvian quesillo; "small cheese")
entries.what: A small fresh cheese of the Andes, made by curdling fresh milk and pressing it into small patties, sold by women at markets and eaten in soups and stews. In Yura (Arequipa) it is also served as a fried dish.

entries.heading: Quesillo (stretched-curd cheese)
entries.what: a fresh, unaged, elastic cheese shaped into long, flat slabs of 300–800 g (usually around 500 g). The main ingredient in Salvadoran pupusas. Retail listings sold in El Salvador are described as Nicaraguan quesillo (the only retail cheese in

entries.heading: Quesillo (Venezuelan quesillo)
entries.what: A local caramel dessert, similar to crème caramel or flan, sweet and jelly-like with a distinct taste.

entries.heading: Evaporated milk (leche evaporada o concentrada)
entries.what: a syrupy milk product from partial evaporation of water, sold sterilised or UHT (UAT) in the Food Code.

entries.heading: Evaporated milk
entries.what: milk with about 60% of its water removed. Canadian evaporated milk must have at least 25% milk solids and 7.5% milk fat; vitamin C and D may be added, and disodium phosphate or sodium citrate with an emulsifier.

entries.heading: Evaporated milk (in tea)
entries.what: Tinned evaporated milk added to tea by some adolescents in the study, in both urban and rural settings.

entries.heading: Evaporated milk (淡奶)
entries.what: Milk concentrated to about 60% less water, sterilised and canned. Classic ingredient in Hong Kong-style milk tea and red bean ice. Brand Black&White named as the best for milk tea (per Wikipedia).

entries.heading: Leche evaporada (evaporated milk; Gloria)
entries.what: Concentrated, sterilised, canned milk; the most consumed dairy product in Peru and widely used in desserts and coffee. Gloria's first product (Arequipa, 1941–42).

entries.heading: Evaporated milk (in karak)
entries.what: Concentrated, sterilised milk tinned for shelf life. In Qatar it is the milk in karak, the spiced sweet tea.

entries.heading: Evaporated milk
entries.what: Evaporated milk is sold in Saudi Arabia under the Luna brand (example only).

entries.heading: Evaporated milk (นมระเหย)
entries.what: milk with water removed but not sweetened. Used in Thai milk tea and in nom yen.

entries.heading: Evaporated milk (evaporated milk, unsweetened canned)
entries.what: milk concentrated by removing roughly 60% of the water; shelf-stable canned product.

entries.heading: Evaporated milk
entries.what: Shelf-stable canned milk with about 60% of its water removed.

entries.heading: Ricotta (or goat cheese, as one food item in the study)
entries.what: a soft whey cheese eaten by Bahraini adults in the same study.

entries.heading: Ricotta (Estonian industrial)
entries.what: ricotta listed among products of Piimatööstus OÜ, with a "Ricotta EST" heading.

entries.heading: Ricotta (ewe's milk, Carlow Farmhouse)
entries.what: Seasonal ricotta made from ewe's milk, one of the farm's fresh products (with a ewe's-milk yoghurt).

entries.heading: Ricotta (poina) and smoked ricotta (poina fumàda), including goat ricotta (poina de caòra)
entries.what: Trentino whey cheeses, fresh and smoked. PAT.

entries.heading: Ricotta
entries.what: A traditional Marche whey cheese, listed among dairy products in the regional list.

entries.heading: Ricotta (sheep whey; ricotta secca, gentile, moliterna, mustia)
entries.what: The usual Sardinian whey cheese, used as a filling in pardulas, culurgiones and rujolos. Commercial ricotta is mostly sheep whey. The Sardinian goat-whey version, ricotta secca, is softer and eaten as a table cheese.

entries.heading: Ricotta (ricotta romana; ricotta di bufala; ricotta salata; ricotta forte)
entries.what: a whey cheese traditionally made from the leftover whey of other cheeses; modern versions often use milk.

entries.heading: Ricotta
entries.what: a fresh whey cheese listed as made in Kenya.

entries.heading: Ricotta (ricotta)
entries.what: Italian whey cheese, used in Monegasque barbagiuan as a filling alongside brousse or Parmesan.

entries.heading: Ricotta (ricotta; Italian whey cheese)
entries.what: whey cheese, widespread in Italy.

entries.heading: Emmentaler (Emmentaler AOP; Emmental, Emmenthaler; "Emmentaler Switzerland")
entries.what: a yellow, medium-hard Swiss cheese with characteristic holes. Protected designation of origin in Switzerland since 2006 (Swiss Federal Court ruling), with a premium "Premier Cru" grade.

entries.heading: Emmentaler AOP
entries.what: A hard cheese with large holes, first made in the Emmental valley in Bern and now made in many cantons. The name came first as a place of origin, not a variety.

entries.heading: Emmentaler (Emmentaler AOP; Emmental)
entries.what: Swiss hard cheese from the Emme valley; its AOP production area is wider than the valley and includes canton Solothurn.

entries.heading: Emmentaler (Emmental; Emmentaler AOP)
entries.what: a yellow, medium-hard Swiss cheese with holes, originating in the Emme Valley, Switzerland.

entries.heading: Emmentaler (Emmentaler AOP, Emmental)
entries.what: the Swiss hard cheese of the Emme valley, made in small rural dairies; the Swiss AOP version has a fixed production area that includes Zug.

entries.heading: Emmentaler (Emmentaler AOP; Emmental, Emmentaler)
entries.what: A protected Swiss cheese. Its AOP area covers several cantons, and Zürich is one of them.

entries.heading: Emmental (Emmentaler)
entries.what: yellow medium-hard Swiss cheese with natural holes, named after the Emme valley.

entries.heading: Emmental
entries.what: a Swiss-style cheese listed as made in Kenya.

entries.heading: Emmental (Swiss-origin cheese; name only in source)
entries.what: A cheese named as a stuffing for a chicken breast dish at a restaurant, L'Auberge Gourmande.

entries.heading: Human donor milk (banco de leche humana)
entries.what: milk donated for premature, surgical, allergic or orphaned infants, and babies whose mothers cannot produce enough.

entries.heading: Lait maternel de don (human donor milk, lactariums)
entries.what: Milk donated by nursing mothers to hospital milk banks (lactariums), given on prescription to very premature babies.

entries.heading: Human donor milk (मानव दूध दान)
entries.what: Donor milk banks in India, mostly set up 2013–2019, with the first at Sion Hospital, Mumbai (1989, called Asia's first).

entries.heading: Human donor milk (Iran hospital milk banks; Persian name not given in the source)
entries.what: Donated human breast milk held by hospital milk banks for preterm and low-birth-weight infants. Iran had 16 active milk banks in university-affiliated hospitals by October 2025, which the source calls the regional leader in milk-bank develo

entries.heading: Human donor milk (Malaysia, online milk-sharing)
entries.what: Breast milk shared between mothers, mostly informally, through online breastfeeding communities in Malaysia. Formal donation is limited.

entries.heading: Human donor milk (MilkBankNG)
entries.what: Nigeria's first human donor milk bank, in Lagos, supplying premature babies in neonatal intensive care.

entries.heading: Donormelk (human donor milk)
entries.what: Expressed breast milk given by one mother to another's baby.

entries.heading: Human donor milk (US milk banks)
entries.what: Pooled human milk from screened donors, given to premature or sick infants.

entries.heading: Human donor milk (sữa mẹ hiến tặng; human milk bank at Da Nang)
entries.what: Donor breast milk from a milk bank at Da Nang Hospital for Women and Children, the first in Vietnam; donor milk also comes informally and through wet nursing (nhũ mẫu).

entries.heading: Kössan (lait caillé)
entries.what: A curdled milk served in Guinea, called lait caillé or kössan, and eaten with maize in the dish Latchiri Kössan in the Moyenne Guinée, central to family ceremonies such as baptisms and weddings. The Fouta Djallon section gives milk as a sta

entries.heading: Lait caillé (Luxlait curd)
entries.what: Curd product sold by Luxlait, described as "frais et sain" and as a product that has stayed central to Luxembourg households.

entries.heading: Lait caillé (French name; local name "sow" per the French Wikipedia cuisine article, language not labelled; no other names confirmed)
entries.what: A curdled, fermented milk eaten widely in Senegal and served with millet dishes such as fondé, lakh sankhal and thiakry. The French Wikipedia cuisine article says it is consumed in large quantity.

entries.heading: Lait caillé (lait caillé, spontaneously fermented milk; "lait caillé" is French, local-language names not identified)
entries.what: The main traditional fermented milk of Burkina Faso, described in the literature as a spontaneously fermented milk product. A 2024 note isolates a Lactococcus lactis starter strain from it and reports it ferments milk faster than the tradit

entries.heading: Lait caillé (sour curdled milk; Senegal, shared with Gambia not confirmed)
entries.what: The main traditional fermented milk in Senegal, naturally curdled. The Senegal milk review calls it the dominant product of that country's dairy market.

entries.heading: Kössan / latchiri kössan (lait caillé, curdled milk)
entries.what: Curdled milk called kössan, served with a maize-based dish called Latchiri Kössan. The article lists "lait caillé (kössan)" among specialities.

entries.heading: Mali curdled milk (lait caillé, cow)
entries.what: curdled milk sold in Mali, sampled with raw milk for microbial quality in a Malian study cited in a review.

entries.heading: Curd milk (lait caillé)
entries.what: a dairy product recorded as a separate category in the Niger household milk survey, alongside fresh milk, cheese and butter.

entries.heading: Lait caillé (lait caillé; kosam / kaadam / tufam in Peul/Fulani usage)
entries.what: The main dairy product of Senegal and the most common traditionally fermented milk in the north. Eaten daily, sold in rural markets, small shops and Dakar at a higher price.

entries.heading: Lait caillé (bah)
entries.what: Curdled milk, locally called bah, used as an ingredient in some bouillies.

entries.heading: Lait caillé (curdled milk; French "lait caillé", local name not found)
entries.what: Curdled milk made in traditional Peul dairies and sold in the local market; the Tridge overview lists curdled milk as a product of the raw-milk trade.

entries.heading: Mozzarella (Estonian industrial)
entries.what: mozzarella listed among products of Piimatööstus OÜ (Kaarlijärv, Tartu County).

entries.heading: Mozzarella (fior di latte, Abruzzo)
entries.what: cow's-milk mozzarella (fior di latte). The page says it is mainly made in Abruzzo in Italy, along with several other southern and central regions.

entries.heading: Mozzarella (fior di latte; Mozzarella di bufala campana)
entries.what: a semi-soft stretched-curd cheese with roots in southern Italy; the best-known fresh cheese of the country.

entries.heading: Mozzarella
entries.what: a stretched-curd cheese made in Kenya by several dairies.

entries.heading: Mozzarella (mozzarella; imported)
entries.what: a commercial cheese sold in Mozambique, recorded as imported trade.

entries.heading: Mozzarella (Omaruru cheese)
entries.what: One of the cheeses made by Tinkie Cornelissen in Omaruru.

entries.heading: Mozzarella (Milka Krem, Philippine Carabao Center)
entries.what: Mozzarella sold at the Milka Krem outlet of the Philippine Carabao Center, in the UPLB branch's list with white cheese.

entries.heading: Mozzarella (as labelled by Hyderabad dairy shops)
entries.what: Five samples labelled "mozzarella cheese", collected from local dairy farms and shops in Hyderabad district, Sindh, for a probiotic study.

entries.heading: Mozzarella (Uruguay)
entries.what: Mozzarella is widely used in Uruguay, in the chivito, figazza, muzzarella pizza, panchos porteños, and milanesa a la napolitana. The Spanish article lists it among the dairy industry's output.

entries.heading: Requesón (River Plate spreadable cheese)
entries.what: in the River Plate countries, requesón names a popular spreadable cheese, linked to the Brazilian requeijão.

entries.heading: Requesón (whey cheese)
entries.what: a whey cheese sold by several Aragonese dairies, including Villa Villera's ricotta-type requesón (bronze at World Cheese Awards 2019).

entries.heading: Requesón (whey cheese, Cantabrian historical mention)
entries.what: a whey cheese made by heating and draining whey; named in the Cantabrian cheese history by Rodrigo de Reinosa as distinct from the cheese (queso) proper.

entries.heading: Requesón (whey cheese, Mallorca)
entries.what: Cottage-style whey cheese sold by Mallorcan producers Formatges Burguera and Formatges Grimalt, and by Muntanya de sa vall.

entries.heading: Requesón (whey cheese, Spain)
entries.what: Soft, granular cheese made from whey; Spanish versions are moister. In Catalonia the equivalent is mató.

entries.heading: Requesón
entries.what: A soft whey-style cheese sold in markets, traditionally wrapped in corn husks.

entries.heading: Requesón (whey cheese, Nicaraguan spelling uncertain)
entries.what: Named in the Nicaraguan dessert list of the English Wikipedia article; no description given.

entries.heading: Requesón (whey cheese, Salvadoran "ricotta")
entries.what: a Salvadoran ricotta, per Culture magazine. Retail listing as "requesón con chile o loroco" at $2.00 in the 2026 elsalvador.com article.

entries.heading: Requesón (Conaprole)
entries.what: Requesón, a curd cheese sold by Conaprole in full-fat, Light (55% less fat) and 0% lactose versions.

entries.heading: Requesón (whey ricotta-style product)
entries.what: A soft product made from whey left after cutting milk, eaten as a spread or ricotta-like product.

entries.heading: Whipped cream (grädde) on the Åland pancake
entries.what: Real dairy cream whipped and served on the Åland pancake, hot or cold, usually with prune jam (raspberry for children). Locally the cream-and-jam topping is called snömos ("snow mash").

entries.heading: Šlehačka (whipped cream)
entries.what: Homemade whipped cream, used in cakes and pastries; served with svíčková (chantilly).

entries.heading: Flødeskum (whipped cream)
entries.what: cream whipped to stiff foam; used in layer cakes, fruit salad, desserts, hot drinks (e.g. hot chocolate). Served with æblekage, citronfromage, risalamande.

entries.heading: Crème chantilly (whipped cream)
entries.what: Sweetened whipped cream, often flavoured with vanilla; a basic French cream preparation.

entries.heading: Whipped cream
entries.what: Whipped cream spread on top of dairy puddings such as Milky.

entries.heading: Slagroom (whipped cream)
entries.what: Cream of 30–40% fat. The name slagroom is legally reserved in the Netherlands for cow's milk cream with at least 30% fat. Tops coffee, hot chocolate, ice cream, pastries, strawberries and advocaat.

entries.heading: Frișcă (whipped cream)
entries.what: Whipped cream; the Romanian name frișcă bătută appears only as an interlanguage link on the English page.

entries.heading: Whipped cream (served on pearl cassava or tapioca)
entries.what: Whipped cream served as a topping on a dessert of pearl cassava (tapioca), sometimes with caramel.

entries.heading: Whipped cream (US forms)
entries.what: Cream whipped to a light foam, sweetened and flavoured; sold fresh or in aerosol cans.

entries.heading: Akkawi (Cyprus listed as a producer)
entries.what: A white brine cheese from the Levant, named after the city of Acre; the English Wikipedia List of cheeses places it in a Cyprus section.

entries.heading: Akawi (Czechoslovak salted white)
entries.what: salted white cheese first made in Czechoslovakia for export to a Lebanese buyer in the early 1960s; the review lists Akawi among Czech market cheeses.

entries.heading: Akkawi (عكاوي; Akko cheese)
entries.what: A white brine cheese named after the city of Acre (Akka), now produced across the region and popular among Arab Israelis.

entries.heading: Akkawi (عكاوي, akkawi / akawi)
entries.what: A white, semi-hard brine cheese from the Levant, named after the port city of Acre. It is one of Jordan's main eating cheeses alongside Nabulsi, per the Nabulsi Wikipedia article.

entries.heading: Akkawi (جبنة عكاوي, جبن عكاوي, جبنة عكاوية; Akawi, Ackawi, Akawieh, Accaoui (Libanlait and Candia spelling); Tscheeky for an aged brined form)
entries.what: A mild, salty, smooth white cheese named after Acre (Akka). Widely eaten in Lebanon as a table cheese, in pastries and in kunafa. Most consumed white cheese in Lebanon per the sources.

entries.heading: Akavi siers (Akkawi; Akavi siers, with caraway version)
entries.what: a Levantine cheese from the port of Akko (Acre), Israel. Latvian Wikipedia records that the company Sērenes piens has produced and sold it in Latvia since 2019, including a localised version with caraway (ķimenes).

entries.heading: Akkawi (عكاوي; Ackawi; Akawi)
entries.what: A Levantine white brine cheese named for the city of Acre (Akka) in Galilee, which was part of Mandate Palestine. Cheese.com calls it a common variety of jibneh baida with a smoother texture and mild, slightly salty taste.

entries.heading: Akkawi (عكاوي; also akawi, akkawieh)
entries.what: A white brine cheese of the Levant, named after the port of Acre (Akka). Mildly salty, smooth, eaten as a table cheese, grated into dishes, or used as a base for other cheeses. Keeps up to about a year.

entries.heading: Cheddar (Australian industrial and farm cheddar)
entries.what: Cheddar is the main cheese of Australia, over 55% of the market per the Wikipedia cheddar article. Australia and New Zealand call it "tasty cheese".

entries.heading: Cheddar (industrial; cheddar cheese)
entries.what: a hard cheese eaten by Bahraini adults in one study; a supermarket cheese.

entries.heading: Cheddar
entries.what: The English cheese named after the village of Cheddar in Somerset, south-west England.

entries.heading: Cheddar
entries.what: A natural, relatively hard cheese, first made in the village of Cheddar, Somerset.

entries.heading: Cheddar (Cheddar; jibini cheddar)
entries.what: a hard pressed cheese, sold in Kenya as an industrial or artisanal product.

entries.heading: Cheddar (Korean-made)
entries.what: Cheddar made in Korea from 1970, after a cheesemaker studied in Europe for about three months.

entries.heading: Cheddar (Omaruru cheese)
entries.what: One of the seven cheeses made by Tinkie Cornelissen in Omaruru.

entries.heading: Cheddar (as labelled by Hyderabad dairy shops)
entries.what: Five samples labelled "cheddar cheese", collected from the same local dairy farms and shops in Hyderabad, Sindh.

entries.heading: Cream cheese (Bega Cheese, Victoria)
entries.what: Bega Cheese sells cream cheese as a bulk core dairy ingredient, alongside cheese and powdered milk. Bulk ingredients make up about 35% of company revenue.

entries.heading: Cream cheese (industrial)
entries.what: a soft fresh cheese eaten by Bahraini adults in the same study.

entries.heading: Queso crema (cream cheese)
entries.what: A commercial cream cheese sold under the Dos Pinos brand. Used as a filling and seasoning in Costa Rican cooking.

entries.heading: Kermajuusto (cream cheese; Finnish high-fat type)
entries.what: A Finnish high-fat cheese type; the name is also used for Valio products such as Ritari and Turunmaa.

entries.heading: Cream cheese (Baladna brand, industrial)
entries.what: Cream cheese, "Original", sold under the Baladna brand in Qatar.

entries.heading: Smetankovyi (Сметанковий, cream cheese)
entries.what: Ukrainian hard cheese made from pasteurised milk, per the List of cheeses.

entries.heading: Cream cheese
entries.what: A fresh spreadable cheese, standardised in the US.

entries.heading: Cream Cheese (Conaprole)
entries.what: Conaprole's Cream Cheese, sold in 400 g and 3.6 kg packs, and a light version.

entries.heading: Flavoured milk (leche aromatizada; leche saborizada)
entries.what: milk with added flavourings, defined in the Food Code.

entries.heading: Leche saborizada (flavoured milk, Lula)
entries.what: Flavoured milk sold under the Lula brand of Dos Pinos.

entries.heading: Flavoured milk (दूध का फ्लेवर)
entries.what: Named as a milk product in an Indian consumer study.

entries.heading: Flavoured milk
entries.what: Milk with chocolate or strawberry flavour, and an infused children's milk.

entries.heading: Flavoured milk (packaged)
entries.what: Packaged flavoured milk given to children as a snack. In a 2022 survey of 447 mothers of 6–10-year-olds in the Balangoda health area, 44.7% said their child was given flavoured milk among packaged snacks.

entries.heading: Flavoured milk (chocolate milk and Shakers)
entries.what: Luxlait's chocolate milk (UHT) and fresh chocolate milk, and "Shakers", flavoured milk drinks in 10 flavours.

entries.heading: Flavoured milk
entries.what: Ready-to-drink flavoured milks and calcium- or vitamin-fortified milks for children and adults, including Anchor CalciYum, Primo and Mega Milk.

entries.heading: Flavoured milk (industrial)
entries.what: flavoured milk sold in Taizz Governorate, from local industries or imports.

entries.heading: Jibneh Arabieh (Arabic: جبنة عربية; other names: jibni, jibna)
entries.what: A soft white cheese with a mild taste, similar to feta but less salty.

entries.heading: Jibneh Arabieh (جبنة عربية; jibni)
entries.what: A soft white brined cheese found across the Middle East; the Israeli list says it is made in the Galilee and Negev.

entries.heading: Jibneh Arabieh (جبنة عربية; also jibni)
entries.what: A mild, white Middle Eastern table cheese, similar to feta but less salty; used in cooking and as a filling in pastries such as knafeh.

entries.heading: Jibneh Arabieh (جبنة عربية / jibneh; also "jibne arabieh", Arabic cheese)
entries.what: A soft white cheese described as traditional to the Arabian Peninsula and found across the Middle East, particularly popular in the Persian Gulf region.

entries.heading: Jibneh Arabieh (جبنة عربية; jibni; jibneh baida)
entries.what: A general Middle Eastern white table cheese; cooked in dishes or eaten as a table cheese, and an ingredient in knafeh-style pastries.

entries.heading: Jibneh arabieh (جبنة عربية, jibni)
entries.what: A soft white cheese found across the Middle East and especially popular in the Persian Gulf region; mild, similar to feta but less salty. Used in cooking and as a table cheese, and in cheese-filled pastries such as knafeh.

entries.heading: Jibneh baida (جبنة بيضاء, salted goat cheese)
entries.what: A salty goat cheese, often made by nomadic Bedouin tribes in the Arab desert, topped with spices, including myrrh, and seeds.

entries.heading: Jibna (جبنة; cheese, general word)
entries.what: the general Arabic word for cheese, given in the dairy list of the Arabic Wikipedia Sudanese cuisine article, and as cheese eaten with bread, falafel and stews in the English article.

entries.heading: Jibneh Arabieh (jibneh baida, "white cheese")
entries.what: A Middle Eastern white cheese, salty and meltable, widely made in the region; Syrian cuisine article lists "jibne baida" as a white hard cheese with strong salt.

entries.heading: Mualebi (milk pudding, muhallebi)
entries.what: milk pudding listed in the Albanian Balkan-sweets section, linked to the Turkish-Balkan muhallebi

entries.heading: Mahalabiya (مهلبية; mehalabeya)
entries.what: Egyptian milk pudding thickened with starch (cornstarch or rice flour), flavoured with vanilla. A variant of muhallebi without the rice.

entries.heading: Muhallebi (mahallebi; milk pudding)
entries.what: a milk pudding (called "milk rice" pudding in the source), used as the custard in galaktoboureko. Flavours include lemon, orange and rose.

entries.heading: Muhallabiya / mahalayeh (مهلبية; محلاية; muhallebi)
entries.what: a milk and rice or starch pudding flavoured with rose or orange-blossom water or mastic; Qamar al-Din popular in Levant during Ramadan

entries.heading: Muhallebi (مهلّبية; mahalabiya, mouhallabiya, balouza in some versions)
entries.what: A milk pudding made with rice or starch, sugar and milk, a common dessert across the Middle East. In Lebanon it is served with orange blossom water in restaurant versions.

entries.heading: Muhallabia (mahalabiya, muhallebi)
entries.what: A milk pudding thickened with rice flour, cornstarch or semolina, flavoured with orange blossom water or rose water.

entries.heading: Muhallabia (مهلبية, muhallebi, mahlabiyeh)
entries.what: milk pudding thickened with rice flour, starch or semolina, flavoured with rose or orange blossom water, topped with nuts or syrup.

entries.heading: Muhallebi (milk pudding)
entries.what: a milk pudding thickened with rice flour, starch or semolina, sold in Istanbul muhallebici shops; the base for tavuk göğsü, kazandibi and keşkül.

entries.heading: Sahlab (سحلب; sahlep)
entries.what: A thick warm drink. Modern versions use hot milk instead of water and a substitute starch (cornstarch or rice flour) instead of orchid tuber flour, flavoured with vanilla and topped with cinnamon.

entries.heading: Sahlab (סַחְלָבּ; saḥlab in Arabic, salep in Turkish)
entries.what: A hot milk drink thickened with starch and flavoured with vanilla, then topped with cinnamon and chopped pistachio. In summer it can be cooled and set, and then it becomes a form of muhallebi.

entries.heading: Sahlab (سحلب; salep)
entries.what: a hot winter milk drink thickened with orchid-tuber starch (salep), flavoured with vanilla and topped with cinnamon and coconut; in summer cooled and garnished with nuts as a muhallebi-like dessert

entries.heading: Sahlab (سحلب)
entries.what: A creamy hot winter drink made with milk, orchid-root flour (salep) or a starch substitute, sugar, and topped with cinnamon. Sold as street food or made at home.

entries.heading: Sahlab (سحلب)
entries.what: a winter drink of sweetened hot milk thickened with salep (or cornstarch or rice flour), flavoured with vanilla, topped with cinnamon, walnuts or coconut.

entries.heading: Sahlab
entries.what: A creamy hot winter drink flavoured with vanilla and topped with cinnamon.

entries.heading: Sohlob (sahlab; sorghum cream with milk)
entries.what: A sorghum cream made with milk, named in the Tunisian cuisine article as "sohlob / sahlab".

entries.heading: Sahlep (sahlab)
entries.what: a winter drink of hot milk flavoured with salep (orchid tuber flour), sugar, cinnamon and sometimes vanilla; Maraş is a major producer of salep flour.

entries.heading: UHT milk (Candia GrandLait; Dairy Khoury UHT milk; flavoured UHT milk)
entries.what: Long-life milk in full-fat, half-skimmed, skimmed, 0% and lactose-free forms, in 125 ml to 1 L packs. Candia also sells flavoured UHT milks (Candy'Up chocolate and strawberry, 125 and 180 ml).

entries.heading: UHT milk (ultra-high-temperature milk)
entries.what: UHT milk sold in Libyan markets.

entries.heading: Leche UHT (industrial long-life milk)
entries.what: Ultra-high-temperature treated milk sold in boxes and bags, one of the industrial milk forms in Peru.

entries.heading: Leche UHT (UHT milk)
entries.what: Shelf-stable ultra-high-temperature milk, named in the local industry as a local product.

entries.heading: UHT milk
entries.what: long-life milk sold as UHT milk.

entries.heading: Leche UHT (ultrapasteurizada, larga vida, fortificada, sin lactosa)
entries.what: Long-life milk sold in cartons, whole or skimmed. Conaprole's range also includes calcium-fortified (Extra Calcio, with vitamins A, D3 and E), iron-and-vitamin whole milk, protein skimmed milk, and 0% lactose skimmed milk.

entries.heading: Sữa tiệt trùng (UHT milk)
entries.what: Long-life milk sold in cans or boxes, sold at room temperature.

entries.heading: UHT milk (industrial)
entries.what: UHT milk sold in Taizz Governorate, from local industries or imports.

entries.heading: Donkey milk (Bulgarian native donkey breed)
entries.what: milk from the Bulgarian native donkey breed, reported as low in fat and energy

entries.heading: Donkey milk
entries.what: Milk from female donkeys, used for milk production in the south-western part of Botswana; described as valued for its health benefits.

entries.heading: Eselsmilch (donkey milk)
entries.what: milk of female donkeys; low in fat and high in lactose, with a composition close to human milk. The whey is sweet-tasting.

entries.heading: Donkey milk (गधी का दूध) — Halari
entries.what: Milk of the Halari donkey breed from Gujarat (Jamnagar, Dwarka, Rajkot), a recently registered Indian breed.

entries.heading: Latte d'asina (donkey milk)
entries.what: donkey milk, historically given to infants and the sick; sold in powder form.

entries.heading: Donkey milk (Kenya, medicinal)
entries.what: milk drunk in some Kenyan communities for its perceived medicinal benefit, mainly against asthma and tuberculosis. Among the Maasai, warm freshly milked donkey milk is given to children with severe coughs or pneumonia. Consumption was repor

entries.heading: Leite de burra (donkey milk)
entries.what: Donkey milk, which a review says is in growing demand in Portugal and other European countries.

entries.heading: Edam (queso bola; queso de bola)
entries.what: A Dutch cheese named after the town of Edam in North Holland. In Gibraltar it appears as "queso bola", the name for the Edam ball used on the local rosto dish.

entries.heading: Edam
entries.what: a Dutch-style cheese listed as made in Kenya.

entries.heading: Queso de bola (Bola de Ocosingo, queso Ocosingo)
entries.what: A ball-shaped ripened cheese of Chiapas; in Yucatán a harder version with small irregular holes; used for queso relleno (stuffed cheese dish).

entries.heading: Edam (Edam; Edammer kaas)
entries.what: Dutch cheese named after the town of Edam in North Holland. Sold in many countries as a standard Dutch cheese.

entries.heading: Edam (Edammer kaas; Edam Holland PDO)
entries.what: A red-waxed ball cheese named after the town of Edam, made since the 14th century. "Edam Holland" is protected since October 2010 under the same Dutch-milk rule as Gouda Holland.

entries.heading: Edam (Peruvian edam)
entries.what: Edam made by Peruvian dairies, one of the foreign-style varieties in national contests.

entries.heading: Queso de bola (queso de bola, keso de bola; Edam)
entries.what: Edam cheese, called queso de bola ("ball cheese") in Spain and former colonies. In the Philippines it is a popular imported/supermarket cheese and a staple of the Christmas table.

entries.heading: Gouda (queso Gouda; imported, used in Cuban-style pizza and soup)
entries.what: Imported Dutch-style cheese that a Cuban-cuisine cooking page says was widely available in Cuba and was the cheese used on Cuban-style pizza; it is also the cheese generally named in a Cuban-style cream-of-cheese soup.

entries.heading: Gouda (goat gouda in Kenya)
entries.what: a Dutch-style cheese made in Kenya by several dairies.

entries.heading: Gouda (Dutch cheese; name only in source)
entries.what: A cheese the article calls the closest thing to Dutch cuisine it could find, sold in a shop.

entries.heading: Goudse kaas (Gouda; Gouda Holland; Goudse boerenkaas)
entries.what: The best-known Dutch cheese, named after the city of Gouda in South Holland, where it was traded for centuries. Most is factory-made; a farmhouse version (boerenkaas) is still made on about 300 farms.

entries.heading: Gouda (Goudse kaas; Gouda Holland PGI)
entries.what: The best-known Dutch cheese, named after the town of Gouda. Traditionally a wheel of about 1–16 kg with an orange-yellow colour from annatto. "Gouda Holland" is an EU protected name that requires Dutch milk and natural ripening of at least

entries.heading: Gouda (Peruvian gouda)
entries.what: Dutch-style gouda made in Peru; winners of gouda awards from Ayacucho and Puno dairies.

entries.heading: Queso Gouda (Conaprole)
entries.what: Gouda-named cheese sold by Conaprole.

entries.heading: Gruyère AOP
entries.what: A Swiss AOP hard cheese. The Swiss cheese list names the cantons of Bern, Fribourg, Vaud, Neuchâtel and Jura and parts of German-speaking Switzerland as its production area.

entries.heading: Gruyère AOP (Gruyère; Gruyère AOP)
entries.what: A hard Swiss cheese whose name comes from the town of Gruyères in the canton of Fribourg; its PDO area takes in several western cantons, Fribourg among them.

entries.heading: Gruyère (AOP)
entries.what: A large-wheel AOP cheese; the protected production area includes the canton of Jura.

entries.heading: Gruyère AOP (Gruyère; Gruyère d'alpage, Gruyère de Gruyères)
entries.what: A protected Swiss hard cheese. The AOP zone includes the canton of Neuchâtel and the Montagnes neuchâteloises, where Gruyère d'alpage is produced. It is listed under Neuchâtel on the French list of Swiss cheeses.

entries.heading: Gruyère (Gruyère AOP; Gruyère, Greyerzer, Gruyère de Vaud)
entries.what: Swiss hard cheese made in several cantons, including Vaud.

entries.heading: Gruyère (Greyerzer, Le Gruyère)
entries.what: hard Swiss cheese from the cantons of Fribourg, Vaud, Neuchâtel, Jura and Bern, named after the town of Gruyères.

entries.heading: Gruyère
entries.what: a Swiss-style cheese listed as made in Kenya.

entries.heading: Gulab jamun (khoa dumplings)
entries.what: a sweet made from milk solids.

entries.heading: Gulab jamun (other names: gulab jamun)
entries.what: Fried balls of milk solids and flour soaked in syrup.

entries.heading: Gulab jamun (गुलाब जामुन)
entries.what: Fried milk-solid balls soaked in rose-cardamom syrup; the best-known Indian sweet abroad.

entries.heading: Gulab jamun (gulab jamun; fried milk-solid balls in syrup)
entries.what: Fried dough balls made from milk solids, soaked in fragrant syrup. Listed among the Indo-Mauritian sweets.

entries.heading: Gulab jamun (khoya balls in syrup)
entries.what: Fried milk-solid balls soaked in syrup; main base is khoya.

entries.heading: Gulab jamun (gulab jamun; Hindustani sweet)
entries.what: A Hindustani sweet made from boiled-down milk, listed among typical Surinamese dishes and sweets.

entries.heading: Gulab jamun
entries.what: fried balls of milk solids soaked in sugar syrup.

entries.heading: Natilla (Colombian Christmas custard)
entries.what: A traditional Colombian Christmas dessert, served alongside manjar blanco, buñuelos and hojuelas.

entries.heading: Natilla (Costa Rican sour cream)
entries.what: A thick, slightly sour cream. It is eaten with gallo pinto, bread and tortillas, and is used in tamal asado, budín, desserts, bizcochos and as a spread on bread or crackers. It is milder than American sour cream.

entries.heading: Natilla
entries.what: A custard dessert of milk, egg yolk and sugar, listed in Cuban cuisine.

entries.heading: Natilla (custard)
entries.what: a thick custard dessert listed among Ecuadorian dishes.

entries.heading: Milk custard (œufs au lait)
entries.what: A milk-and-egg custard dessert listed in French Guianese cuisine.

entries.heading: Custard (other names: custard)
entries.what: A sweetened, thickened dish of milk or cream with egg or egg yolk.

entries.heading: Natilla (milk custard)
entries.what: a custard named as the cream-and-cheese base of the Salvadoran quesadilla, a sweet or savory sponge cake made with rice or corn flour.

entries.heading: Tres leches (milk cake)
entries.what: A wet cake made mostly of milk and sugar. Served after lunch or dinner. Also appears as a queque variant.

entries.heading: Tres leches (cake)
entries.what: A sponge cake soaked in three milks and topped with whipped cream. The Dominican Republic lists it as a dessert.

entries.heading: Tres leches (milk-soaked sponge cake)
entries.what: a sponge cake soaked in three milks, eaten across Latin America, including Honduras.

entries.heading: Tres leches (three-milk cake)
entries.what: A dessert listed by name in Panamanian cuisine.

entries.heading: Tres leches (Peruvian version)
entries.what: A sponge cake soaked in a mix of three milks and topped with whipped cream and cinnamon; widely eaten in Peru, sometimes with Peruvian flavours such as lúcuma or algarrobina (per a Lima guide, not confirmed by the recipe page). Origin is Ce

entries.heading: Tres leches (Puerto Rican version)
entries.what: A sponge cake soaked in a mix of canned and fresh milk, topped with whipped cream. One Puerto Rican recipe site adds coconut milk and calls the mix "a fifth type of leche."

entries.heading: Tres leches (cake)
entries.what: A cake made with three kinds of milk, listed among the most consumed desserts in El Salvador.

entries.heading: Kumis (Colombian kumis)
entries.what: A fizzy, sour, kefir-like fermented milk drink made in rural and urban south-west Colombia.

entries.heading: Kumisz (kumis)
entries.what: Fermented mare's milk, carbonated, slightly sweet, slightly sour; described as one of the most characteristic drinks of the Hungarians before the conquest.

entries.heading: Airag (айраг; kumis, kumiss, airag)
entries.what: The national drink of Mongolia, fermented mare's milk, drunk in summer and at ceremonies. Known as kumis in other Central Asian languages.

entries.heading: Kymyz (kumis; qymyz; mare milk drink)
entries.what: A fermented mare's milk drink, listed in the Central Asian food atlas under its Turkmen name "Kymyz".

entries.heading: Kımız (kumis, mare's milk)
entries.what: a traditional fermented mare-milk drink from Central Asia, historically drunk by Turkic peoples; the review calls it a traditional Turkish drink and "Turkistan boza".

entries.heading: Qimiz (qimiz; kumis)
entries.what: Mare's milk fermented with lactic acid bacteria and yeasts. Drunk by nomadic herding peoples; foams when poured.

entries.heading: Brimsen (Bryndza)
entries.what: Salted fresh sheep cheese. In the German article it is the same product as Bryndza.

entries.heading: Bryndza (bryndza; Slovak name, also made in Moravia)
entries.what: Soft mixed, salted cheese originating in Slovakia, also produced in Moravia and eaten in Czechia.

entries.heading: Bryndza (brindza)
entries.what: a sheep cheese placed in Central and Eastern Europe, most notably Slovakia and Poland.

entries.heading: Bryndza (bryndza; Polish and Slovak)
entries.what: A soft, creamy sheep's-milk cheese made in Central and Eastern Europe, mainly in Slovakia and Poland. In Poland it is linked with the Podhale region.

entries.heading: Bryndza (Balkan brined sheep cheese variant)
entries.what: a brined cheese listed with Serbia among its origins

entries.heading: Bryndza (bryndza; Slovak and Polish; also "Liptauer" in Austria)
entries.what: a white, crumbly, slightly moist sheep cheese with a tangy, strong flavour and a noticeable butyric-acid taste; central to Slovak cooking, especially bryndzové halušky (the national dish) and bryndzové pirohy.

entries.heading: Dèguè (thiakry)
entries.what: A sweet millet pudding or beverage, also called thiakry, made with millet mixed in milk or yoghurt, often with dried fruit and spices.

entries.heading: Dèguè (millet-and-milk dish, given as fermented milk in one source)
entries.what: A dessert or drink of fermented milk with millet grains. The French Wikipedia cuisine page calls it "lait fermenté avec granulés de mil", of Mandingo origin.

entries.heading: Chakery (thiakry, thiacry; Wolof cakri; Fula bodé; Bambara dèguè)
entries.what: A sweet millet couscous dessert with dried fruit and spice, eaten as an after-meal sweet across West Africa. The Gambian and Senegalese versions are the ones the source describes first.

entries.heading: Thiakry (millet couscous dessert with milk or yoghurt)
entries.what: Sweet millet couscous with milk, condensed milk, or yoghurt, with dried fruit and spices. Listed in the Guinea-Bissau cuisine article.

entries.heading: Dégué
entries.what: a dessert of curdled milk and millet semolina, named in the French Malian cuisine article.

entries.heading: Thiakry (thiacry, thiakry; wolof cakri; Fula bodé; Bambara dèguè)
entries.what: A sweet dessert of millet couscous eaten with yoghurt or sour milk. Served as a snack, dessert and at iftar in Senegal and Gambia. A family of dishes spread across West Africa.

entries.heading: Kasseri (Κασέρι; Kaseri)
entries.what: A protected stretched-curd cheese; its PDO names Xanthi, which lies in this region, as one of its production areas.

entries.heading: Kasseri (Κασέρι)
entries.what: A stretched-curd cheese made from sheep milk, with a smooth, chewy texture and a hard rind. PDO.

entries.heading: Kasseri (Κασέρι; Kaseri; kaşar; kashkaval)
entries.what: A pale yellow, smooth, chewy stretched-curd cheese with a hard rind.

entries.heading: Kasseri (κασέρι)
entries.what: A PDO sheep-milk cheese from Greece's pasta filata family.

entries.heading: Kasseri (Κασέρι; Π.Ο.Π.)
entries.what: Smooth, chewy cheese with a hard rind.

entries.heading: Kasseri (כשרי)
entries.what: A pale yellow Greek-origin cheese brought to Israel by Greek Jews and now made locally, used on salads and pizza.

entries.heading: Kulfi (কুলফি)
entries.what: an indigenous frozen dessert of the subcontinent; the Wikipedia infobox lists Bangladeshi cuisine among its associated cuisines; Shahnaz et al. 2004 describes it as an indigenous ice cream, popular in hot summers.

entries.heading: Kulfi (कुल्फ़ी; qulfi)
entries.what: Dense frozen dessert, not whipped or churned (not ice cream); "traditional Indian ice cream".

entries.heading: Kulfi (kulfi; frozen milk dessert)
entries.what: Indian-subcontinent frozen dessert. Denser than ice cream because it is not churned.

entries.heading: Kulfi (कुल्फी)
entries.what: A frozen dairy dessert that the Nepali Wikipedia article says arose in the Indian subcontinent in the 16th century and is popular in Nepal (also Bangladesh, Myanmar, Sri Lanka and the Middle East). No Nepal-specific form is described.

entries.heading: Kulfi
entries.what: Frozen dairy dessert, denser than ice cream, not churned. Listed among popular Pakistani desserts.

entries.heading: Kulfi
entries.what: dense frozen dessert of thickened, sweetened milk, "traditional Indian ice cream".

entries.heading: Qumësht i papërpunuar (raw milk, sold by farmers)
entries.what: milk sold unprocessed, mainly by farmers direct to urban buyers. In the Tirana sampling, raw cow milk was a minority category of the milk on sale.

entries.heading: Raw milk (leche cruda)
entries.what: Raw cow's milk, produced and consumed directly by farmers and in rural communities; consumption linked to beliefs about health.

entries.heading: Leche cruda (raw cow milk)
entries.what: Raw milk is sold and used in Costa Rica alongside pasteurised and UHT milk.

entries.heading: Lait cru (raw milk)
entries.what: Milk not heat-treated after milking; the reference product for French raw-milk cheeses and fresh milk sold on farms.

entries.heading: Rauwe melk (raw milk)
entries.what: Milk as it leaves the cow, the starting material for the dairy industry. The Dutch dairy herd is TB-free, so raw milk is allowed for sale. Farms may sell it, with a clear label that it must be boiled before use.

entries.heading: Lait cru (raw milk, sold informally)
entries.what: Raw milk is commonly traded and consumed without treatment in some areas; it is often sold in plastic bottles in the south.

entries.heading: Burrino / Manteca (burrino, manteca; also butirro in Calabria; Manteca del Cilento in Campania)
entries.what: A seasonal, hand-made cheese: an outer layer of the same stretched curd used for scamorza, with a butter core. Some versions have a ricotta and cream filling. Recognised as a PAT.

entries.heading: Manteca (burrino; Manteca del Cilento)
entries.what: a seasonal cheese: an outer layer of the same stretched curd as scamorza, with a butter core (a variant has a ricotta and cream filling).

entries.heading: Manteca (also burrino or butirro; cow's milk; PAT)
entries.what: A seasonal cheese made from cow's milk fat and leftover whey. Outer shell of stretched curd (like scamorza); inner core of butter. A variant has a ricotta and cream filling.

entries.heading: Manteca (butter)
entries.what: Butter, sold by the dairy industry, and used in cooking.

entries.heading: Manteca (butter)
entries.what: Butter, sold by Conaprole as mantequilla, and used in baking, including the butter-based medialuna pastries.

entries.heading: Mizithra (Μυζήθρα; Myzithra, Mizithra)
entries.what: A whey cheese sold fresh (like ricotta), or dried and salted as a grating cheese (like ricotta salata). Xynomizithra is the salted, aged, drier form.

entries.heading: Mizithra (Μυζήθρα; other names: myzithra, mizithra; also used in "xynomyzithra", the salted and aged form)
entries.what: A whey cheese made in many parts of Greece. Fresh (soft) and aged/salted (hard) forms are both made.

entries.heading: Mizithra (Μυζήθρα)
entries.what: A traditional whey cheese made across Greece; the Wikipedia article's photo caption names Achaea.

entries.heading: Myzithra (μυζήθρα; sweet and dry)
entries.what: the soft whey cheese made from tyrogalo, sold fresh or dried.

entries.heading: Mizithra (Μυζήθρα)
entries.what: a Greek whey cheese, primarily made on Crete but widespread across Greece.

entries.heading: Mizithra (Μυζήθρα)
entries.what: Soft, moist fresh cheese similar to ricotta; also sold salt-dried as a grating cheese similar to ricotta salata.

entries.heading: Panir (panir; fresh cheese, uncertain)
entries.what: a fresh dairy product named in Afghan cooking; the diaspora study lists it both among Afghan dishes that remain and among those that have disappeared.

entries.heading: Paneer (পনির; ponir)
entries.what: the pressed form of chhana, widespread across the Indian subcontinent; in Bangladesh it appears as a dairy term.

entries.heading: Paneer (पनीर; panir)
entries.what: Non-melting acid-set cheese, the basic Indian cheese; widespread across the subcontinent.

entries.heading: Ponir (Bengali/Odia; পনির)
entries.what: Bengali and Odia hardened curd: chhena kneaded into a dough, heavily salted and hardened.

entries.heading: Paneer
entries.what: an Indian-style fresh cheese listed as made in Kenya.

entries.heading: Paneer (Punjabi cottage cheese; fresh acid-set cheese)
entries.what: Fresh cottage cheese widely used in Punjabi cooking, in dishes such as palak paneer, matar paneer, shahi paneer, paneer kofta and paneer paratha. The Punjabi article covers both Indian and Pakistani Punjab.

entries.heading: Panir (панир; pinir, panir)
entries.what: The Tajik-language Wikipedia describes panir as a nutritious food product made from soured or curdled milk, usually yellow, sometimes with holes.

entries.heading: Qishta (قشطة)
entries.what: A creamy surface layer collected from milk heated slowly in shallow pans; used as a filling in knafeh, mafrouke and atayef.

entries.heading: Qishta / ghishta (قشطة; qishta, ghishta, kishta)
entries.what: a highly perishable cream made by heating fresh milk in shallow pans until a thick cream layer forms; eaten as a dessert, used in dishes, and filling for qatayef and halawet el jibn

entries.heading: Qishta (قِشْطَة; ashta, kishta, kashta, ghishta, eshta)
entries.what: A thick cream formed on heated whole milk. Eaten fresh as a dessert or used as filling and topping. The Wikipedia "Ashta" entry redirects here.

entries.heading: Qishta (قشطة, cream)
entries.what: thick layer of cream formed on milk heated gently; used as a dessert with fruit, honey or syrup, as filling, and as the cream topping in madlouqa (Palestinian knafeh-type dish).

entries.heading: Qishta (cream) (القشطة; cream)
entries.what: cream, named in the dairy list of the Arabic Wikipedia Sudanese cuisine article.

entries.heading: Qishta (qishteh, ashta, kashta)
entries.what: A thick cream formed on heated milk, eaten fresh as a dessert or used as a filling.

entries.heading: Qishta (sweet clotted cream on lahoh)
entries.what: sweet clotted cream, qishta, eaten on lahoh with honey, butter or ghee.

entries.heading: Raw camel milk (drunk unpasteurised)
entries.what: Camel milk taken from pastoral and semi-pastoral herds and drunk raw.

entries.heading: Raw camel milk
entries.what: camel milk is typically drunk raw in most pastoral societies in the Horn of Africa. Ethiopian camels are kept by Afar, Somali, Borana, Beja, Rashaida and Karayu groups in the Afar, Somali, eastern and southern Oromia regions.

entries.heading: Raw camel milk (شیر شتر; consumed in Golestan)
entries.what: Raw milk from one-humped camels in Golestan province, a source of native probiotic bacteria.

entries.heading: Raw camel milk (حليب الإبل, halib al-ibil)
entries.what: Raw dromedary milk from camels in the Kuwaiti desert, sold fresh in retail stores and consumed raw, often for perceived therapeutic benefit.

entries.heading: Raw camel milk (Sudan)
entries.what: raw camel milk, the basic product of camel herders.

entries.heading: Raw camel milk (caano)
entries.what: Raw camel milk is the basic traditional milk of Somali pastoralists, consumed unprocessed.

entries.heading: Ricotta salata (Umbria)
entries.what: A ricotta-based cheese listed for Umbria in the table.

entries.heading: Ricotta salata
entries.what: A traditional Marche whey cheese, listed as a dairy product.

entries.heading: Ricotta salata (Abruzzo)
entries.what: a salted, pressed form of ricotta, linked on the cuisine page to ricotta secca.

entries.heading: Ricotta salata (ricotta secca)
entries.what: an aged sheep's-milk ricotta, grated over dishes; key in Sicilian cooking, such as pasta alla Norma.

entries.heading: Ricotta salata (Sardinian)
entries.what: A salted, aged whey cheese listed among Sardinian cheeses.

entries.heading: Sbrinz AOP
entries.what: A very dry, long-keeping hard cheese with a salt content of 12–16 g/kg. The name comes from Brienz in the Berner Oberland, which was the main trading point for this cheese in the Middle Ages.

entries.heading: Sbrinz (Sbrinz AOP; also "Alp-Sbrinz")
entries.what: A very hard cheese made in central Switzerland; one of the oldest cheeses in Europe. It is made by hand in copper kettles in Luzern, Obwalden and Nidwalden.

entries.heading: Sbrinz AOP (Sbrinz; Sbrinz, German)
entries.what: A hard cheese protected as Swiss AOP. Its production area includes Nidwalden, among Lucerne, Schwyz, Obwalden, Zug, Bern and St. Gallen.

entries.heading: Sbrinz (Sbrinz; Sbrinz DOP/AOP)
entries.what: one of Europe's oldest cheese varieties. The German article says it is made mainly in the cantons of Lucerne, Obwalden and Nidwalden; most is now made in valley dairies (Talkäsereien), with some alp versions in Nidwalden and Obwalden.

entries.heading: Sbrinz (Sbrinz AOP; Alp-Sbrinz; former name Spalenkäse)
entries.what: a long-keeping hard cheese of Central Switzerland, made in valley and alp dairies and aged for a long time; it is one of the Swiss protected cheeses.

entries.heading: Sbrinz (Spalenkäse, Alp-Sbrinz)
entries.what: very hard Swiss cheese from Central Switzerland, grated over pasta or eaten with bread and wine.

entries.heading: Tarator (cold yoghurt and cucumber sauce)
entries.what: cold summer side or sauce of cucumber, garlic and yoghurt

entries.heading: Tarator (таратор) — cold yoghurt soup
entries.what: a traditional cold dairy soup and a popular summer dish in Bulgaria, usually an appetiser; some drink it with mastika or rakia

entries.heading: Tarator
entries.what: A cold soup of yogurt and cucumber, using Bulgarian yogurt in Israel.

entries.heading: Tarator (таратор; cold yoghurt soup or salad)
entries.what: Cold soup or salad in Macedonian, Turkish and Balkan cuisine, popular in spring and summer.

entries.heading: Tarator (таратор; cold yogurt-cucumber dish)
entries.what: cold summer soup or liquid salad of yogurt, cucumber, garlic, oil, dill and sometimes walnut; a Balkan dish shared with Bulgaria, Turkey (cacık) and Greece (tzatziki).

entries.heading: Tarator (cold yoghurt soup)
entries.what: a cold soup of yoghurt, water and cucumber or herbs, in the summer.

entries.heading: Urdhë (urdha, urdhë; urda)
entries.what: an unaged cheese made by boiling whey left over from draining other cheeses; often shaped in half-sphere moulds; similar to ricotta in production.

entries.heading: Orda (urda, zsendice)
entries.what: a whey cheese made by heating whey left after draining another cheese.

entries.heading: Urdă (whey cheese)
entries.what: Soft, fine, ricotta-like whey cheese, common in Southeast Europe and Hungary; Moldova lists it as a country of origin.

entries.heading: Урда / Изварка (urda, izvarka; also урда, изварка in Macedonian)
entries.what: A dairy product high in protein; soft, fine-grained or spreadable, with a mild milky smell. Traditionally a use for whey and buttermilk. Served in Macedonian dishes such as pepper stuffed with urda and burek with urda; "Пиперки со урда" is

entries.heading: Urdă
entries.what: A ricotta-like whey cheese, soft and mild, slightly sweeter than ricotta, common across Romania and the Balkans.

entries.heading: Urdă (whey curd)
entries.what: soft, crumbly fresh curd made by boiling whey left from making caș; similar to ricotta.

entries.heading: Urda (урда; изварка; urdă, whey-type dairy)
entries.what: High-protein dairy product made from by-products of milk processing; the Macedonian article names изварка as the Macedonian term.

entries.heading: Urda (Slovak whey curd)
entries.what: The thick layer that forms when žinčica whey is boiled and is skimmed off with a ladle.

entries.heading: Amasi (mafi in Sesotho; amasi, emasi, maas; other names)
entries.what: A thick, sour, curdled milk product, eaten as a snack in Lesotho, South Africa and Zimbabwe. Sources compare its texture to cottage cheese or plain yogurt, with a much stronger flavour.

entries.heading: Amasi (maas in Afrikaans; also amasi/umasi; not a cheese, closer to a soured or fermented milk)
entries.what: A thick, sour, fermented milk product of southern Africa, widely eaten in South Africa and Lesotho. The Zulu, Xhosa, Ndebele, Swazi and Sotho use it, and it is also common in South African Indian cooking, where it is used like curd.

entries.heading: Amasi (amasi, amasi; Ndebele and Nguni languages; sour milk)
entries.what: a soured milk product from southern Africa, popular as a snack in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Lesotho, per Wikipedia.

entries.heading: Madila (sour milk; other names: madila, amasi)
entries.what: A sour cultured milk, fermented until fully matured, eaten on its own or added to porridge. Also sold commercially in Botswana.

entries.heading: Emasi (emasi, sour milk; amasi in Zulu/Xhosa/Ndebele)
entries.what: a thick, sour, curdled fermented milk, the everyday staple of rural Swazi households. The Swazi name is "emasi".

entries.heading: Amasi (amasi; maas, emasi, mafi in some sources)
entries.what: A thick, sour, curdled milk, often compared to cottage cheese or plain yoghurt but sharper. Staple in pre-colonial times; now a common snack. Sold commercially as well as made at home.

entries.heading: Amasi (amasi, mukaka wakakora in Shona context; "maas" in Afrikaans; other names: soured milk)
entries.what: Thick soured milk with whey separated out, traditionally eaten with pap (sadza-type maize porridge) and also drunk. Its name is used in Ndebele; Zimbabwe is named as one country where it is now a popular snack.

entries.heading: Baladi
entries.what: A soft, smooth, creamy and mild cheese; each Middle Eastern country has its own version.

entries.heading: Baladi cheese (جبنة بلدي; baladi, "local" cheese)
entries.what: A soft, white, mildly rich cheese listed as one of the characteristic cheeses of Iraqi cuisine. The English article describes it as originating in the wider Middle East.

entries.heading: Baladi cheese (جبنة بلدي; "local cheese")
entries.what: A mild but rich cheese made by shepherds in Lebanon's high mountains, per Wikipedia.

entries.heading: Baladi cheese (جبنة بلدي; jibnah baladi; Jibneh Khadra)
entries.what: A traditional fresh Levantine cheese, sold as "mountain cheese" or "village cheese".

entries.heading: Baladi cheese (جبنة بلدي / جبنة بلدية, "village" or "country" cheese; also green cheese)
entries.what: A soft white cheese of the Arab world, made by shepherds in Lebanon's mountains, sometimes called mountain cheese.

entries.heading: Barfi (burfi; khoa sweet)
entries.what: a milk-based sweet from the Indian subcontinent with a fudge-like consistency.

entries.heading: Barfi (other names: barfi, burfi)
entries.what: A fudge-like sweet made from milk solids and sugar.

entries.heading: Barfi (barfi; milk-solid sweet)
entries.what: A sweet made from milk solids (khoa) and sugar. Listed among the Indo-Mauritian sweets.

entries.heading: Barfi
entries.what: A sweet made from thickened milk, sometimes mixed with lentils, fruit or flour; the simplest version is milk and sugar.

entries.heading: Barfi (burfi)
entries.what: milk-based fudge-like sweet.

entries.heading: Djathë i bardhë (djathë i bardhë; "white cheese")
entries.what: the most popular cheese in Albania, per the kashkaval article; the Albanian cuisine article lists it in the dairy section and it links to the sirene and whey-cheese (urda) articles.

entries.heading: Lefko tyri (λευκό τυρί; white cheese)
entries.what: a white cheese named on the Naxos page.

entries.heading: Gvina levana (גבינה לבנה, "white cheese"; also quark-like soft white cheese)
entries.what: A soft white Israeli cheese, similar to quark and cream cheese, one of the best-selling cheeses in Israel and a key ingredient in Israeli cheesecake.

entries.heading: White cheese (unnamed local white cheese, filling for khbeiza)
entries.what: the Libyan cuisine article describes khbeiza, a Libyan dish, as filled with "white cheese with dried mint". No name is given for the cheese.

entries.heading: Beyaz peynir (white cheese; Ezine, Çanakkale, Thrace)
entries.what: The main Turkish table cheese, with a name meaning "white cheese." Compared with feta but milder. Eaten at breakfast, in salads, and in cooked dishes.

entries.heading: Brie (King Island Dairy, Tasmania)
entries.what: King Island's signature brie, launched in April 1985 according to the King Island Dairy page.

entries.heading: Brie (Brie de Meaux, Brie de Nangis, Brie de Melun)
entries.what: A soft cow's-milk cheese named after the Brie region around Seine-et-Marne; pale, under a white mould rind that is typically eaten.

entries.heading: Brie
entries.what: a soft bloomy-rind cheese made in Kenya.

entries.heading: Brie (Luxlait)
entries.what: Brie sold by Luxlait, described as having a subtle taste.

entries.heading: Brie (Omaruru cheese)
entries.what: One of the cheeses made by Tinkie Cornelissen in Omaruru.

entries.heading: Butter tea (yak or cow milk; Wakhi and highland use)
entries.what: tea churned with butter and salt, drunk in the highlands.

entries.heading: Suja (butter tea)
entries.what: Tea made with tea leaves, salt and butter, churned together. In Bhutanese culture it is drunk at special occasions such as weddings and Losar. Guests are often served suja with zao (puffed rice roasted with butter and sugar).

entries.heading: Butter tea (酥油茶, suyu, po cha, bho jha)
entries.what: Tea mixed with yak butter, salt and tsampa, drunk by most Tibetans, often several cups a day. Chinese name 酥油茶.

entries.heading: Butter tea (bho jha / po cha / su chya)
entries.what: A strong tea churned with butter, salt and water, a staple in Tibetan and Himalayan Nepal. Sherpa name su chya or phe chya. Often eaten with tsampa (roasted barley flour mixed with melted butter).

entries.heading: Butter tea (noon chai variant; gur gur chai / local names not confirmed)
entries.what: Salty, Tibetan-style tea with butter, drunk in the north.

entries.heading: Caciocavallo silano (multi-region PDO)
entries.what: A PDO caciocavallo made across several southern regions, including Molise, with the Sila as the production zone named in the infobox.

entries.heading: Caciocavallo silano (DOP)
entries.what: a DOP caciocavallo made mainly in Calabria, Basilicata, Molise, Puglia and Campania. Listed here because Campania is part of its protected area.

entries.heading: Caciocavallo silano (PDO, Apulia part of its area)
entries.what: A PDO caciocavallo made with cow's milk in Basilicata, Calabria, Campania, Molise and Apulia; recognised in 1993. Shaped as a teardrop with hard edible rind, tastes somewhat like aged provolone; the two forms are tied together with rope and

entries.heading: Caciocavallo silano (cow's milk; PDO, multi-region incl. Basilicata)
entries.what: The PDO caciocavallo, a teardrop-shaped stretched-curd cheese with a hard edible rind, aged hanging over a stick, typically in pairs tied with rope.

entries.heading: Caciocavallo Silano (caciocavallo silano; DOP)
entries.what: Oval or truncated-cone cheese, 1–2.5 kg per wheel, named for its horse-head shape with hanging ties. Mild and sweet young, spicier with age.

entries.heading: Café con leche
entries.what: coffee with milk, served at breakfast; historically with ensaimadas in Buenos Aires and with chipá in Mesopotamia.

entries.heading: Café con leche (coffee with milk)
entries.what: Coffee with heated milk, "half coffee and half heated milk", a standard Colombian drink.

entries.heading: Café con leche (coffee with milk)
entries.what: Coffee served with milk, the usual way to take coffee in Costa Rica.

entries.heading: Café con leche (café con leche; leche con café not confirmed)
entries.what: The traditional Cuban breakfast drink, usually served with buttered, toasted pan cubano.

entries.heading: Café con leche (Dominican)
entries.what: Dominican coffee made in a greca (stovetop pot) and served with hot milk; a breakfast drink.

entries.heading: Camembert (King Island Dairy, Tasmania)
entries.what: A King Island Dairy product listed as "Camembert".

entries.heading: Camembert (Camembert de Normandie)
entries.what: A moist, soft, creamy, surface-ripened cow's-milk cheese first made in the late 18th century in Camembert, Normandy.

entries.heading: Camembert
entries.what: a soft bloomy-rind cheese made in Kenya.

entries.heading: Camembert (made in Mexico)
entries.what: A French-style bloomy-rind cheese also made in Mexico.

entries.heading: Camembert (Omaruru cheese)
entries.what: One of the cheeses made by Tinkie Cornelissen in Omaruru.

entries.heading: Chocolate milk (leche chocolatada; leche achocolatada)
entries.what: a milk drink with cocoa or chocolate, defined in the Food Code.

entries.heading: Kakaomælk (chocolate milk)
entries.what: cold chocolate milk, widely drunk in Denmark.

entries.heading: Kókómjólk (chocolate milk)
entries.what: Chocolate-flavoured milk drink made by Mjólkursamsalan since 1973. Variants include strawberry (2002), reduced sugar (2006) and white chocolate (2023).

entries.heading: Chocolate milk (cocoa mixed with milk; "chocolate milk")
entries.what: A cold or warm drink of cocoa powder mixed with milk, sometimes sweetened. The Wikipedia article credits its origin to Jamaica, where the first recorded milk-and-cocoa recipe is linked to the 1494 cacao-brewing practice; it was popularised

entries.heading: Chokladmjölk (chokladdryck; chocolate milk)
entries.what: A chocolate drink made from cocoa powder and sugar mixed with milk or water. Sold cold and ready to drink in cartons; Pucko is named as another brand of cold ready-to-drink chocolate milk, and one brand name has become a generic word for th

entries.heading: Grana Padano (cross-region, includes Piemonte)
entries.what: PDO hard cheese produced and grated across about thirty-two provinces in Emilia-Romagna, Lombardy, Piemonte, Trentino-Alto Adige and Veneto.

entries.heading: Grana Padano (Grana Padano DOP)
entries.what: a hard, crumbly cow's-milk cheese from the Po Valley; the Lombard cuisine article says it descends from Granone Lodigiano, attributed to monks of the Chiaravalle Abbey in the 12th century.

entries.heading: Grana Padano (Grana Padano DOP)
entries.what: A large DOP hard cheese made across the Po Valley. Veneto is one of the regions of the DOP zone, so it is also made here, under the general DOP rule (cows, milk, cheese and ageing must all be in the zone).

entries.heading: Grana Padano
entries.what: A hard, long-aged cow's-milk grana cheese, protected under the DOP scheme, made across several northern regions including Emilia-Romagna.

entries.heading: Grana Padano
entries.what: a hard grana cheese from the Po Valley, made from partly skimmed cow's milk.

entries.heading: Jameed (جميد; dried salted yogurt curd)
entries.what: a dried, salted yogurt product used as a preserved food in Bedouin cooking.

entries.heading: Jameed (ג'מיד; Hebrew: אבן יוגורט, "yogurt stone")
entries.what: A hard, dried yogurt or labneh ball, used in Bedouin cooking, including mansaf, and kept without refrigeration.

entries.heading: Jameed (جميد, jameed; also jamid, jameed/kashk-like; "rock cheese" in some travel sources)
entries.what: A hard, dried fermented dairy product, central to Jordan's national dish mansaf, where it forms the fermented yogurt sauce. Wikipedia calls it a dried yogurt, unique to Jordanian cuisine, and similar to kashk.

entries.heading: Jameed (جميد; dried yogurt)
entries.what: A dried yogurt product sold in balls, used in mansaf and other dishes.

entries.heading: Jameed (جميد; also جميدة, "dried yoghurt")
entries.what: a hard, salty, dried ball of fermented milk; the key ingredient of mansaf, Jordan's national dish, and the sauce for mansaf and other dishes

entries.heading: Jameed (جميد)
entries.what: hard dried yoghurt, rehydrated into a thick yoghurt for mansaf, the national dish. Used as the sour base of mansaf and in the dip mthawamet bandora (roasted tomatoes with jameed).

entries.heading: Jameed (جميد; dried fermented yoghurt)
entries.what: Dried, salted yoghurt balls used to make sauces and stews; in Saudi cuisine it is the base of Mulayhiya and Mansaf.

entries.heading: Matsun (մածուն; matzoon, matsoni, matsun)
entries.what: The main dairy product of Armenian cuisine. Used on its own, in soups, sauces and cakes, and as the base for tan, butter and chortan. Armenia is named as its place of origin.

entries.heading: Matsoni (მაწონი; მაწვნი in genitive; Armenian: մածուն)
entries.what: traditional Georgian sour milk product. Armenian origin is claimed by Armenia as well; Georgian matsoni has been a protected geographical indication since 24 January 2012.

entries.heading: Katyk (катык)
entries.what: Thick sour milk of Turkic peoples, Tatars and neighbouring republics; source of suzma and kurut.

entries.heading: Katyk (катик; matsun)
entries.what: Fermented dairy drink found in Central Asia, Caucasus and Crimean Tatar cuisine; base for suzma, kurt and ayran.

entries.heading: Katyk (katyk; Uzbek katiq, Russian katyk)
entries.what: Fresh cow or goat milk fermented with lactic acid bacteria, with a distinct taste, smell and consistency. It is the base for suzma, qurut and katykli soup in Uzbek cooking.

entries.heading: Kefalograviera (Κεφαλογραβιέρα; Kefalograviera)
entries.what: A hard table cheese, salty with a rich aroma, often pan-fried as saganaki or grated over pasta. Sometimes sold outside Greece as Kefalotyri.

entries.heading: Kefalograviera (Κεφαλογραβιέρα), Epirus artisanal example
entries.what: a Greek hard cheese made in the same artisanal style as Feta; an artisanal example was sampled in Epirus.

entries.heading: Kefalograviera (Κεφαλογραβιέρα; other names: kefalograviera)
entries.what: A white to yellowish full-fat cheese with a salty, piquant flavour, made to a protected recipe with a longer, sharper finish than feta

entries.heading: Kefalograviera (Κεφαλογραβιέρα, ΠΟΠ)
entries.what: a hard table cheese, salty, with nutty and buttery notes, used in cooking and for saganaki.

entries.heading: Kefalograviera (Κεφαλογραβιέρα; Π.Ο.Π. Western Macedonia, Epirus, Aetolia-Acarnania, Evrytania)
entries.what: Salty hard cheese with a rich aroma; fried in triangles for saganaki and grated over pasta. Closely resembles kefalotyri and is sometimes sold under that name.

entries.heading: Lassi (লাচ্ছি; lachhi)
entries.what: a drink of yoghurt blended with water and either spices or sweet flavourings.

entries.heading: Lassi (लस्सी; lachhi, lassi)
entries.what: A yoghurt-based drink from Punjab, blended with water and spices or sugar, and sometimes fruit. Served in a clay cup (kulhar) in Varanasi and Rajasthan; the name is a Hindi borrowing first attested in 1882.

entries.heading: Lassi (mango)
entries.what: A drink sold by Luxlait as a traditional Indian/Pakistani fermented drink, here in mango flavour.

entries.heading: Lassi (Malaysian Indian)
entries.what: A yoghurt-based drink with savoury and sweet varieties, popular in Malaysian Indian cuisine.

entries.heading: Lassi (Punjabi / Urdu: لسی; other names: lassi, lassee)
entries.what: A yoghurt drink with a smoothie-like texture, from the Indian subcontinent and originating in Punjab. Pakistani Punjab is part of that region.

entries.heading: Nabulsi
entries.what: A brined white cheese from Nablus, Palestine, sold in the UAE.

entries.heading: Nabulsi (جبنة نابلسية)
entries.what: A Palestinian white brined cheese from Nablus, used in knafeh and widely in the Middle East.

entries.heading: Nabulsi (نابلسي, nabulsi; mashmouleh is a cow/sheep mix)
entries.what: A Palestinian white brined cheese named after the city of Nablus in the West Bank. Wikipedia says it is one of the main cheeses eaten in Jordan.
