entries.heading: Nabulsi (نابلسي; Nabulsi cheese; Naboulsi)
entries.what: A white brined cheese named after Nablus in the West Bank. The Wikipedia article calls it a Palestinian cheese and one of Jordan's principal cheeses, and it is the cheese used in knafeh.

entries.heading: Nabulsi cheese (جبن نابلسي)
entries.what: A semi-salty cheese named after Nablus in the West Bank. It is used in Syrian and Levantine sweets (nabulsiyyeh, knafeh) and eaten in Jordan.

entries.heading: Pasteurised milk (Fan Milk)
entries.what: Early product of the Ghanaian dairy company Fan Milk, founded in 1960 as the "Ghanaian Milk Company".

entries.heading: Pasteurised milk (低温殺菌牛乳, teion sakkin gyūnyū)
entries.what: Milk heat-treated at low temperature to keep flavour and protein. Most market milk in Japan is UHT, so low-temperature pasteurised milk is a niche, mainly sold by some makers and farm shops.

entries.heading: Pasteurised milk (pasteurized milk)
entries.what: Pasteurised milk was one of four milk and cheese products collected from Kuwaiti hospitals and tested for antibiotic residues (50 samples).

entries.heading: Pasteurised milk (fresh and bottled, industrial)
entries.what: milk pasteurised by a processor and sold in packs or as fresh pasteurised milk, mainly through the formal channel.

entries.heading: Pasteurised milk (melk, consumptiemelk)
entries.what: Pasteurised milk for drinking, sold at a government-capped maximum price. In the 2008 data, about 45% of the roughly 30,000 l of dairy consumed per day was produced locally.

entries.heading: Raib (soured raw milk, butter base)
entries.what: Spontaneously soured raw milk that is churned to make smen and fresh butter.

entries.heading: Rayeb (fermented milk, Libya row; Latin spelling as in source)
entries.what: a traditional fermented milk the review lists under Egypt, Libya and Tunisia.

entries.heading: Raib (rayeb, raïb, ikkil; رايب)
entries.what: Naturally soured milk, eaten as natural yoghurt and churned to make lben. Sold as a packaged product under a brand name (Raibi Jamila) as well.

entries.heading: Raib (Raïb; cultured milk, possibly the same word as rayeb)
entries.what: The Chadian name for cultured (soured) cow, sheep or goat milk, from which rouaba is made.

entries.heading: Rayeb (whole fermented milk)
entries.what: A fermented whole milk sold mainly through N'Djamena milk bars; its success is what drives dairy consumption outside the home in the city.

entries.heading: Rayeb (raïb, rayeb; Tunisian fermented milk)
entries.what: A traditional Tunisian dairy beverage, consumed directly or further processed into leben.

entries.heading: Raw (fresh) cow milk sold at open-air markets
entries.what: Milk sold raw to the public at open-air markets across Cameroon, sampled in the Far North, North and West regions. It is sold without regulation for human consumption.

entries.heading: Raw (unpasteurised) cow milk
entries.what: milk sold and used raw, from small and mid-size farms and informal channels.

entries.heading: Raw (unpasteurised) fresh milk
entries.what: Fresh milk sold raw by hawkers, door to door, and to small collectors and processors.

entries.heading: Raw (unboiled) fresh cow's milk (Dinka, Nuer and other cattle-keeping pastoralists)
entries.what: Fresh, unprocessed cow's milk drunk by herders in cattle camps, and sold raw at camp points of sale.

entries.heading: Raw (unprocessed) cow milk, sold informally
entries.what: The largest share of marketed milk in Uganda, sold unprocessed.

entries.heading: Raw cow milk (fresh, unprocessed)
entries.what: most milk is sold and supplied raw. Milk products are mostly made at household level from raw milk.

entries.heading: Raw cow milk (شیر خام)
entries.what: Unpasteurised cow milk sold in Iran alongside pasteurised and UHT milk.

entries.heading: Raw cow milk (sold at market)
entries.what: milk sold directly by sellers at markets (Table 1 of PMC11900221 "Cow milk").

entries.heading: Raw cow milk (amata y'inka)
entries.what: unheated milk drunk or sold directly from the farm, a large share of which is consumed raw in Rwanda.

entries.heading: Raw cow milk (fresh milk)
entries.what: fresh raw milk from cows, the base for all mabisi. Sold by smallholder dairy farmers; in some areas historically sold to Indian traders near villages.

entries.heading: Ryazhenka (ражанка; ryazhenka)
entries.what: A baked, caramelised sour milk drink, thick and brown, made from fermented baked milk. Described as traditional in Belarus, Russia and Ukraine; the English article gives Ukraine as its origin and notes Russian and Soviet sources calling it

entries.heading: Rjaženka (ryazhenka; rjaženka)
entries.what: highly pasteurised sour milk, creamy, golden-brown, mild yoghurt-like taste

entries.heading: Riażenka (riażenka, ryazhenka; baked milk drink)
entries.what: A milk drink made by fermenting milk that has been heat-treated for several hours. Also spelled riażanka, rażanka, prażanka; the misspelling "rjażenka" is used in Poland.

entries.heading: Ryazhenka (ряженка)
entries.what: Sour drink of milk baked until brown, then fermented; yellowish-brown, caramel flavour. Russian, Belarusian and Ukrainian product.

entries.heading: Ryazhenka (ряжанка; baked milk)
entries.what: Milk baked for hours until it turns golden-brown and creamy, then fermented. Named in Ukrainian for "baked milk"; the English article lists Ukraine as its origin, shared with Russia and Belarus.

entries.heading: Scamorza (Abruzzo)
entries.what: a stretched-curd cheese recognised as a traditional product of several regions, including Abruzzo (with Campania and Basilicata).

entries.heading: Scamorza (Campanian variant, with buffalo milk)
entries.what: a ball-shaped stretched-curd cheese, made in Campania, sometimes from buffalo milk.

entries.heading: Scamorza (Puglian sheep variant noted)
entries.what: A stretched-curd cheese similar to mozzarella, traditional across southern Italy, including Puglia. Egg-shaped with a waist, around 0.15–0.25 kg.

entries.heading: Scamorza (cow's milk, general; PAT in Basilicata)
entries.what: A stretched-curd cheese like mozzarella, egg-shaped, tied in the middle.

entries.heading: Scamorza
entries.what: a southern stretched-curd cheese, made across Italy.

entries.heading: Skyr (skyr; súrostur, "ferskur súrostur")
entries.what: A thick, strained, soured fresh dairy product that Iceland is known for. Traditionally eaten with a spoon; sold today mostly in cartons.

entries.heading: Norse-era skyr (skyr; Old Norse skyr; other names: sour milk curd)
entries.what: A sour milk product similar to quark, named in the 13th-century Konungs skuggsjá as part of Norse Greenlanders' diet.

entries.heading: Skyr (Glenisk)
entries.what: Skyr, listed as a new high-protein product by Glenisk.

entries.heading: Skyr (skyr; skyr.is; ísskyr, other names)
entries.what: A thick, mild, high-protein sour dairy product, eaten cold with spoons, often with cream. It has been part of Icelandic food for centuries and is mentioned in medieval sagas, though no medieval description survives. Commonly classed as a fr

entries.heading: Skyr (Icelandic-style strained fermented milk)
entries.what: Sold by Luxlait as "d'inspiration islandaise", high-protein and 0% fat. Available as Nature (450 g and 150 g), Vanille, Citron and Myrtille (150 g).

entries.heading: Skyr (skjør in Norwegian)
entries.what: a fat-free dairy product with traditions in Icelandic and Norwegian culture; thicker than yoghurt, slightly sour with some residual sweetness; sold in flavoured versions. The Norwegian variant is written skjør in Bokmål and Nynorsk rules. Q

entries.heading: Tilsiter
entries.what: semi-hard cheese created by Prussian-Swiss settlers from Emmental in Tilsit (East Prussia) in the mid-19th century; the recipe was taken back to Switzerland, where it has been made since 1893.

entries.heading: Tilsiter (Holsteiner Tilsiter)
entries.what: A semi-hard cheese named after the former East Prussian town of Tilsit (now Sovetsk); made as a wheel or block.

entries.heading: Tilsiter (made in Estonia)
entries.what: the German-origin Tilsiter cheese, which the source says is also made in Estonia.

entries.heading: Tilsiter
entries.what: a German-style washed-rind cheese listed as made in Kenya.

entries.heading: Tylżycki (ser tylżycki, tilsiter; Tilsit cheese)
entries.what: A semi-hard rennet cheese named after Tylża (Tilsit, now Sovetsk in Russia, formerly East Prussia). Pale yellow interior with small holes, dark brown rind.

entries.heading: Wagashi (Gassirè / Gassiré; also wagasi, wara, amo, gasaru; other names: warakashi)
entries.what: A soft, mild, white cheese made by the Peulh (Fulani) in northern and central Benin and sold widely in Parakou, Dassa and Nikki and in markets across Benin and neighbouring countries. Widely eaten as a meat or fish substitute, fried or boil

entries.heading: Wagashi (wagashi, wagashie, waagashie, woagashie; also Hausa/Fulani "wagashi" and "wara" in some sources)
entries.what: A soft, unripened cottage-type cheese made mostly from cow's milk, widely eaten in Ghana, particularly in the Northern and Volta regions. Often sold fried in markets and at waakye stalls, where it is eaten as a meal or with other foods.

entries.heading: Wagashi (Gassire in Fulfulde; wagasi in Zarma-Songhai; wagashi/wara/warankashi elsewhere in West Africa)
entries.what: A soft, mild West African cheese made from cow milk, eaten fried or boiled, or in sauces and stews as a meat or fish substitute. The Niger-Benin paper calls it the most appreciated dairy product in Benin and Niger alongside fermented milk.

entries.heading: Wara (warankasi; wara-kasi; wara; awara)
entries.what: A soft, unripened white curd cheese of Yoruba and northern-Nigerian Fulani tradition, sold in whey, in calabashes or in small bags, and eaten fresh, boiled, or deep-fried. Wikipedia calls wara a name also used for foreign cheeses in general

entries.heading: Wagashi (FAO multi-country entry that lists Nigeria)
entries.what: A West African soft cheese, listed by FAO among nine West African countries including Nigeria. Usually fried before eating and used as protein in soups and stews.

entries.heading: Wagashi (Peul soft cheese, Togo)
entries.what: The Togo name for the West African soft cheese, made by Peul women and sold in the north; the Tridge overview lists "local cheeses (e.g., Peulh/Wagashi)" among the products of raw-milk processing.

entries.heading: Appenzeller (Appenzeller Käse; Appenzeller)
entries.what: A Swiss cheese from the Appenzellerland, sold in full-fat and quarter-fat versions and in mild to strong ripeness grades. Its brand organisation is based in Appenzell town.

entries.heading: Appenzeller (Appenzeller; Classic, Surchoix, Extra)
entries.what: A Swiss cheese from the Appenzell region, with the cheese first mentioned in a document from 1282. It is produced in village dairies and is a specialty of both half-cantons, Appenzell Innerrhoden and Appenzell Ausserrhoden.

entries.heading: Appenzeller (Appenzeller Käse; Appenzeller Extra, Surchoix, Classic)
entries.what: a Swiss hard-to-semi-hard cow's milk cheese famous for its herbal brine, made in the Appenzell region of north-east Switzerland

entries.heading: Appenzeller (Appenzeller Käse)
entries.what: Swiss cheese from the Appenzell region, famous for its herbal brine; used in the Appenzeller cheese tart (Chäsfladen).

entries.heading: Batzos (Μπάτζος, also μπάτσος; batzos)
entries.what: A traditional brined cheese from shepherds of the Pindus and Kaimaktsalan mountains, with a salty, slightly sour, piquant taste and many irregular holes. It originated at Voio in Western Macedonia and now also comes from Central Macedonia a

entries.heading: Batzos (Μπάτζος; Batzos)
entries.what: A traditional Greek brined cheese with irregular holes, low in fat, salty and slightly sharp. Eaten plain, fried or with eggs.

entries.heading: Batzos (μπάτζος; Mpatzos)
entries.what: A traditional Greek brined cheese, with a PDO whose area includes Thessaly; also the base stage for hard cheeses such as kefalograviera and kefalotyri.

entries.heading: Batzos (Μπάτζος; Π.Ο.Π. Macedonia and Thessaly)
entries.what: Traditional Greek brined cheese; salty with a mild bite; low in fat (fat removed in whey, used to make butter or manouri).

entries.heading: Caciocavallo podolico
entries.what: a Podolica-cow caciocavallo, ripened long, with pasture and scrubland aromas.

entries.heading: Caciocavallo podolico
entries.what: A stretched-curd cheese made only from the milk of Podolica cows, a breed raised free-range. Typical of Puglia and nearby regions; aged for five or six years it develops complex pasture aromas, and is served as a "noble" cheese at the end o

entries.heading: Caciocavallo podolico (cow's milk, Podolica breed; PAT, Basilicata named)
entries.what: A stretched-curd cheese made only from the milk of Podolica cows, in the traditional way and only in certain months of the year. Aged 5–6 years or more it develops pasture and scrubland aromas; it is served as a fine table cheese, usually a

entries.heading: Caciocavallo podolico (caciocavallo podolico)
entries.what: Caciocavallo made from Podolica cow milk, a regional variant listed for Calabria.

entries.heading: Cacioricotta (salentino / pugliese)
entries.what: A cheese made with a hybrid of cheese-making and ricotta-making, used grated over pasta; the Cucina pugliese page calls the Puglian one "cacioricotta salentino".

entries.heading: Cacioricotta (sheep or goat milk; hybrid cheese and ricotta method)
entries.what: A traditional southern Italian cheese combining cheesemaking and ricotta-making.

entries.heading: Cacioricotta (Cacioricotta)
entries.what: A traditional cheese from the south of Italy, listed for Calabria.

entries.heading: Cacioricotta
entries.what: a southern cheese that combines ricotta-style and hard-paste steps.

entries.heading: Caciotta (Umbria)
entries.what: A small cylindrical cheese, up to 1 kg, of which Umbria lists plain caciotta and caciotta al tartufo.

entries.heading: Caciotta (Caciotta del Montefeltro / Caciotta del Fermano)
entries.what: The most widespread cheese of the region, with two main styles: the Fermano style, eaten young and slightly sweet-sour, and the Montefeltro style, aged and more savoury. Montefeltro caciotta is aged 2–6 months.

entries.heading: Caciotta (family)
entries.what: a family of cheeses with many regional variants in central and southern Italy.

entries.heading: Caciotta (caciotta; Italian semi-hard cheese family)
entries.what: a family of small Italian cheeses; name is a Tuscan-dialect form.

entries.heading: Milchkaffee / Schale (milk coffee)
entries.what: Milk coffee drink; in Switzerland it is called "Schale" after the bowl it is served in.

entries.heading: Café au lait (Kurokawa Onsen café au lait, Kumamoto)
entries.what: A coffee milk made from over 90% Jersey milk, sweetened only with sugar, with French coffee and no powdered milk or stabilisers, sold by Yama no Ibuki.

entries.heading: Milchkaffee (milk coffee)
entries.what: Coffee served with milk, listed in Liechtenstein as a typical accompaniment to Ribel.

entries.heading: Milk coffee (café au lait; milk drink)
entries.what: Coffee with milk. The Mauritian cuisine article calls it a Franco-Mauritian non-alcoholic drink, well liked by Franco-Mauritians.

entries.heading: Chechil (չեչիլ; also chechil panir, tel panir, husats panir, chil panir, chivil panir)
entries.what: A braided or skein-wound string cheese, dry and stringy, made mainly in Shirak. Each coil is about 3–4 kg and very salty, so it is usually soaked in water before eating.

entries.heading: Tel panir (Թել պանիր; a type of chechil)
entries.what: A traditional Armenian string cheese from the Armenian Highlands, described as a type of chechil with a braided or threaded form.

entries.heading: Çeçil pendir (chechil, string cheese; Armenian and Georgian origin claimed)
entries.what: A brined string cheese, rolled into braided ropes; named in the Azerbaijani popular list.

entries.heading: Chechil (ჩეჩილი) — also Adjaruli Chechili (აჭარული ჩეჩილი) and Meskhuri Chechili (მესხური ჩეჩილი)
entries.what: A brined string cheese pulled into thin strands and usually braided. In Georgia it is linked to Meskheti (Meskhuri) and Adjara (Adjaruli); in Georgian registers it appears as Adjaruli and Meskhuri chechili.

entries.heading: Chechil (чечил; Armenian/Georgian stretched-curd cheese)
entries.what: Brined string cheese, similar to mozzarella, pulled into thin strands and usually braided. Popular in Armenia and Georgia, produced in Turkey; the article names Russian industrial production in the former Soviet countries.

entries.heading: Falooda with condensed milk (other names: falooda, faluda)
entries.what: A chilled dessert of milk, rose syrup, vermicelli and basil seeds, sometimes with ice cream or kulfi.

entries.heading: Falooda (फालूदा; faluda)
entries.what: Chilled milk drink with rose syrup, vermicelli and sweet basil seeds; often served with kulfi.

entries.heading: Faluda (with ice cream)
entries.what: Popular cold dairy refreshment in Sri Lanka, with syrup, ice cream, jelly pieces and basil seeds; mango and gooseberry (nelli) versions exist.

entries.heading: Falooda (faluda)
entries.what: Cold Mughlai dessert drink with rose syrup, vermicelli and basil seeds in milk; often served with kulfi.

entries.heading: Formaggio di fossa (Umbria, infobox only)
entries.what: A cheese aged in sealed tufa pits, historically made between Romagna and the Marche.

entries.heading: Formaggio di fossa (Fossa di Sogliano DOP; Ambra di Talamello; formaggio in fossa)
entries.what: A cheese matured in pits dug into tufa. Named Formaggio di Fossa di Sogliano DOP in the regional list. Ambra di Talamello is the local name for the same product from Talamello. Historically the Marche region's cheese; since 2009 the towns o

entries.heading: Formaggio di fossa
entries.what: a pit cheese from Emilia-Romagna, aged in underground tufa pits.

entries.heading: Formaggio di fossa (formaggio di fossa; pit cheese)
entries.what: a cheese aged in underground pits; traditional to Romagna, Marche, Tuscany and Montefeltro according to the Wikipedia articles.

entries.heading: Leche de vaca (leche fresca; fresh cow milk)
entries.what: Milk from dairy cows. In a 2014 survey of 516 herds in Camagüey, the main milk-producing province, average yield was 1024 kg per cow per year (95% CI 996–1051 kg). The paper gives national output as 1134 million litres at the 1989 peak, 353

entries.heading: Fresh cow milk (lait frais; raw fresh milk)
entries.what: Fresh cow's milk, the main fresh milk supply in Mauritius. Cowkeepers supply about 95% of the country's fresh milk.

entries.heading: Fresh cow milk (raw milk, sold in very small quantities)
entries.what: Fresh milk is scarce on Norfolk Island. A cheesemaking family on the island recalled drinking fresh milk as a rarity. Most of the island's cattle are raised only for beef (about 99 percent, per the same source).

entries.heading: Fresh cow milk (liquid, full cream and low fat)
entries.what: ordinary drinking milk, full cream and low-fat/skimmed.

entries.heading: Fromage blanc
entries.what: An acid-coagulated fresh cheese from northern France and southern Belgium; also called maquée.

entries.heading: Fresh white cheese (fromage blanc, Ferme de lait-Quateur)
entries.what: A fresh white cheese (fromage blanc) from the dairy farm "la ferme de lait-Quateur", named with its fresh milk and yoghurts as widely present in small and large Guianese retail.

entries.heading: Fromage Blanc (Kyodo Gakusha Shintoku; Japanese name not in sources)
entries.what: A fresh fromage blanc from Kyodo Gakusha Shintoku Farm, listed in a Hokkaido product roundup.

entries.heading: Fresh white cheese (unnamed; Arabic جبنة بيضاء طازجة)
entries.what: a fresh white cheese, not given a specific name in the source, used in Yemeni cooking.

entries.heading: Kashk (Afghan use; dried yogurt / drained-curd product)
entries.what: a sour, salty, long-keeping dried dairy product widely used in Iran, Central Asia and the Middle East. In Afghanistan it is listed as a dish component in the Hazara cuisine ("kashk/ayran, yogurt") served with aash.

entries.heading: Kashk (Persian کشک; Kurdish کەشک; also kishk, qurut, jameed)
entries.what: A dried sour-dairy product of the Caucasus, Central Asia and Middle East; a staple in Iran, used in ash reshteh and kashk-e bademjan (aubergine with kashk and mint).

entries.heading: Kashk (کشک; also qurut, keshk, tow, jortan, lech)
entries.what: A sour, dried dairy product made from yogurt or doogh, eaten as a staple, especially in winter; used to thicken and flavour soups and stews (e.g. kalle joosh, kashk-e bademjan, ash reshteh). Also made as a liquid industrial product.

entries.heading: Kashk (كشك, dried drained yoghurt)
entries.what: dried, shaped yoghurt; in Palestinian cuisine lists it appears as a dish or ingredient.

entries.heading: Kashk
entries.what: A dried, salty fermented milk product with a long shelf life.

entries.heading: Kefalotyri (Kefalotiri, Greek Κεφαλοτύρι)
entries.what: A hard cheese made in Greece and Cyprus, with roots in the Byzantine era. Its whey is used to make anari.

entries.heading: Kefalotyri (Κεφαλοτύρι; Kefalotiri)
entries.what: A hard, salty cheese; the name means "head cheese", possibly from the wheel's shape.

entries.heading: Kefalotyri (Κεφαλοτύρι)
entries.what: a hard, salty yellow cheese; the Cretan list on Greek Wikipedia names it.

entries.heading: Kefalotyri (Κεφαλοτύρι)
entries.what: Hard, salty white-to-yellow cheese from Greece and Cyprus. Suited to grating, eating as is, or frying for saganaki.

entries.heading: Kettugol and lébol (milk fat)
entries.what: milk-fat products used in light cooking and in hair weaving.

entries.heading: Kettugol and lébol (milk-fat butter-like products)
entries.what: Fats derived from milk fat, named in the Fula article.

entries.heading: Kettugol and lébol (milk fats)
entries.what: Fats derived from milk, used in light cooking and in hair weaving.

entries.heading: Kettugol and lébol (Fulbe milk fat)
entries.what: two Fulbe milk-fat products, used in light cooking and in hair weaving.

entries.heading: Kheer (rice pudding)
entries.what: a pudding or porridge, usually rice pudding, popular in the Indian subcontinent.

entries.heading: Kheer (meetha bhat; other names: kheer, sweet rice)
entries.what: A sweet rice pudding made by simmering milk with sugar or jaggery and rice.

entries.heading: Kheer (rice pudding)
entries.what: Milk pudding with rice, sugar or jaggery; common in Pakistan (Pakistani rice-dish category lists it).

entries.heading: Kheer (rice pudding)
entries.what: sweet pudding of rice (or vermicelli) boiled in milk with sugar, nuts and dried fruit.

entries.heading: Khoa (khoya, khowa, mawa; खोया)
entries.what: Dried-down milk solids used across South Asia (India, Nepal, Pakistan) in sweets and savoury dishes.

entries.heading: Khoa / mawa (খোয়া; mawa)
entries.what: the base of many traditional Bangladeshi sweets; Shahnaz et al. 2004 calls it a partially dehydrated whole milk product.

entries.heading: Khoa / khova / mawa (खोया; khoya, pachotta)
entries.what: Dried milk solid used as the base of many Indian sweets; about 5.5% of India's milk goes into it, and about 600,000 t a year are made.

entries.heading: Khoya (khoa / mawa; dried milk solid)
entries.what: Soft milk solid used as a base for sweets, used across South Asia including Pakistan.

entries.heading: Khoa (khoya, mawa, milk solids)
entries.what: milk reduced to a soft dough-like solid.

entries.heading: Kishk (كشك; dried kishk; kishk akhdar when wet)
entries.what: A traditional Lebanese fermented, dried milk-and-cereal product, ground into powder for winter soups, stews and porridges; also used in manakish and kibbeh.

entries.heading: Kishk (كشك; kishk / kashk)
entries.what: a dried, powdered mix of bulgur with milk and laban, fermented, stored dry; used as a soup or porridge base

entries.heading: Kishk (كشك)
entries.what: A dried, powdery food of Levantine origin made from burghul fermented with milk and yoghurt. Standard form is a dry powder; a soft intermediate called kishk akhdar is eaten during production.

entries.heading: Kishk (كشك)
entries.what: A powdery mix of burghul fermented with milk and laban, dried for winter.

entries.heading: Kishk (كشك)
entries.what: A powdery product of cracked wheat (burghul) fermented with milk and yogurt, used in cooking and as a base for soups and dishes.

entries.heading: Kossam (Fulfulde: milk in general; semi-manufactured yoghurt)
entries.what: In Adamawa, "kossam" is the generic Fulfulde term for dairy products on the market, meaning milk; for one product it is the label of a semi-manufactured yoghurt sold alongside a manufactured yoghurt. The Wikipedia Fulani article also gives

entries.heading: Kossam (fresh milk and yoghurt, Fulbe)
entries.what: Kossam is the general Fulbe term for fresh milk (miraɗam) and for yoghurt (pendidan); central to Fulbe identity.

entries.heading: Kossam (milk) and pendidan (yoghurt) — Fulbe generic
entries.what: Kossam is the general Fula word for milk, covering fresh milk (miraɗam) and yoghurt (pendidan); valued as a drink or as processed forms such as yoghurt and cheese.

entries.heading: Kossam (fresh milk and yoghurt, Fulfulde; miraɗam and pendidan)
entries.what: kossam is the general Fulfulde term for both fresh milk (miraɗam) and yoghurt (pendidan).

entries.heading: Manouri (Μανούρι)
entries.what: A whey cheese made from the whey left after feta or hard cheese production, with fresh sheep or goat milk or cream added. Richer than feta, with a light, slightly sour and nutty taste. PDO.

entries.heading: Manouri (Μανούρι; Manouri)
entries.what: A creamy white cheese, less salty than feta, used in salads, pastries and desserts, and as a cream-cheese substitute.

entries.heading: Manouri (μανούρι)
entries.what: A creamy, mild whey cheese, mostly eaten fresh at the table or in appetisers; PDO-protected.

entries.heading: Manouri (Μανούρι; Π.Ο.Π.)
entries.what: By-product of feta production; cream added to the whey, making it creamier than feta; about 36–38% fat, 0.8% salt.

entries.heading: Mascarpone
entries.what: a soft, milky-white product made from cow's cream; often called a cheese but technically a cream because it does not form a true curd.

entries.heading: Mascarpone
entries.what: a soft dairy product from Lombardy, associated with Lodi; often called a cheese but the source calls it a cream.

entries.heading: Mascarpone
entries.what: a fresh cream cheese listed as made in Kenya.

entries.heading: Mascarpone (mascarpone; Italian cream cheese)
entries.what: a rich fresh cheese made from cream, widespread in Italy.

entries.heading: Milo (malted chocolate milk drink)
entries.what: A chocolate and malt powder, developed in Sydney in 1934 by Thomas Mayne, a Nestlé industrial chemist. Usually stirred into hot or cold milk, or sprinkled on top, in Australia and New Zealand. Formula: malt extract, milk powder, cocoa, suga

entries.heading: Milo (malted chocolate drink; made with milk)
entries.what: A chocolate-flavoured malted powder, made by Nestlé, typically mixed with milk, hot water or both. Its standard recipe is malted barley, milk powder, sugar and cocoa.

entries.heading: Milo (malted drink mixed with milk)
entries.what: A malted chocolate powder traditionally mixed with hot or cold milk, or sprinkled on top.

entries.heading: Milo (malt chocolate drink), including Milo Dinosaur and Milo ais/peng
entries.what: malted chocolate powder made by Nestlé; standard recipe has malted barley, milk powder, sugar and cocoa. Usually mixed with milk, hot water, or both.

entries.heading: Pecorino romano (DOP)
entries.what: DOP pecorino, mainly Sardinia and Lazio; its DOP area includes the province of Grosseto, Tuscany. Some ~2 % of production is in Toscana (per Pecorino page).

entries.heading: Pecorino Romano (pecorino romano DOP; Lazio is the origin area)
entries.what: A sheep's-milk hard cheese protected by PDO. It originated in Lazio but nearly all production has moved to Sardinia, per the EN article.

entries.heading: Pecorino Romano (Sardinian production)
entries.what: The historic pecorino, with about 97% of production now in Sardinia (a 2018 figure cited on Italian Wikipedia). Made in Sardinia, Lazio and the province of Grosseto.

entries.heading: Pecorino Romano
entries.what: a hard, salty sheep's-milk cheese; the name Pecorino is the sheep-cheese family in Italy.

entries.heading: Provolone Valpadana (Provolone Valpadana DOP)
entries.what: a DOP stretched-curd cheese made in the Po Valley in two versions, sweet and sharp (piccante); may be smoked.

entries.heading: Provolone Valpadana (DOP)
entries.what: DOP provolone made in the Po Valley.

entries.heading: Provolone Valpadana (Provolone Valpadana DOP)
entries.what: A DOP stretched-curd cheese made in the Po Valley. In Veneto it is made mainly in the west of the Verona province, per PMC11675318.

entries.heading: Provolone Valpadana
entries.what: A stretched-curd cow's-milk cheese protected under DOP, made in the Po Valley; Emilia-Romagna is one of its regions.

entries.heading: Queso blanco (Colombian use)
entries.what: A Latin American fresh white cheese, used in Colombia as a generic fresh cheese.

entries.heading: Queso blanco
entries.what: A fresh white cheese of Mexico and Latin America; in Mexico it is a close relative of queso fresco.

entries.heading: Queso blanco (queso blanco del país; queso fresco)
entries.what: A white fresh cheese that the source says is "a firm cheese used for frying" in Puerto Rican cuisine, typically served with guava paste. Its alternate names include queso blanco del país.

entries.heading: Queso blanco (Venezuelan white cheese; queso blanco duro; queso semi-blando)
entries.what: The common white cheese of Venezuelan cuisine, made across the country with varying flavour and texture. Its regional varieties are named for the region (llanero, paisa, palmita, guayanés). It is grated on pabellón or pasta, used as an arep

entries.heading: Roquefort
entries.what: The French cheese given the first administrative appellation of origin (1925), a blue-veined sheep cheese from the Causses area of Aveyron.

entries.heading: Roquefort
entries.what: A sheep-milk blue cheese from southern France; white, tangy, creamy, slightly moist, veined with blue mould; no rind.

entries.heading: Roquefort (French blue cheese; name only in source)
entries.what: A blue cheese named as a topping for a snail dish, stuffed into cherry tomatoes.

entries.heading: Roquefort (as listed in Uruguay)
entries.what: Named as dairy output in Uruguay. Roquefort is a French protected cheese.

entries.heading: Taleggio (cross-region, Novara province)
entries.what: PDO cheese produced and aged only in set areas: eight Lombard provinces, the province of Novara (Piemonte), and the province of Treviso (Veneto).

entries.heading: Taleggio (Taleggio DOP)
entries.what: a semi-soft cheese from Val Taleggio, Lombardy, with a thin pinkish-brown rind and a creamy, pale yellow interior.

entries.heading: Taleggio (Taleggio DOP)
entries.what: A DOP cheese from Lombardy, Piedmont and Veneto. The Veneto part of its DOP zone is Treviso province.

entries.heading: Taleggio
entries.what: a washed-rind cheese named after Val Taleggio in Lombardy.

entries.heading: Tan (թան)
entries.what: A savoury, lightly salted yoghurt drink. Armenian origin, widespread in the Caucasus mountains and Central Asia. Sold still or carbonated; often flavoured with herbs such as parsley, mint, basil or sumac, and vegetables such as cucumber.

entries.heading: Doogh
entries.what: A yoghurt-based beverage, sometimes carbonated. The List of dairy products names Armenia among the countries where it is popular, alongside Iran, Afghanistan, Azerbaijan, Iraq, Syria and Turkey.

entries.heading: Doogh (دوغ; also dugh, tan)
entries.what: A cold, savoury Iranian drink made from fermented milk, served with meals (e.g. dizi, chelow kabab); it is not simply diluted yogurt. Sold industrially in PET bottles as well as made at home.

entries.heading: Tan
entries.what: A fermented dairy drink made with lactic bacteria and dairy yeast, with water and salt added. Listed with the Turkmen name "Tan".

entries.heading: Tan (tan)
entries.what: A fermented dairy drink made with a starter culture of lactic acid bacteria, dairy yeast, water and salt; named in Kazakh, Uzbek, Kyrgyz, Tajik and Turkmen.

entries.heading: Vacherin Mont-d'Or (Vacherin Mont d'Or, Swiss version; Vacherin du Haut-Doubs in France)
entries.what: soft, washed-rind cheese from the Jura villages of the Vallée de Joux in canton Vaud (Switzerland) and the French Haut-Doubs (Franche-Comté). Traditionally made in winter, when cows come down from alpine pastures and there is not enough mil

entries.heading: Vacherin Mont d'Or
entries.what: seasonal soft cheese made in villages of the Jura in France and Switzerland; the Swiss version is eaten warm like fondue.

entries.heading: Mont d'Or (Vacherin Mont-d'Or; Vacherin du Haut-Doubs)
entries.what: A very soft cow's-milk cheese from the Jura, sold in a spruce box, made on the Doubs/Jura side of the region and also in Vaud.

entries.heading: Vacherin Mont d'Or
entries.what: A cow's-milk cheese from the Jura/Doubs; the French form (mont d'Or) is distinct from Swiss Vacherin.

entries.heading: Vacherin du Haut-Doubs
entries.what: The French form of Vacherin, an unpasteurised cow's-milk cheese from the Doubs/Jura, wrapped in a spruce band.

entries.heading: Ziger (Zieger in Germany and Austria; sérac in French; ricotta in Italian; mascarpa or zigra in Ticino)
entries.what: A fresh whey cheese made from the liquid left after hard Swiss-type cheese is made. The de.wikipedia Appenzeller article records it as once widespread in Appenzellerland before the rennet method spread in the mid-16th century.

entries.heading: Ziger (Sérac, Zieger)
entries.what: whey cheese (similar to ricotta) from Swiss dairies; the basis of Schabziger.

entries.heading: Sérac
entries.what: fresh cheese made from whey left after making pressed cooked cheeses like gruyère or comté.

entries.heading: Zieger (fresh flavoured cheese)
entries.what: A fresh flavoured cheese. PAT.

entries.heading: Aaruul (Mongolian dried curd)
entries.what: Hard, air-dried Mongolian curd, shapes and sizes vary by region, sold in Inner Mongolia.

entries.heading: Aaruul (ааруул; aaruul, aarul)
entries.what: The main Mongolian dried curd; a hard, sour, snack-type product stored for months without refrigeration. Usually eaten plain or sweetened, sometimes with dried berries.

entries.heading: Aaruul (ааруул; Mongolian) — Russian region not confirmed
entries.what: Mongolian dried dairy product; Tuvan and Kyrgyz use the word курут for it.

entries.heading: Aaruul (ааруул; dried curd)
entries.what: Hard, dried curd that keeps for months without refrigeration; a staple of the white foods and a winter/spring food when fresh milk is scarce. Also sold sweetened and in shapes.

entries.heading: Asiago (DOP)
entries.what: DOP cheese whose protected area includes part of the Province of Trento.

entries.heading: Asiago (Asiago DOP; Asiago pressato, Asiago d'allevo; other names: Pegorin, historic sheep form)
entries.what: A DOP cow's-milk cheese from the Asiago plateau and the foothills of Vicenza, Trento and parts of Padua and Treviso. It is one of the best-known Veneto cheeses; its pressed fresh form is eaten young and its aged form is grated.

entries.heading: Asiago
entries.what: a cow's-milk cheese from the Asiago plateau.

entries.heading: Bandung (sirap bandung)
entries.what: A pink, sweet milk drink flavoured with rose syrup; popular in Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore.

entries.heading: Sirap bandung (air bandung, bandung, iced bandung, rose syrup drink)
entries.what: A pink, rose-flavoured milk drink.

entries.heading: Bandung (rose-milk drink)
entries.what: milk-based drink flavoured with rose syrup, pink in colour.

entries.heading: Banon (Banon AOC/AOP; chèvre de Banon; other names: Banon à la feuille)
entries.what: a cheese from the old village of Banon and its surroundings, protected since 2003.

entries.heading: Banon
entries.what: A French goat cheese made near the town of Banon in Provence; also called Banon à la feuille.

entries.heading: Banon (Banon; Banon de Provence)
entries.what: A small French goat cheese from the Banon area of Provence, wrapped in chestnut leaves. Monaco's Wikipedia article calls it a popular local choice.

entries.heading: Bleu de Gex (Bleu de Gex Haut-Jura; bleu de Septmoncel)
entries.what: 6–9 kg wheel from the Haut-Jura plateaus; AOC 1977, AOP 2008 (the page gives two AOP dates).

entries.heading: Bleu de Gex (incl. Bleu du Haut-Jura, Bleu de Septmoncel, pérassu)
entries.what: A blue-veined cow's-milk cheese from the Haut-Jura plateaus, about 7.5 kg on average.

entries.heading: Bleu de Gex (Bleu du Haut-Jura, Bleu de Septmoncel)
entries.what: A creamy, semi-soft blue cheese from unpasteurised milk in the Jura, named for the Pays de Gex.

entries.heading: Sauerkäse (Werdenberger Sauerkäse; Bloderkäse; Surchäs in Werdenberg; Ploderkäse; Sauerchäs)
entries.what: a sour-milk cheese from eastern Switzerland; the Werdenberg and Obertoggenburg (incl. Ebnat-Kappel, Wildhaus-Alt St. Johann, Nesslau, and Amden) are part of its protected production area. The same name family also covers Liechtenstein and t

entries.heading: Bloderkäse (Sauerkäse, Werdenberger and Liechtensteiner Sauerkäse)
entries.what: sour-milk cheese with 4–15% fat, from Toggenburg, Werdenberg, Liechtenstein and Montafon (Vorarlberg).

entries.heading: Liechtensteiner Sauerkäse (Sura Käs; Bloderkäse; Sauerkäse)
entries.what: A sour-milk cheese made in eastern Switzerland, Liechtenstein and the Montafon valley of Vorarlberg. Fat content 4 to 15 percent. Sold at three ripening stages.

entries.heading: Queso Azul (blue cheese)
entries.what: a blue-veined cheese defined in the Food Code.

entries.heading: Blue cheese (jibini buluu; "blue highland" at Doinyo Lessos)
entries.what: a blue-veined cheese listed as made in Kenya.

entries.heading: Blue cheese (Omaruru cheese)
entries.what: One of the cheeses made by Tinkie Cornelissen in Omaruru.

entries.heading: Booza (بوظة; Jordanian mastic booza)
entries.what: a Levantine stretched frozen dairy dessert made with sahlab and mastic; the Jordanian version is mastic-flavoured and salep-based

entries.heading: Booza (بوظة، ice cream, Levantine elastic ice cream)
entries.what: a Syrian-origin elastic ice cream made with sahlab, mastic and often qishta; firm enough to be shaped into a roll.

entries.heading: Booza (بوظة)
entries.what: A dense, elastic ice cream from Damascus, with mastic and sahlab in the base; often served shaped into a roll.

entries.heading: Brânză de vaci (cow's-milk cheese)
entries.what: Moldovan cow's cheese, eaten with mămăligă, sour cream or șorici.

entries.heading: Brânză de vaci
entries.what: A common Romanian fresh cow's cheese, like tvorog or twaróg; used for breakfast and as pastry filling, including in pasca.

entries.heading: Cow's milk cheese (unnamed, industrial)
entries.what: Cow's milk cheese, described as rarer than goat cheese, sold in the same outlets.

entries.heading: Brousse
entries.what: A whey cheese of Provence and Languedoc, originally made from goat-cheese whey.

entries.heading: Brousse (regional brousse, whey cheese)
entries.what: the general brousse of Provence and the Mediterranean south (Provence, Côte d'Azur, Alpes du Sud, Languedoc). Not protected in the article's terms.

entries.heading: Brousse (brousse; brousse de Provence)
entries.what: A fresh white whey cheese from Provence, also found in Languedoc and the Comtat Venaissin. The French Monaco-cuisine article names it as a filling for barbagiuan.

entries.heading: Brynza (ovčí, ewe's milk)
entries.what: Carpathian brined cheese; the review lists a Czech brynza made from ewe's milk.

entries.heading: Brynza (брынза) — Russian North Caucasus usage
entries.what: Brined cheese; Russian-language article says it is integral to the cuisine of the North Caucasus of Russia.

entries.heading: Brynza (Uzbek industrial brined cheese)
entries.what: A brined white cheese. Uzbek Wikipedia lists brinza as a salty cheese that matures in brine, and says Uzbek dairies have set up production of soft cheese and brinza.

entries.heading: Buffalo milk (भैंस का दूध)
entries.what: India's main milk source at about 49% (indigenous 35%, non-descript 14% in 2017–18), with higher fat (7–7.5%) than cow milk.

entries.heading: Latte di bufala (buffalo milk)
entries.what: milk of water buffalo, used for dairy products in Campania.

entries.heading: Buffalo milk (ကျွဲနို့)
entries.what: milk from water buffalo; in areas with many buffalo, it is drunk in place of cow's milk.

entries.heading: Cabécou
entries.what: small goat cheese of the Massif central (Quercy, Rouergue, Périgord, Velay, Limousin, Haute-Auvergne).

entries.heading: Cabécou
entries.what: The generic name for a small goat-milk cheese family of the Massif central (Quercy, Rouergue, Périgord, Velay, Limousin, Haute-Auvergne).

entries.heading: Cabécou
entries.what: A small soft goat cheese from the Midi-Pyrénées/Quercy and Périgord area; one of Aquitaine's famous foods.

entries.heading: Canestrato (formaggio di Rovereto, Canestrato trentino)
entries.what: A savoury table cheese with a rough rind from the canestro mould; can turn spicy. A variant includes crushed pepper grains.

entries.heading: Canestrato (Canestrato calabrese)
entries.what: A cheese recognised as a Calabrian traditional agri-food product (PAT).

entries.heading: Canestrato (Canestrato di Moliterno; Canestrato pugliese)
entries.what: a hard cheese from a mix of sheep and goat milk; grated or eaten at table.

entries.heading: Karak (كرك; chai karak)
entries.what: tea mixed with milk, served as the morning breakfast drink in Bahrain.

entries.heading: Karak (kark; karak chai) — milk tea drink
entries.what: Strong black tea boiled with evaporated milk, sugar and spices (cardamom common). Popular across the Gulf.

entries.heading: Chai karak (spiced milk tea)
entries.what: A spiced milk tea popular in the Gulf Arab region as chai karak.

entries.heading: Chal (camel milk and water product; script not given)
entries.what: A fermented product made from camel milk mixed with water; a camel-milk product named for Iran and Turkmenistan.

entries.heading: Chal (çal; ч́ал, "chal"; camel chal)
entries.what: A white, slightly sparkling, sour fermented camel milk drink. English Wikipedia calls it the drink Turkmenistan is best known for, and it is hard to export because it spoils quickly.

entries.heading: Qumron (Uzbek name for shubat, chal; camel milk)
entries.what: Fermented camel milk, called shubat (Kazakh), chal (Turkmen, Uzbek, Kazakh), khoormog (Mongolian) or qumron (Uzbek). Described as sparkling and sour; resembles a drinkable yoghurt.

entries.heading: Chaource
entries.what: A soft cow's-milk cheese named after Chaource, Aube, with a protected area that extends into the Yonne.

entries.heading: Chaource
entries.what: Soft bloomy-rind cheese from the Aube; its production zone also reaches part of the Yonne.

entries.heading: Chaource
entries.what: A cow's-milk cheese originally made in Chaource (Aube), Champagne-Ardenne; the cheese gives its name to the town.

entries.heading: Chugo (chhurpi; also churkam, chogo, chugu)
entries.what: A very hard, dried milk cheese cut into small cubes and chewed or sucked throughout the day, especially in rural areas. Per 2018 Department of Livestock figures, the third most-produced dairy product after datshi and butter.

entries.heading: Chhurpi (Tibetan/Himalayan cheese, also churpi, durkha, chogo/chugo)
entries.what: Himalayan cheese from yak buttermilk, sold soft and as an extremely hard chew; origin given as Nepal and Tibet.

entries.heading: Chhurpi (Himalayan, incl. Sikkim, Nepal, Bhutan, Tibet)
entries.what: Traditional Himalayan cheese, "one of the hardest cheeses in the world" in its hard form.

entries.heading: Clabber (Scotland)
entries.what: unpasteurised milk left to sour until it thickens or curdles.

entries.heading: Bainne clabhair (clabber)
entries.what: A fermented milk eaten with bread, one of the traditional forms of milk in Gaelic Ireland, listed alongside milk, cheese and yoghurt. A separate "fermented milk drink" described as Irish is also listed.

entries.heading: Clabber
entries.what: Unpasteurised milk left to sour into a thick, tangy, yogurt-like substance.

entries.heading: Condensed and evaporated milk (炼乳 / 淡奶; 奶精 is a non-dairy substitute)
entries.what: Milk concentrated to about a quarter of its water content and sweetened; unsweetened evaporated milk is 淡奶. Used in cha chaan teng milk tea, cha jau (茶走), desserts, drizzled on fruit and shaved ice.

entries.heading: Condensed and evaporated milk (lait concentré; Cèbon brand as example)
entries.what: sweetened or concentrated tinned milk sold in Gabon.

entries.heading: Condensed and evaporated milk (UK uses)
entries.what: milk concentrated by evaporation, with sugar added for condensed milk.

entries.heading: Coulommiers
entries.what: Soft Brie-type cheese; the list page tags it to Île-de-France and Champagne.

entries.heading: Coulommiers (Coulommiers; Brie de Coulommiers)
entries.what: a disc-shaped soft cheese from the town of Coulommiers, a smaller, rounder cousin of Brie; fat content given as 40 % (English article) and 45–50 % (French article).

entries.heading: Coulommiers
entries.what: A soft ripened cheese from Coulommiers, Seine-et-Marne, shaped as a disc with a white bloomy rind (Penicillium candidum).

entries.heading: Crema (spreadable unripened white cheese)
entries.what: named in the El Salvador section of the English Wikipedia List of cheeses as a spreadable, unripened white cheese.

entries.heading: Crema (Honduran salted sour cream)
entries.what: a salty, soured cream spooned over breakfast, baleadas, beans and tacos fritos. Often called crema or sometimes queso fresco/crema on street food.

entries.heading: Crema (Mexican cream, used as a filling and topping)
entries.what: Cream used as a filling or topping; the source lists "crema" among taco fillings (from rice to meat to cream to vegetables) and as a torta filling with beans and chile.

entries.heading: Crema (cream; crema pura)
entries.what: Natural, unskimmed cream, served with the typical Salvadoran breakfast and added to some soups; cream soups (crema de langosta, crema de camarones) are also listed.

entries.heading: Crema catalana (crema andorrana served as a Catalan-style cream)
entries.what: A custard of milk, egg yolk and sugar, flavoured with lemon zest and cinnamon or vanilla, with a caramelised sugar top. Named in Andorra as a typical dessert by about 21.5% of respondents in a 2017 survey, far more than any other milk dish.

entries.heading: Crema catalana (crema catalana; "crema cremada", "Crema de Sant Josep")
entries.what: A milk custard flavoured with cinnamon and lemon zest, topped with a layer of caramelised sugar, served at room temperature.

entries.heading: Crema catalana (milk custard dessert)
entries.what: a baked or chilled custard dessert, listed in the Honduran gastronomy article.

entries.heading: Crème fraîche (épaisse et fluide)
entries.what: Non-sterilised cream, cultured with lactic bacteria to thicken and sour it; French usage requires fat of at least 30% for the term "fraîche".

entries.heading: Crème fraîche
entries.what: A lightly soured cream, less acidic than gräddfil; can be boiled without curdling, whipped, or used as a dip. Flavoured variants exist. Introduced to Sweden in the early 1980s.

entries.heading: Crème fraîche (industrial cream)
entries.what: A cultured cream made by La Laiterie du Berger under the Dolima brand, sold in shops and supermarkets in Dakar and regional towns.

name: Drinking yoghurt
names: Sữa chua uống and functional yoghurt drinks

entries.heading: Drinking yoghurt (yoghurt drink)
entries.what: sweetened drinkable yoghurt sold in Europe, the UK and the US.

entries.heading: Drinking yoghurt
entries.what: Drinking yoghurt, sold as a probiotic and functional product.

entries.heading: Sữa chua uống and functional yoghurt drinks (drinking yoghurt)
entries.what: Industrial drinking yoghurt and "functional" yoghurts with probiotics, calcium, zinc or vitamins, marketed in Vietnam by Vinamilk, Friesland Campina, Nestlé, Nutifood and Yakult.

entries.heading: Eggnog (lait de poule)
entries.what: milk or cream, sugar, raw eggs, a spirit and spices such as vanilla or nutmeg; commercial versions use gelatin and other thickeners with less egg and cream.

entries.heading: Lait de poule (eggnog-style hot milk drink)
entries.what: Milk, cream, sugar and egg yolks flavoured with nutmeg or cinnamon; often with rum, brandy or whisky; served at Christmas.

entries.heading: Eggnog
entries.what: A chilled, sweetened drink of milk and/or cream, sugar and whipped eggs, often with spirits; tied to the US holiday season from Thanksgiving to Christmas.

entries.heading: Fontina (Danish-made)
entries.what: the Italian fontina type, which has spread to Denmark and other countries. Danish fontina is milder, softer and has more holes than Italian fontina.

entries.heading: Fontina (Fontina; Fontina d'Aosta, Fontina DOP)
entries.what: The best-known cheese of Valle d'Aosta, a semi-hard cow's-milk cheese with a natural rind that turns tan to orange-brown and a pale paste with small openings. Mature Fontina is nutty and still melts well.

entries.heading: Fontina (Fontina Valle d'Aosta)
entries.what: a cow's-milk cheese first made in the Aosta Valley, creamy and mild, nuttier with age.

entries.heading: Fresh goat cheese (queso fresco de cabra, Aragón)
entries.what: the fresh goat cheese traditional to Aragón, which the guide says was eaten fresh and grilled ("a la plancha") in Campo de Cariñena.

entries.heading: Fresh goat cheese (local, unnamed)
entries.what: A fresh goat cheese made in Morocco, named only as a traditional product in a microbiology study; the Zayanes of Khénifra also eat goat cheese as a staple.

entries.heading: Fresh goat cheese (queso fresco de cabra, family goat farms)
entries.what: Artisanal fresh goat cheese made on family goat farms in Durango, Campeche and Querétaro.

entries.heading: Gāri (milk porridge)
entries.what: a fluid or porridge made from flour (millet, sorghum or maize) and milk.

entries.heading: Gāri (milk and cereal porridge or fluid)
entries.what: A fluid or porridge of millet, sorghum or maize flour with milk; described as a Fulani meal.

entries.heading: Gāri (Fulbe milk porridge)
entries.what: a fluid or porridge of flour from cereals (millet, sorghum or corn) and milk.

entries.heading: Ghee / clarified butter (ঘি)
entries.what: clarified butterfat, about 99.7% milk fat, a concentrated energy source in Bangladeshi cooking. Mughal cooks used it heavily; it is used in khichuri (with cumin and fenugreek), polao, biriani, roast, korma; an ingredient of darbesh.

entries.heading: Ghee / clarified butter (ერბო)
entries.what: pure milk fat freed from plasma; about 98% fat; white or pale yellow, soft.

entries.heading: Ghee / clarified butter (топлёное масло)
entries.what: Butter with water and milk solids removed (about 99% fat). Russian article describes the Kyrgyz method (sary may) and a Buryat photo caption only.

entries.heading: Giuncata (Zuncà, Giuncà; Savona)
entries.what: a fresh cheese named after the rush basket (fascera) in which the curd is shaped. It is made in southern Italy and in Liguria.

entries.heading: Giuncata
entries.what: A fresh soft cheese, cylindrical or spindle-shaped, with its form from the rush basket that holds the curd. Recognised in Puglia, Calabria and Liguria as a traditional regional agri-food product.

entries.heading: Giuncata (giuncata, cream cheese)
entries.what: Fresh soft cheese made in Calabria, Puglia and Liguria; a Sila and Sibari-plain speciality per the Calabrian source.

entries.heading: Goat and sheep milk (farm milk, Atakora and Donga)
entries.what: small-ruminant milk taken from farms in north-west Benin.

entries.heading: Goat and sheep milk (drunk mixed with water)
entries.what: milk of small stock, consumed commonly diluted with water.

entries.heading: Goat and sheep milk (minor)
entries.what: Small-ruminant milk, sold and drunk only occasionally in Nigeria; no named product found.

entries.heading: Goat milk infant formula (UK sales)
entries.what: goat-milk-based infant formula sold in the UK.

entries.heading: 산양분유 (goat-milk infant formula)
entries.what: A goat-milk formula produced by Namyang Dairy, referenced from 2012.

entries.heading: Goat-milk infant formula
entries.what: Infant formula made from goat milk protein.

entries.heading: Gorgonzola (cross-region, Lombardy and Piemonte)
entries.what: blue cheese made in Lombardy and Piemonte; the Piemonte part of the production area is the provinces of Biella, Cuneo, Novara, Verbano-Cusio-Ossola and Vercelli, plus some municipalities in Alessandria. Novara has been the leading producer

entries.heading: Gorgonzola (Gorgonzola DOP)
entries.what: an Italian blue cheese named after the town of Gorgonzola near Milan, made in two versions: "dolce" (sweet, creamy, mild) and "piccante" (spicy, firmer and stronger, also called naturale or montagna).

entries.heading: Gorgonzola
entries.what: an Italian blue cheese from unskimmed cow's milk, named after the town of Gorgonzola (Milan).

entries.heading: Graviera (produced in Trikala and Larisa, Thessaly)
entries.what: Graviera samples collected from producers in the Trikala and Larisa (Larissa) areas for origin studies.

entries.heading: Graviera (Γραβιέρα)
entries.what: A hard cheese sold with regional names (Kritis, Naxou, Agrafon); a 105-sample origin study placed Peloponnese among nine production regions.

entries.heading: Graviera (Γραβιέρα; Π.Ο.Π. Kritis, Agrafon, Naxou)
entries.what: Greece's second most popular cheese after feta. Wheels with a crisscross rind pattern from the draining cloth.

entries.heading: Südlü sıyıq (milk porridge)
entries.what: milk porridge listed in the Azerbaijani cuisine dairy gallery.

entries.heading: Milk porridge (grautur boiled in milk)
entries.what: Ground corn or cereal porridge boiled in milk and served thin. Also porridge boiled in milk, mixed with skyr.

entries.heading: Grøt (milk porridge)
entries.what: traditional Norwegian breakfast porridge made from flour or groats boiled with milk, in types including rømmegrøt (with sour cream) and risgrøt (with rice).

entries.heading: Hong Kong-style milk tea (港式奶茶, silk-stocking milk tea, 絲襪奶茶)
entries.what: Ceylon black tea with evaporated milk (or sometimes condensed milk), made in cha chaan teng diners. Originated mid-20th century under British rule; often attributed to Lan Fong Yuen (1952).

entries.heading: Hong Kong-style milk tea (港式奶茶; silk-stocking milk tea, 絲襪奶茶)
entries.what: A strong black tea blend, poured with evaporated milk and sugar, and made in cha chaan teng and dai pai dong. Its name comes from the cloth filter bag, which resembles silk stockings.

entries.heading: Hong Kong-style milk tea (silk-stocking milk tea; 港式奶茶)
entries.what: strong black-tea blend mixed with evaporated milk, served hot or iced. Common in Hong Kong and in Macau's cha chaan teng diners.

entries.heading: Idiazábal (Idiazabal; Idiazábal, Idiazabal gazta in Basque; other names: queso de Idiazábal)
entries.what: A cylindrical sheep cheese with a DO (Denominación de Origen) since 1987, also registered as a DOP. Its area covers the Basque Country and Navarra, excluding the Valle de Roncal municipalities, which make Roncal instead.

entries.heading: Idiazabal (Idiazabal gazta; Idiazábal; Artzai Gazta Idiazabal Baserrikoa as a farm-style variant)
entries.what: A Basque sheep's cheese with a PDO created in 1987. It is eaten young as a fresh-ish cheese, often with quince jam, or aged until firm and sharp enough to grate.

entries.heading: Idiazábal (queso Idiazábal)
entries.what: Traditional smoked or unsmoked sheep's-milk cheese from the southern Basque Country (and Navarre).

entries.heading: Queijo industrial (industrial cheese; Novagrolider, Aldeia Nova)
entries.what: factory cheese made by local dairies. Novagrolider is described as specialised in cheese and derivatives; Aldeia Nova makes cheese among its butter and yoghurt.

entries.heading: Industrial cheese (domestic market)
entries.what: cheese made by defined fermentation, heat treatment and enzymatic processing for the domestic market, alongside yoghurt.

entries.heading: Industrial cheese (Uganda processors)
entries.what: Cheeses made by licensed processing companies in Uganda, sold alongside their butter, yoghurt and milk.

entries.heading: Irimshik (Kyrgyz: Sir; Kazakh: irimshik)
entries.what: a "national delicacy" made from curd of sour milk slow-cooked for several hours, with a golden-brown colour and sweet, creamy taste, per the atlas paper; the Kyrgyz name is "Sir", the same word as the generic cheese word.

entries.heading: Irimshik (ірімшік; ақ ірімшік, қызыл ірімшік; ирімшик)
entries.what: Traditional Kazakh cheese. Sources describe it as a spring-made, pressed dried curd, eaten dry or in dishes such as zhent and kazyzhent.

entries.heading: Irimshik (Turkmen label "Peýnir" in Table 2)
entries.what: a curd-based dish made from sour milk, slow-cooked for several hours.

entries.heading: Irimshik (ірімшік)
entries.what: Spring curd made from boiled unskimmed milk with added sour cream.

entries.heading: Jben (Aguissi)
entries.what: A fresh Maghreb cheese, drained and salted or not to taste; industrial versions use cow milk and animal rennet.

entries.heading: Jben (جبن, جبن البربري; jben)
entries.what: Traditional soft cheese of Morocco, made in farms and by informal producers, and sold in dairy shops (mhlaba) and markets.

entries.heading: Jben (جبن; the name is shared with Moroccan and Algerian cheeses)
entries.what: A fresh Tunisian cheese, eaten at breakfast with bread and olive oil, often homemade.

entries.heading: Kashkaval (кашкавал; yellow cheese)
entries.what: the typical yellow cheese of Bulgaria, one of the two main Bulgarian cheese categories; used in kashkavalka pastry, princesa snack, pizza.

entries.heading: Kashkaval (קשקבל; qashqawan)
entries.what: A yellow melting cheese, widely used in pizza, sandwiches and pastries; Balkan and Levant tradition.

entries.heading: Кашкавал (kaškaval / kashkaval; Šarplaninski ovčji kaškaval for the sheep version)
entries.what: A yellow cheese in North Macedonia; "kashkaval" is also used in everyday speech for yellow cheeses generally (Gouda and Emmental are sometimes called kashkaval).

entries.heading: Kumis / qymyz (қымыз; kumys, koumiss, kimiz, cosmos)
entries.what: Fermented mare's milk, the classic steppe drink of Kazakhs and other Turkic and Mongolic peoples; often ends a meal with tea.

entries.heading: Kumys (fermented mare's milk, medicinal use in Poland)
entries.what: A Central Asian fermented mare's milk drink. In Poland recorded only as a medicinal drink.

entries.heading: Kumys (кумыс)
entries.what: Traditional steppe drink of mare's milk, mildly alcoholic, carbonated and sour. Russian name "кумыс". Used in Russian medical spa treatment from the 1850s.

entries.heading: Laguiole (fourme de Laguiole is a separate listed name; this entry is the Laguiole cheese)
entries.what: large farmhouse-style cheese from the Aubrac plateau; AOC 1961, AOP 2008.

entries.heading: Laguiole (Fourme de Laguiole)
entries.what: The Aubrac cheese of the Laguiole type, sold as Laguiole; the page also covers the Fourme de Laguiole.

entries.heading: Laguiole (Tome de Laguiole)
entries.what: A pressed uncooked cheese from the Aubrac plateau (Aveyron), also called Tome de Laguiole or fourme de Laguiole.

entries.heading: Lakh (ngalakh; lax in Wolof means "milk")
entries.what: A rolled millet porridge from Senegalese and Gambian cooking, served sweet. The Wolof name literally means milk.

entries.heading: Lakh (لاخ; lakh)
entries.what: Curds or yoghurt topped with grated coconut and served over sweet millet porridge (عصيدة الدخن الحلوة).

entries.heading: Lakh (lakh araw; ngalakh with baobab sauce)
entries.what: A pudding of millet or sorghum porridge (rolled flour) in sour milk. Ngalakh is the Senegalese and Gambian form with a baobab-fruit, peanut-paste, vanilla and orange-blossom sauce.

entries.heading: Leche asada (baked milk custard)
entries.what: Baked milk and egg dessert with caramel, similar to flan but baked directly so the top browns. Served at room temperature or cold.

entries.heading: Leche asada
entries.what: A baked custard similar to flan but less sweet; a typical Colombian dessert (listed with Peru, Argentina, Chile).

entries.heading: Leche asada (baked milk custard, Peruvian flan)
entries.what: A Peruvian baked custard that the source says descends from the medieval flan ("flaon"); eaten cold after refrigeration and keeps 3–4 days.

entries.heading: Liptauer
entries.what: Spicy cheese spread served on bread, a Heuriger snack; common in Austrian, Hungarian and Slovak cuisine.

entries.heading: Liptauer (liptói túró; körözött)
entries.what: a paprika-spiced spread made from a white cheese base, sour cream, butter or margarine, and finely chopped onion; chives and caraway are common, and some recipes add beer.

entries.heading: Liptauer (liptauer; Šmirkás in Slovak; spicy cheese spread)
entries.what: a spicy cheese spread from Slovak, Austrian and Hungarian cuisine, listed in Wikipedia's Slovak cheeses category.

entries.heading: Queso Manchego (queso manchego, Spanish)
entries.what: The best-known cheese of Castilla-La Mancha, with a strong, slightly spicy flavour and a greasy-looking rind. Protected by a denominación de origen; a PDO in the EU.

entries.heading: Manchego (Manchego; queso manchego)
entries.what: Sheep's-milk cheese from the La Mancha region of Castile-La Mancha, one of Spain's best-known cheeses.

entries.heading: Manchego (Mexican)
entries.what: A Mexican cheese named after the Spanish manchego style; widely sold in Mexico, grated when aged.

entries.heading: Mató (fresh curd cheese, Casa Raubert)
entries.what: A fresh curd cheese made at Casa Raubert, listed among its whey and cottage cheeses. The Catalan dessert mel i mató uses this cheese.

entries.heading: Mató
entries.what: A fresh, soft, creamy, unripened cheese, widespread across Catalonia; central Catalonia is cited as traditional territory.

entries.heading: Mató
entries.what: Fresh, unsalted, slightly sweet Catalan curd cheese, mostly eaten as a dessert, traditionally with honey (mel i mató).

entries.heading: Maziwa lala (Swahili "sour milk"; also "mala")
entries.what: a yoghurt-like sour milk produced and eaten by livestock-keeping peoples in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania.

entries.heading: Maziwa lala (yogurt-like fermented milk)
entries.what: a yoghurt-like fermented milk made by livestock-keeping peoples in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania.

entries.heading: Maziwa lala
entries.what: A yoghurt-like fermented milk produced by livestock-keeping communities in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania.

entries.heading: Milk powder and infant formula (奶粉, 乳粉; 配方奶粉)
entries.what: Milk powder made by processing and drying milk; forms include whole, skim, modified (调制), and infant/children's/adult/elderly/pregnant formulas. Infant formula is registered in China.

entries.heading: Milk powder and infant formula (industrial; شیر خشک)
entries.what: Industrial milk powders and infant formulas sold on the Iranian market, and infant complementary foods.

entries.heading: Milk powder and infant formula (粉乳, 調製粉乳)
entries.what: Dried milk in Japan includes whole milk powder (全粉乳), skim milk powder (脱脂粉乳), sweetened milk powder (加糖粉乳), buttermilk powder, and infant formula (調製粉乳) and its liquid form (調製液状乳).

entries.heading: Milkshake (milchéyk)
entries.what: A milkshake, drunk regularly in Haiti, as the cuisine article reports.

entries.heading: Milkshake (ミルクセーキ, mirukusēki)
entries.what: A Japanese milk-shake made with milk, egg and sugar (and vanilla), served cold or occasionally warm. A Nagasaki variant made with condensed milk and crushed ice is eaten as a dessert.

entries.heading: Milkshake
entries.what: Milk, ice cream and flavouring blended together; US soda-fountain and fast-food staple.

entries.heading: Montasio (Montasio DOP)
entries.what: A DOP mountain cheese made in Friuli-Venezia Giulia and in the Veneto provinces of Treviso, Belluno, Venice (as far as Chioggia) and the north of Padua.

entries.heading: Montasio (Montâs, Friulian; Montasio DOP)
entries.what: DOP cheese named after the Montasio plateau in the Carnic Alps; sold fresh, medium and aged, with a soft white paste and "occhiatura" (eyes) when fresh, becoming harder and more aromatic with age.

entries.heading: Montasio
entries.what: a semi-hard cow's-milk cheese from northeast Italy; rind stamped with production date.

entries.heading: Mozzarella di bufala campana (DOP, Lazio share)
entries.what: Buffalo-milk mozzarella under the Campania-named PDO, produced in several regions including Lazio.

entries.heading: Mozzarella di bufala campana (PDO, Molise zone)
entries.what: The PDO buffalo mozzarella, produced in Campania, Lazio, Molise and Puglia. In Molise, production is limited to the comune of Venafro (IS).

entries.heading: Mozzarella di bufala campana (mozzarella di bufala campana DOP)
entries.what: a fresh stretched-curd cheese from buffalo milk, the best-known Campanian cheese and a PDO product.

entries.heading: Munster
entries.what: A washed-rind cheese named as a regional cheese in Franche-Comté's cuisine article, though its usual home is the Vosges.

entries.heading: Munster (Munster; Géromé in Lorraine; Munster fermier; Munster Géromé)
entries.what: Soft, washed-rind cylindrical cheese, 13–19 cm across and 2.4–8 cm thick, 450 g to 1.5 kg. A small "petit munster" (7–12 cm, at least 120 g) is also made.

entries.heading: Munster
entries.what: A soft, strong-smelling cheese made mainly in the Vosges (Alsace, Lorraine, Franche-Comté); also called Munster-géromé or Minschterkaas.

entries.heading: Niter kibbeh (niter kebbeh)
entries.what: A spiced, buttery clarified fat spooned over lentils and rice; also eaten with lahoh at breakfast, with honey and tea.

entries.heading: Niter kibbeh (ናይጋ / tesmi in Tigrinya, Eritrea and Ethiopia)
entries.what: A seasoned clarified butter used in Ethiopian and Eritrean cuisine. It is the fat base for kitcha fit-fit and ga'at sauces.

entries.heading: Niter kibbeh (nitir kibe / neter kibe; spiced clarified butter, ghee)
entries.what: clarified butter simmered with spices, the core fat of Ethiopian and Eritrean cooking. Spices named include besobela (sacred basil), koseret, fenugreek, cumin, coriander, turmeric, korarima, cinnamon and nutmeg. Vegetable-oil version is cal

entries.heading: Omashikwa (fermented buttermilk; Herero and Ovambo; Namibia with southern Angola)
entries.what: a traditional fermented buttermilk of the Herero and Ovambo communities. A review of southwest Angolan transhumance names it as made by the Herero and Ovambo of northern Namibia and southern Angola.

entries.heading: Omaere (sour milk; Herero, Himba)
entries.what: a sour milk that Herero women prepared in pre-colonial times (named omaere in the Herero article). The Himba article describes a sour-milk staple with maize porridge made from milk of cows and goats, without naming it.

entries.heading: Omaere (fermented buttermilk; other names: omashikwa in Ovambo, mpofu in Rukwangali)
entries.what: Buttermilk acidified to a sour product, eaten by Herero and other peoples; mass-produced in Namibia.

entries.heading: Omaere (omashikwa, mpofu, oruhere ruomaere; other names: fermented buttermilk, sour milk)
entries.what: A Namibian fermented dairy product made by acidifying buttermilk. Eaten with cooked oruhere (maize meal porridge); drunk daily by many groups.

entries.heading: Ossau-Iraty (ossau-iraty; Basque/Béarnais "brebis" cheese)
entries.what: A cylindrical sheep cheese from the French Basque Country and Béarn, mostly in the Pyrénées-Atlantiques, with a hard yellow-orange to grey rind and an ivory interior.

entries.heading: Ossau-Iraty
entries.what: A sheep cheese from the Basque and Béarn mountains, PDO 1999.

entries.heading: Ossau-Iraty (Esquirrou)
entries.what: A Basque sheep's-milk cheese from southwestern France (Northern Basque Country and Béarn), named after the Ossau valley and the Iraty forest.

entries.heading: Fallone di Gravina (pallone di Gravina)
entries.what: A fresh, mild cheese made specifically in Gravina in Puglia; eaten very fresh, ideally on the day it is made.

entries.heading: Pallone di Gravina (cow's milk; traditional regional product)
entries.what: A semi-hard spun-paste cheese made from raw cow's milk, shaped into a ball, weighing 1.5–10 kg.

entries.heading: Pallone di Gravina
entries.what: a semi-hard, rennet-set cheese stretched in hot water and hand-shaped into a ball; best after a year.

entries.heading: Parmigiano Reggiano (Parmigiano-Reggiano)
entries.what: A hard, long-aged cow's-milk grana cheese, protected under the DOP scheme. Wheels are large, about 40 kg on average (legal minimum 30 kg).

entries.heading: Parmigiano Reggiano (Parmigiano-Reggiano; Parmesan)
entries.what: a hard, granular cheese from unpasteurised cow's milk, aged long enough to be sold as a grating cheese.

entries.heading: Parmigiano-Reggiano (parmesan)
entries.what: Italian hard grating cheese used as a filling and topping for barbagiuan and in the savoury tourte de blettes (listed in the French Monaco-cuisine article).

entries.heading: Pecorino toscano (DOP)
entries.what: the main Tuscan pecorino, DOP, made in all of Tuscany and in a few municipalities of Umbria and Lazio.

entries.heading: Pecorino toscano (Umbrian part)
entries.what: A DOP sheep cheese made in Tuscany and Lazio; the Italian page also lists two Umbrian municipalities in its production zone.

entries.heading: Pecorino Toscano
entries.what: a firm sheep's-milk cheese from Tuscany with a long history (Pliny the Elder), traditionally called marzolino because it began in March.

entries.heading: Peda / "Pera" (khoya sweet; other names: peda, pera)
entries.what: A soft, round milk sweet made from khoa and sugar, flavoured with cardamom.

entries.heading: Peda
entries.what: A thick, semi-soft sweet made from reduced milk, offered to Hindu gods in Nepal. Traditional flavour is cardamom; brown peda is brown.

entries.heading: Peda (pera)
entries.what: round semi-soft sweet made from khoa and sugar.

entries.heading: Petit-suisse
entries.what: an unripened, unsalted, smooth fresh cheese with cream added, about 60 g a cylinder, about 10 g fat per 100 g.

entries.heading: Petit-suisse
entries.what: A fresh, unripened, unsalted cheese from Normandy, with a texture closer to thick yogurt.

entries.heading: Petit Suisse (Tiviski, plain and with dates)
Pont-l'Évêque
entries.what: a square Normandy cheese from the Pont-l'Évêque area; AOC.

entries.heading: Pont-l'Évêque
entries.what: AOC Norman cheese whose zone includes Mayenne.

entries.heading: Pont-l'Évêque
entries.what: A square, uncooked, unpressed cow's-milk cheese from Normandy.

entries.heading: Prostokvasha (prostokvasha)
entries.what: Soured milk made by naturally present bacteria; the English article ties it to Russia and Ukraine.

entries.heading: Prostokvasha (простокваша)
entries.what: Russian name for soured milk; the everyday sour milk drink, traditionally soured naturally or started from an existing sour product.

entries.heading: Prostokvasha (простокваша; Russian soured milk)
entries.what: Russian soured milk, paired in the English article with the Ukrainian kysliak as traditional fermented milk.

entries.heading: Provolone (Provolone Valpadana; Provolone del Monaco; Provolone piccante; Provolone dolce)
entries.what: an aged stretched-curd cheese that began near Vesuvius, shaped as pears, sausages or cones; now made mainly in the northwest, especially Cremona.

entries.heading: Provolone
entries.what: a stretched-curd cheese listed as made in Kenya.

entries.heading: Provolone (Peruvian provolone)
entries.what: A smoked, semi-matured provolone sold by the Chugur quesería in Cajamarca, used for cheese boards and grilling.

entries.heading: Los Beyos (Queso de Los Beyos)
entries.what: IGP cheese from Ponga and Amieva in Asturias and Oseja de Sajambre in León (shared with León).

entries.heading: Queso de Los Beyos (Los Beyos; Ponga and Amieva in Asturias, and Oseja de Sajambre in León)
entries.what: a small cheese (up to 500 g) from Asturian and Leonese valleys; mild aroma, slightly acidic, soft flavour; holes in the paste indicate warm milk and fast whey drainage.

entries.heading: Queso de Los Beyos
entries.what: Asturian cheese from Los Beyos.

entries.heading: Tronchón (queso de Tronchón; also "queso Tronchón"; Valencian heading in the Wikipedia list)
entries.what: a cured cheese from the village of Tronchón (Teruel) in the Maestrazgo, cited by Cervantes in Don Quixote and already famous across Spain by 1615. The guide calls it the most emblematic Aragonese cheese.

entries.heading: Queso de Tronchón
entries.what: A round, matured sheep (or goat) cheese with a volcano-shaped mark on both faces and a flower-like pattern on the rind; weighs about 0.5–2 kg; sheep flavour sharpens with age.

entries.heading: Queso de Tronchón (Aragon)
entries.what: Aragonese sheep's-milk cheese; cited by Cervantes in Don Quixote.

entries.heading: Queso fresco (queso fresco; also queso blanco, queso sierra, queso enchilada)
entries.what: The most common fresh cheese of Mexico, made in nearly all regions and tied to ranch culture in the north. Used to crumble over dishes.

entries.heading: Queso fresco (queso blanco; "queso fresco")
entries.what: The most-produced cheese in Peru, a mild, firm and crumbly white cheese, and the everyday cheese used in Peruvian dishes.

entries.heading: Queso fresco (fresh white cheese)
entries.what: a locally made fresh white cheese, sold on retail shelves in Salvadoran shops and markets. Eaten fresh.

entries.heading: Queso frito (queso blanco; queso de freír)
entries.what: A dense, salty white cheese meant to be fried in hot oil rather than eaten raw. Served in Dominican breakfast plates, e.g. with mangú, fried salami and fried eggs ("los tres golpes" context).

entries.heading: Queso frito (fried cheese)
entries.what: A cheese served fried, sold as street food. It is an optional accompaniment to "tajadas con ensalada" (fried plantain slices with salad).

entries.heading: Queso frito (fried cheese, Puno)
entries.what: A Puno dish of fried cheese, served as a regional dish.

entries.heading: Rasgulla (রসগোল্লা)
entries.what: Chhena and semolina balls boiled in sugar syrup; staple dessert of West Bengal and Odisha.

entries.heading: Rasgulla (rasgulla; milk-based sweet in syrup)
entries.what: Small balls of chhena simmered in sugar syrup. Listed among the Indo-Mauritian sweets.

entries.heading: Rasgulla (rasgula)
entries.what: spongy balls of chhena (milk curd) in light sugar syrup.

entries.heading: Raviggiolo
entries.what: A soft, fresh cheese from the Tuscan-Romagnol Apennines, recognised as a traditional food product (PAT). Also known as raveggiolo or ravaggiolo.

entries.heading: Raviggiolo (Umbria PAT)
entries.what: A fresh, soft, mildly sweet and buttery cheese, 3–4 cm high, 20–25 cm across, 800 g to 1.4 kg.

entries.heading: Raviggiolo
entries.what: A fresh soft cheese made in the Apennine areas of central Italy, traditionally in the autumn and winter months. Listed as a traditional product in Marche.

entries.heading: Biraadam (raw fresh milk, Fulfulde)
entries.what: The Fulfulde term, used in Adamawa, for raw, fresh, non-fermented, unskimmed milk. It is the starting milk for the Adamawa fermented products (pendidam is made from skimmed biraadam).

entries.heading: Raw fresh milk (कच्चा दूध)
entries.what: Fresh milk from household or village sources; often boiled before drinking; preferred by many rural and trusted-source buyers.

entries.heading: Raw / fresh milk (cow, goat, sheep)
entries.what: Locally produced fresh milk, with sheep, goat and cow the primary sources of milk production.

entries.heading: Rocamadour (cross-region: made mostly in Lot, Occitanie; some communes in Corrèze and Dordogne)
entries.what: A small raw-milk goat cheese from the Quercy, named after the village of Rocamadour; AOC 1995, AOP 1999.

entries.heading: Rocamadour
entries.what: A small goat cheese of the Quercy area, part of the cabécou family.

entries.heading: Rocamadour
entries.what: A small French goat cheese from Périgord and Quercy, named after the village of Rocamadour.

entries.heading: Saint-Paulin
entries.what: a trademarked cheese, first made by Trappist monks at Saint-Paulin, now mostly industrial, about 2 kg per wheel.

entries.heading: Saint-Paulin
entries.what: A creamy, mild, semi-soft cheese originally made by Trappist monks at Saint-Paulin; a cousin of Port-Salut.

entries.heading: Saint-Paulin
entries.what: A pressed uncooked cheese, first made by Trappist monks in Quebec, now also made in France and Réunion.

entries.heading: Lait de brebis (sheep's milk)
entries.what: Sheep's milk, richer in fat and protein than cow's milk; can be drunk, but in France mostly used for cheese and yoghurt.

entries.heading: Sheep's milk (ewe milk)
entries.what: Sheep were Iceland's main dairy animals for centuries. Milk was drunk fresh, or made into butter, cheese and skyr.

entries.heading: Sheep's milk
entries.what: Milk from sheep kept by the Toposa, mentioned in one sentence.

entries.heading: Shubat (fermented camel milk; no Chinese name given in the sources)
entries.what: Traditional fermented camel milk, a staple of nomadic communities in northern China for centuries. Shubat was also sampled in Inner Mongolia's Xilin Gol and in Mongolia in a fermented-dairy microbiome study.

entries.heading: Shubat (шубат)
entries.what: Fermented camel's-milk drink, listed in the atlas as Kazakh, Kyrgyz and Tajik. The atlas describes it as a fermented dairy drink made from camel's milk.

entries.heading: Shubat (fermented camel milk; Kazakh drink in Turkmenistan)
entries.what: Kazakh fermented camel milk drink. A review says it is consumed by Kazakhs living in neighbouring countries, including Turkmenistan.

entries.heading: Stilton (Blue Stilton; White Stilton)
entries.what: An English blue cheese sold blue or white; cylindrical, with its own crust, unpressed, with blue veining from the centre.

entries.heading: Stilton
entries.what: An English strong blue cheese; white Stilton is milder and semi-soft.

entries.heading: Stilton (made in NZ)
entries.what: A cheese the NZ cuisine article says some NZ farmers began making in the 1980s.

entries.heading: Stracchino (Crescenza)
entries.what: soft fatty cheese; stracchino is aged, crescenza is very fresh.

entries.heading: Stracchino (crescenza)
entries.what: a soft, creamy, usually square cheese eaten very young, with a mild, slightly acidic taste. Alternative name crescenza.

entries.heading: Stracchino (stracchino; Italian soft cheese family)
entries.what: a family of soft Italian cheeses (general knowledge; the Wikipedia page was not re-read for this line).

entries.heading: Sutlijaš (sutlija; rice and milk pudding)
entries.what: A sweet rice-and-milk dessert typical of the Balkans and Turkey; the name comes from Turkish süt (milk). Listed as a Bosnian dish in the Bosnian cuisine article.
